title: מבנה הסוגיות – Shevuot
note: חלוקה לסוגיות ולשלבי הדיון שנוצרה בבינה מלאכותית באתר talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).
note_de: KI-erzeugte Einteilung in Sugjot und Argumentationsschritte von talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum); englisch, hebräisch wo dort vorhanden.
note_en: AI-generated sugya sections and argument steps from talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Four categories of two that are four
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Four categories of two that are four
items.desc_en: The mishnah introduces the tractate by listing four topics—oaths, impurity awareness, Sabbath labors, and plague signs—each described as 'two that are four'.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens the tractate by listing four topics—oaths, impurity awareness, Sabbath labors, and plague signs—each described as 'two that are four'.

items.text: First case: awareness at both ends
items.text_en: First case: awareness at both ends
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that if one has awareness of impurity at the beginning and end, with forgetfulness in between, the sacrifice is the sliding-scale offering.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states the first case: one who has awareness of impurity at the beginning and end, with forgetfulness in between, brings the sliding-scale offering.

items.text: Second case: awareness at beginning only
items.text_en: Second case: awareness at beginning only
items.desc_en: The mishnah explains that if there is awareness at the beginning but not at the end, the inner goat and Yom Kippur suspend punishment until knowledge is gained, then a sliding-scale offering is brought.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states the second case of impurity: awareness at the beginning but not at the end, where the inner goat and Yom Kippur suspend punishment until knowledge is gained, then a sliding-scale offering is brought.

items.text: Third case: awareness at end only
items.text_en: Third case: awareness at end only
items.desc_en: The mishnah teaches that if there is no awareness at the beginning but awareness at the end, the outer goat and Yom Kippur atone, based on a scriptural analogy.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states the third case: when there is no awareness at the beginning but awareness at the end, the outer goat and Yom Kippur atone, based on a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the inner goat.

items.text: Fourth case: no awareness at all, and a dispute
items.text_en: Fourth case: no awareness at all, and a dispute
items.desc_en: The mishnah concludes with the case of no awareness at either end: Rabbi Yehuda says the goats of festivals and new moons atone, while Rabbi Shimon says only festival goats atone, and questions what new moon goats atone for.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah introduces the fourth case: one who had no awareness at either end, and states that the goats of festivals and new moons atone.
The mishnah attributes the previous statement to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Shimon disagrees, stating that only the festival goats atone, but not the new moon goats.
The gemara asks: for what sin do the new moon goats atone?

items.text: Opening Mishnah: first clause
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: first clause
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins by stating that a goat-offering atones for a pure person who ate impure food.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a goat-offering atones for a pure person who ate impure food.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's opinion
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's opinion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir asserts that all goat-offerings have equal atonement, namely for impurity of the Temple and its sacred objects.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir states that all goat-offerings share equal atonement, specifically for impurity of the Temple and its sacred objects.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's opinion
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's opinion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between different goat-offerings: New Moon goats atone for a pure person who ate impure food, Festival goats for cases with no knowledge at all, and Yom Kippur goats for cases with initial knowledge but final forgetfulness.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon distinguishes the atonement functions of New Moon, Festival, and Yom Kippur goat-offerings for different levels of awareness of impurity.

items.text: Dispute on interchangeability of goats
items.text_en: Dispute on interchangeability of goats
items.desc_en: The Sages ask Rabbi Shimon whether goats of different types may be offered for each other. He permits it, but they object that since their atonements differ, how can they be interchangeable? He responds that all come to atone for impurity of the Temple and its sacred objects.

sub.desc_en: The Sages ask Rabbi Shimon whether goats designated for different occasions may be offered interchangeably.
Rabbi Shimon permits the interchangeability of the goats.
The Sages object that since the atonements of the goats are not equal, how can they be offered for each other?
Rabbi Shimon resolves that all goats come to atone for impurity of the Temple and its sacred objects, so they are fundamentally interchangeable.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda's version
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda's version
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda reports in Rabbi Shimon's name a different formulation: New Moon goats atone for a pure person who ate impure food; Festival goats add atonement for cases with no knowledge; Yom Kippur goats add atonement for cases with initial knowledge but final forgetfulness.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda reports in Rabbi Shimon's name that New Moon goats atone for a pure person who ate impure food, and Festival goats add atonement for cases with no knowledge at all.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda adds that Yom Kippur goats further atone for cases with initial knowledge but final forgetfulness.

items.text: Second dispute on interchangeability
items.text_en: Second dispute on interchangeability
items.desc_en: The Sages again ask Rabbi Shimon about interchangeability. He permits it, but they object that Yom Kippur goats could be offered on New Moons, but how can New Moon goats be offered on Yom Kippur to atone for a different atonement? He responds that all come to atone for impurity of the Temple and its sacred objects.

sub.desc_en: The Sages ask Rabbi Shimon whether the goats of different festivals may be substituted for one another.
Rabbi Shimon permits the interchangeability of the goats.
The Sages object that while Yom Kippur goats could be offered on New Moons, New Moon goats cannot be offered on Yom Kippur to atone for a different atonement.
Rabbi Shimon resolves that all goats come to atone for impurity of the Temple and its sacred objects, so they are interchangeable.

items.text: Mishnah: other atonements and distinctions
items.text_en: Mishnah: other atonements and distinctions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues: for intentional impurity of the Temple, the inner goat and Yom Kippur atone; for other sins, the scapegoat atones; and it distinguishes between Israelites, priests, and the anointed priest regarding the bull-offering. Rabbi Shimon draws parallels between the goats and the bull.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for intentional defiling of the Temple or its sacred foods, the inner goat and Yom Kippur itself atone.
The Mishnah states that for all other transgressions in the Torah, the scapegoat atones.
The Mishnah states that Israelites, priests, and the anointed priest are all atoned by the scapegoat, but the bull atones for priests regarding defiling the Temple or its sacred foods.

Rabbi Shimon draws parallels: as the blood of the inner goat atones for Israelites, so the blood of the bull atones for priests; as the confession over the scapegoat atones for Israelites, so the confession over the bull atones for priests.

items.text: Gemara's opening question
items.text_en: Gemara's opening question
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since the Tanna just finished tractate Makkot, why did he choose to teach Shevuot next? It answers: because he taught that one is liable for two on the head, one from here and one from there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since the Tanna just finished tractate Makkot, why did he choose to teach Shevuot next?
The Gemara answers: because he taught that one is liable for two on the head, one from here and one from there.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the principle of oaths: two categories that become four, and the Tanna teaches all four cases for oaths.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the principle that oaths have two categories that become four, and the Tanna teaches all four cases.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's structure
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's structure
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tanna lists all four cases for oaths and impurity but not for Shabbat or plagues. It answers that oaths and impurity are written together in the Torah and are similar in their sliding-scale sacrifice, so the Tanna taught them together; having started with two, he taught all four. For Shabbat and plagues, since their details are brief, he first finishes them and then returns to the longer topic of oaths.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tanna lists all four cases for oaths and impurity but not for Shabbat or plagues.

The Gemara answers that oaths and impurity are written together in the Torah and are similar in their sliding-scale sacrifice, so the Tanna taught them together; having started with two, he taught all four.
The Gemara explains that for Shabbat and plagues, since their details are brief, he first finishes them and then returns to the longer topic of oaths.

items.text: Mishnah's full text of the four topics
items.text_en: Mishnah's full text of the four topics
items.desc_en: The Mishnah elaborates on each of the four topics: oaths (two for future, two for past), impurity (two types of awareness, two for sacred and Temple), Shabbat (two types of carrying, two for poor and homeowner), and plagues (two primary colors, two with their secondary shades).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the first topic: oaths, listing two types (future) that become four (including past).
The Mishnah elaborates the second topic: awareness of impurity, two types (sacred and Temple) that become four.
The Mishnah elaborates the third topic: Shabbat carryings, two types (poor and homeowner) that become four.
The Mishnah elaborates the fourth topic: plague appearances, two primary colors that become four with their secondary shades.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah cannot be either Rabbi Yishmael or Rabbi Akiva, as each holds a different view on liability for impurity. It then resolves that it could be either, by explaining that the Mishnah includes some cases for liability and some for exemption, thus accommodating both opinions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the Mishnah, noting it cannot be Rabbi Yishmael or Rabbi Akiva because each holds a different view on liability for impurity.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah could be either Rabbi Yishmael or Rabbi Akiva, because it includes some cases for liability (חיוב) and some for exemption (פטור), accommodating both opinions.
The Gemara objects: how can the Mishnah include cases for exemption (פטור), since the Mishnah only lists cases of liability?

items.text: Gemara's defense of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Gemara's defense of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the Mishnah's listing of oaths parallels the plagues of leprosy, where all cases are for liability, so here too all oaths are for liability.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the Mishnah's listing of oaths parallels the plagues of leprosy, where all cases are for liability, so here too all oaths are for liability.

items.text: Refinement of Rabbi Yishmael's liability
items.text_en: Refinement of Rabbi Yishmael's liability
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yishmael exempts from a sacrifice for past oaths but imposes lashes, citing Rava's principle that the Torah equates a false oath to a vain oath regarding the past.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yishmael exempts from a sacrifice for past oaths but imposes lashes.
Rava's principle is cited: the Torah explicitly equates a false oath (שבועת שקר) to a vain oath (שבועת שוא) regarding the past.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding future oaths
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding future oaths
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yishmael would impose lashes for a future oath not fulfilled, which is a negative commandment without an action, and answers that Rabbi Yishmael holds that one is lashed for such prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yishmael would impose lashes for a future oath not fulfilled, which is a negative commandment without an action (לאו שאין בו מעשה).
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yishmael holds that one is lashed for a negative commandment without an action (לאו שאין בו מעשה).

items.text: Contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's rulings
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's rulings
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one is not lashed for a future oath not fulfilled because it is a negative commandment without action, yet he also rules that the halakha follows an anonymous Mishnah that implies liability.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one is not lashed for a future oath not fulfilled (a negative commandment without action) conflicts with his own ruling that the halakha follows an anonymous Mishnah that implies liability.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's principle that the halakha follows an anonymous Mishnah, and then cites a case where both Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish rule that one who swears to eat a loaf and fails is not lashed—Rabbi Yochanan because it is a negative commandment without action, Reish Lakish because it is a warning of uncertainty.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Yochanan found a different anonymous Mishnah
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Yochanan found a different anonymous Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan found another anonymous Mishnah (about one who leaves over or breaks a bone) that supports his view, and analyzes whether that Mishnah follows Rabbi Yaakov or Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan found another anonymous Mishnah to support his view.
The Gemara asks which anonymous Mishnah Rabbi Yochanan found, suggesting it might be the one about one who leaves over or breaks a bone.

The Gemara analyzes that the case of breaking a bone in a disqualified offering is explained by a verse, but the case of leaving over in a pure offering must be because it is a לאו שאין בו מעשה (a prohibition without an action), for which one is not lashed.

The Gemara objects that the anonymous Mishnah might follow Rabbi Yehuda, who exempts from lashes only because the verse provides a positive commandment after the prohibition, not because it is a לאו שאין בו מעשה.

A baraita is cited showing that Rabbi Yehuda explains the exemption from lashes for leaving over due to a positive commandment after the prohibition, while Rabbi Yaakov explains it because it is a לאו שאין בו מעשה (a prohibition without an action).

items.text: Identification of the alternative anonymous Mishnah
items.text_en: Identification of the alternative anonymous Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the anonymous Mishnah as one dealing with an oath not to eat a loaf, which implies liability for eating it, thus aligning with Rabbi Yochanan's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan found a different anonymous Mishnah about an oath not to eat a loaf, which he follows.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for shevu'at bituy one is liable only once, with lashes for intentional violation and a sliding-scale offering for inadvertence.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for shevu'at bituy one is liable only once, with lashes for intentional violation and a sliding-scale offering for inadvertence.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies that lashes apply only to this case, implying that 'I will eat' without eating does not incur lashes. It then asks why the Mishnah contradicts another anonymous Mishnah, and resolves that Rabbi initially held that a prohibition without action is punishable by lashes, then retracted, but the Mishnah remained unchanged.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's wording 'this is the case where one is liable for lashes for its intentional violation,' implying that for saying 'I will eat' without eating, one is not lashed.
The Gemara asks why this anonymous Mishnah contradicts another anonymous Mishnah, and why it follows one rather than the other.
The Gemara objects that according to the questioner's reasoning, Rabbi himself would be inconsistent for issuing two contradictory anonymous Mishnayot.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi initially held that a prohibition without action is punishable by lashes, then retracted, but the Mishnah remained unchanged.

items.text: Attempt to explain the Mishnah as Rabbi Yishmael's view for lashes
items.text_en: Attempt to explain the Mishnah as Rabbi Yishmael's view for lashes
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to interpret the Mishnah as Rabbi Yishmael's view, applying it to lashes. It questions how the topics of negaim and Shabbat exits involve lashes, and answers that negaim involve cutting off a bright spot (a prohibition), and Shabbat exits are a prohibition given for the warning of court-imposed death, but Rabbi Yishmael holds that such a prohibition is punishable by lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Mishnah can be explained as Rabbi Yishmael's view for lashes, given that the topic of negaim (plague marks) does not obviously involve lashes.

The Gemara answers that the lashes apply to one who cuts off his bright spot (בהרת), citing Rabbi Avin in the name of Rabbi Ila'a that any place where the Torah says 'הִשָּׁמֶר' (beware), 'פֶּן' (lest), or 'אַל' (do not) is a negative commandment (לא תעשה) punishable by lashes.

The Gemara asks how the topic of Shabbat exits (יציאות שבת) involves lashes, since it is a prohibition given for the warning of court-imposed death (לאו שניתן לאזהרת מיתת בית דין), which normally is not punishable by lashes.

The Gemara answers that this is why the Mishnah is established as Rabbi Yishmael's view, because Rabbi Yishmael holds that even a prohibition given for the warning of court-imposed death (לאו שניתן לאזהרת מיתת בית דין) is punishable by lashes.

items.text: Objection: the Mishnah mentions 'knowledge' not 'warnings'
items.text_en: Objection: the Mishnah mentions 'knowledge' not 'warnings'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah is about lashes, it should discuss 'warnings' (hatra'ot) rather than 'knowledge' (yedi'ot). It further notes that the Mishnah's structure of 'two that are four' and the requirement of knowledge at the start and end with forgetfulness in between are irrelevant to lashes, and the mention of a sliding-scale offering is inappropriate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah is not as previously assumed, it would stand according to Rabbi Akiva, and then questions why the Mishnah mentions 'knowledge' (ידיעות) instead of 'warnings' (התראות) for lashes.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's term 'knowledge' (ידיעות) actually refers to 'knowledge of warnings' (ידיעות דהתראות), meaning awareness of the prohibition before the act.

The Gemara objects further that if the Mishnah is about lashes, the structure of 'two that are four' is inappropriate, the concept of forgetfulness (העלם) is irrelevant to lashes, and the mention of a sliding-scale offering (עולה ויורד) is out of place.

items.text: Rav Yosef's resolution: Rabbi's compilation from different Tannaim
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's resolution: Rabbi's compilation from different Tannaim
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the Mishnah is Rabbi's, who adopted the section on 'knowledge' according to Rabbi Yishmael and the section on 'oaths' according to Rabbi Akiva, thus reconciling the contradictions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah is Rabbi's compilation, who adopted the section on 'knowledge' according to Rabbi Yishmael and the section on 'oaths' according to Rabbi Akiva.

items.text: Rav Ashi's refinement: Rabbi's own reasoning
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's refinement: Rabbi's own reasoning
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi, citing Rav Kahana, refines that Rabbi did not merely compile from Tannaim but expressed his own view, as a baraita shows Rabbi deriving the requirement of knowledge at the start and end from the double occurrence of 've-ne'elam', while Rabbi Akiva also uses that derivation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that he stated the teaching before Rav Kahana, who corrected him that Rabbi did not merely compile from Tannaim without holding his own view.

Rav Kahana asserts that Rabbi expresses his own reasoning, citing a baraita where Rabbi Akiva derives the requirement of knowledge at the start and end from the double occurrence of 'וְנֶעְלַם' (and it was hidden).
The baraita concludes with Rabbi's own view that the derivation is unnecessary, implying he has his own reasoning.

items.text: Derivation of two knowledges from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation of two knowledges from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verse uses 'hidden' implying prior knowledge, and 'he knows' giving two knowledges. It then asks why the Torah repeats 'hidden' twice, and answers: to impose liability for both forgetfulness of impurity and forgetfulness of the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verse uses 'וְנֶעְלַם' (hidden) implying prior knowledge, and 'וְהוּא יָדַע' (he knows), yielding two knowledges.
The Gemara asks why the Torah repeats 'וְנֶעְלַם' (hidden) twice.
The Gemara answers that the repetition imposes liability for both forgetfulness of impurity and forgetfulness of the Temple.

items.text: Applying the same logic to oaths
items.text_en: Applying the same logic to oaths
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we found a reason for knowledges (from the verse), but for oaths, which have no explicit reason, how do we derive liability? It answers that it is logical. A second version says: we found that Rabbi Yishmael holds one way for knowledges, but for oaths, where Rabbi Akiva holds differently, how do we derive? Again, it is logical.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we found a reason for knowledges (from the verse), but for oaths, which have no explicit reason, how do we derive liability?
It answers that it is logical.
A second version says: we found that Rabbi Yishmael holds one way for knowledges, but for oaths, where Rabbi Akiva holds differently, how do we derive?
Again, it is logical.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's method and Rabbi's parallel
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's method and Rabbi's parallel
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva, who imposes liability for past oaths, uses the method of ribbui u'miut (amplifications and restrictions). Rabbi also uses ribbui u'miut, as shown in a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva's liability for past oaths stems from his use of ribbui u'miut (amplifications and restrictions), and Rabbi also uses this method.

items.text: Baraita on redeeming a firstborn: Rabbi vs. Rabbis
items.text_en: Baraita on redeeming a firstborn: Rabbi vs. Rabbis
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi says one may redeem a firstborn with anything except documents, while the Rabbis exclude slaves, documents, and land. The Gemara explains that Rabbi uses ribbui u'miut to include everything except documents, while the Rabbis use klal u'prat to include only movable property with intrinsic monetary value, excluding land, slaves, and documents.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita presenting the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis regarding what may be used to redeem a firstborn.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi derives his ruling through the hermeneutic principle of ribbui u'miut (amplification and limitation), which includes everything except documents.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the Rabbis' position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Rabbis' position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Rabbis derive their ruling through the principle of klal u'prat (general and specific), which limits redemption to movable property with intrinsic monetary value, excluding land, slaves, and documents.

items.text: Objection: Rabbi uses klal u'prat, not ribbui u'miut
items.text_en: Objection: Rabbi uses klal u'prat, not ribbui u'miut
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges Amemar: Does Rabbi really use ribbui u'miut? He cites a baraita where Rabbi uses klal u'prat regarding the awl for piercing a slave's ear. The Gemara then notes the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda over the method of exegesis.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects to Amemar's claim that Rabbi uses ribbui u'miut, citing that Rabbi actually uses klal u'prat.

Ravina cites a baraita about piercing a slave's ear with an awl (מרצע), where Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda uses a ribbui (ולקחת) to include all hand-held tools, while Rabbi uses a klal u'prat (מרצע) to limit to metal tools.
The Gemara explains that the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda is precisely over whether to use klal u'prat (Rabbi) or ribbui u'miut (Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda).

items.text: Interpretive methods: ribbui/mi'ut vs. kelal/perat
items.text_en: Interpretive methods: ribbui/mi'ut vs. kelal/perat
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts two hermeneutic approaches: 'ribbui and mi'ut' (expansion and limitation) vs. 'kelal and perat' (general and specific), using the verse 'in water, in water' (Leviticus 11:34) as a test case. The school of Rabbi Ishmael applies the latter, while Rabbi Akiva's school uses the former, leading to different rulings on impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the two hermeneutic methods: amplifications and restrictions.
Ameimar explains that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi generally uses generalizations and details, but here follows the school of Rabbi Ishmael.
The school of Rabbi Ishmael teaches that the double phrase 'in water, in water' is not a generalization and detail but an amplification and restriction.
Ravina explains that the Rabbis, following the Western tradition, place the detail between two adjacent generalizations and expound them as generalization and detail.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty: regarding oaths, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi formulated the mishna according to Rabbi Akiva, but does not hold that view himself.

items.text: Liability in shevuot requires prior knowledge and concealment
items.text_en: Liability in shevuot requires prior knowledge and concealment
items.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that for an oath to incur liability, the swearer must have had prior knowledge of the fact and then concealed it (he'lem). Rabbi Akiva derives this from the double 'ne'elam' in the Torah, while Rabbi argues that 'ne'elam' already implies knowledge, so the extra phrase 'vehu yada' adds a second awareness requirement.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by asking for the source that liability requires awareness at the beginning and end with concealment in between, and cites Rabbi Akiva's derivation from the double 'וְנֶעְלַם' (and it was concealed).

Rabbi argues that the double 'וְנֶעְלַם' is unnecessary for the awareness requirement, as 'וְנֶעְלַם' implies prior knowledge and 'וְהוּא יָדַע' (and he knew) adds a second awareness; instead, the extra 'וְנֶעְלַם' teaches liability for concealment of impurity and concealment of the Temple.
The Gemara asks how the phrase 'וְנֶעְלַם' (and it was concealed) implies prior knowledge.
Rava answers that the inference comes from the fact that the verse does not write 'וְהִיא עֲלוּמָה מִמֶּנּוּ' (and it was concealed from him), which would indicate no prior knowledge.

items.text: The sotah case and the principle of prior knowledge
items.text_en: The sotah case and the principle of prior knowledge
items.desc_en: The Gemara applies the same logic to the sotah (suspected adulteress) procedure. The verse 've-ne'elam me'einei ishah' implies the husband knew beforehand, otherwise the water test wouldn't work. Abaye and Rav Papa debate whether 'yediat beit rabo' (knowledge of one's teacher) counts as 'yediah' for liability purposes, using the example of a child captured by gentiles.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbi's logic by asking whether the sotah (suspected adulteress) verse 'וְנֶעְלַם מֵעֵינֵי אִישָׁהּ' implies prior knowledge, which would make the water test impossible if the husband knew.
The Gemara cites a baraita that the sotah water tests the wife only when the husband is free from sin, reinforcing Abaye's objection.
Abaye raises a second objection from the Torah (Job 28:21) where 'וְנֶעֶלְמָה' cannot imply prior knowledge since no human knows its value.

Abaye resolves the difficulty by stating that Rabbi holds that 'knowledge of one's teacher' (ידיעת בית רבו) counts as valid knowledge, so the sotah's husband had prior knowledge through the court's warning.
Rav Papa asks Abaye: if everyone has knowledge of their teacher, how can the Mishnah describe a case with no prior knowledge at all?
Abaye answers that one can find such a case in a child captured by gentiles who never learned Torah and thus lacks knowledge of a teacher.

items.text: Shabbat labor categories: avot vs. toladot and the unique case of hotza'ah
items.text_en: Shabbat labor categories: avot vs. toladot and the unique case of hotza'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares the Mishnah's listing of Shabbat labor categories: 'two that are four' (inside/outside) vs. 'two that are four within and two that are four without' (for carrying). It explains that where Shabbat is the primary focus, both avot (primary) and toladot (derivative) are taught; but here (shevuot) only avot are taught because liability is the issue. The unique case of 'hotza'ah' (carrying out) has two subtypes (carrying in/out) but is counted as one avot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah here teaches only 'two that are four' for Shabbat labors, while in tractate Shabbat it teaches 'two that are four inside and two that are four outside'.

The Gemara answers that in tractate Shabbat, where Shabbat is the main subject, both אבות (primary categories) and תולדות (derivative categories) are taught; here, where Shabbat is not the main subject, only אבות are taught.
The Gemara objects that the אבות (primary categories) are 'יציאות' (carrying out), which are only two, not four.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of a possible answer
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of a possible answer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possible answer that some are for liability and some for exemption, noting that the Mishnah's parallel to 'מראות נגעים' (appearances of plagues) shows all are for liability.
Rav Papa answers that in tractate Shabbat, both liability and exemption cases are taught; here, only liability cases are taught.
The Gemara objects that liability cases are only 'יציאות' (carrying out), which are two; but the Mishnah counts two for carrying out and two for carrying in.
Rav Ashi resolves that the Tanna also calls 'הכנסה' (carrying in) by the term 'הוצאה' (carrying out), and the Gemara asks for the source of this.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'one who carries from domain to domain' without specifying which domains, suggesting it might include carrying from public to private domain, which is also called 'hotza'ah'. The Tanna considers any removal of an object from its place as 'hotza'ah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'המוציא מרשות לרשות' (one who carries from domain to domain), asking whether it might refer to carrying into a domain (הכנסה) yet still be called 'הוצאה' (carrying out).
The Gemara objects that perhaps the Mishnah simply means carrying from private to public domain, and questions why it uses the vague phrase 'מרשות לרשות' (from domain to domain).
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah includes even carrying from public to private domain, and the Tanna (תנא) calls any removal of an object from its place 'הוצאה' (carrying out).

items.text: Ravina's proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Ravina's proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Ravina argues that the Mishnah itself supports this interpretation, as it lists 'hotza'ot' (carrying out) but then explains 'hachnasa' (carrying in), showing that both are included under the term 'hotza'ah'.

sub.desc_en: Ravina (רבינא) argues that the Mishnah itself supports this interpretation, because it lists 'יציאות השבת' (carrying out on Shabbat) and then proceeds to explain cases of carrying in (הכנסה).

items.text: Rava's alternative reading
items.text_en: Rava's alternative reading
items.desc_en: Rava offers a different explanation: the Mishnah's phrase 'reshuyot' (domains) refers to the categories of domains in Shabbat, not to the act of carrying.

sub.desc_en: Rava (רבא) offers an alternative explanation: the Mishnah's phrase 'רשויות' (domains) refers to the general category of 'רשויות שבת' (Shabbat domains), which are two.

items.text: Mishnah on plague-mark colors
items.text_en: Mishnah on plague-mark colors
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah listing the four shades of plague marks: bright white like snow, its secondary like lime of the Temple, swelling like white wool, its secondary like the membrane of an egg.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah about 'מראות נגעים' (appearances of skin afflictions), which lists two primary shades (בהרת and שאת) and their secondary shades (as white as snow, lime of the Temple, white wool, and the membrane of an egg).

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's objection to Rabbi Akiva's view
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's objection to Rabbi Akiva's view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina argues that the Tanna of this Mishnah cannot be Rabbi Akiva, because Rabbi Akiva holds that shades are strictly ordered by brightness, which would make it impossible to classify lime of the Temple (secondary to bright white) alongside the swelling (primary white), as it is neither a direct derivative of bright white nor of the same category.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina (רבי חנינא) asks who is the Tanna (תנא) of this Mishnah, and suggests it is not Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא), because Rabbi Akiva holds that shades are ranked above each other, which would leave the lime of the Temple (סיד ההיכל) without a partner for combination.

Rabbi Chanina opens by questioning the identity of the Tanna of the Mishnah on appearances of plagues, arguing it cannot be Rabbi Akiva, because Rabbi Akiva's view that shades are strictly ordered would exclude lime of the Temple from being classified alongside the bright white.
The Gemara objects that if lime is combined with בהרת (bright white), there is שאת (white wool) which is brighter; if combined with שאת, it is not a derivative (תולדה) of that primary shade.
The Gemara extends the objection to the membrane of an egg (קרום ביצה), asking with which shade it can combine, since it is inferior to both primary shades and not a derivative of either.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's inclusion of 'lime of the Sanctuary' as a shade of white, noting that while the 'membrane of an egg' is not problematic because it is subordinate to the 'se'et', the 'lime of the Sanctuary' poses a difficulty, implying the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Akiva.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's inclusion of 'lime of the Sanctuary' as a shade of white, arguing that this implies the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Akiva.

items.text: Inquiry about Rabbi Akiva's source
items.text_en: Inquiry about Rabbi Akiva's source
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks where Rabbi Akiva's view that shades are considered above one another is found.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where we find that Rabbi Akiva holds that one shade of white is above another.

items.text: First attempted proof from Rabbi Yosei's testimony
items.text_en: First attempted proof from Rabbi Yosei's testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei reports that Yehoshua ben Rabbi Akiva asked his father why the shades of negaim are two that are four. Rabbi Akiva responded that they should say 'from the membrane of an egg and above is impure', and then explained that the purpose is to teach that a priest must be expert in the shades and their names.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita where Rabbi Yosei reports that Yehoshua ben Rabbi Akiva asked his father why the shades of negaim are two that are four, and Rabbi Akiva responded that otherwise they would simply say 'from the membrane of an egg and above is impure'.
Rabbi Akiva explains that the purpose of listing multiple shades is to teach that they combine (מצטרפין) with each other.
Yehoshua objects that the same lesson could be taught by simply stating both rules explicitly.
Rabbi Akiva resolves that the detailed enumeration teaches that a priest must be expert in the shades and their names to examine negaim.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Akiva did not say 'from the lime of the Sanctuary and above', implying he holds that all shades combine with the se'et.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rabbi Akiva's omission of 'from the lime of the Sanctuary and above' that he holds all shades combine with the se'et.

items.text: Counter-proposal: perhaps only se'et and its offspring
items.text_en: Counter-proposal: perhaps only se'et and its offspring
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that perhaps Rabbi Akiva only meant that the se'et and its offspring combine, not all shades.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that perhaps Rabbi Akiva only meant that se'et and its offspring combine, and baheret and its offspring combine, not all shades together.

items.text: Second proof from Rabbi Chanina's mashal
items.text_en: Second proof from Rabbi Chanina's mashal
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from Rabbi Chanina, who gave a parable of four cups of milk with varying drops of blood, all being shades of white, one above the other, supporting Rabbi Akiva's view of gradation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Chanina's analogy of four cups of milk with drops of blood, showing that Rabbi Akiva considers all shades of white as distinct levels, one above the other.

items.text: Challenge: Rabbi Akiva's view only in mixed shades, not pure
items.text_en: Challenge: Rabbi Akiva's view only in mixed shades, not pure
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rabbi Akiva's view may apply only to mixed shades (patukh), not pure ones (chaluk), and even in mixed shades, his statement about 'adamdam' like diluted wine suggests he does not hold that all shades are above one another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Akiva's view about shades being above one another may apply only to mixed shades (פתוך), not pure ones (חלוק).
The Gemara raises a further objection: even if one assumes Rabbi Akiva holds this view for mixed shades, it is not clear that he holds it even for mixed shades.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Akiva describes the reddish shades (אדמדם) of the bright and dim white as diluted wine, implying he does not hold that all shades are hierarchically above one another.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the color of baheret
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the color of baheret
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if baheret is as white as snow, the Mishnah should have said 'snow-white' instead of 'white like wool.' It then cites a baraita where Rabbi Nathan reports that Rabbi Akiva actually said 'snow-white' and not 'wool-white.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if baheret is snow-white, the Mishnah should have said 'white like snow' instead of 'white like wool.'
The Gemara resolves that indeed the Mishnah should have said 'snow-white,' and cites a baraita where Rabbi Nathan reports that Rabbi Akiva actually said 'snow-white' and not 'wool-white.'

items.text: Proof that baheret is intense white
items.text_en: Proof that baheret is intense white
items.desc_en: Abaye derives from the verse 'If the baheret is white' that it is white and no other white is as white, indicating its intensity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that baheret is intense white?
Abaye answers by citing the verse 'If the baheret is white' — it is white, and no other white is as white, proving its intensity.

items.text: Baraita on the meanings of baheret, se'et, and sapachat
items.text_en: Baraita on the meanings of baheret, se'et, and sapachat
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that baheret is deep like the sun's appearance, se'et is high, and sapachat is a secondary attachment. It then derives that sapachat attaches to both se'et and baheret through a verbal analogy and a scriptural placement.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines baheret as deep (like the sun's appearance), se'et as high, and sapachat as a secondary attachment, citing biblical verses for each.
The gemara asks: we found that sapachat attaches to se'et, but from where do we derive that it attaches to baheret?
Rabbi Zeira derives via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'לבנה' (white) used for both se'et and baheret that just as se'et has a secondary attachment, so too baheret has one.
A baraita in the Mishnah supports this by noting that the verse placed sapachat between se'et and baheret, teaching that just as it attaches to se'et, so too it attaches to baheret.

items.text: Definition of 'clean white wool'
items.text_en: Definition of 'clean white wool'
items.desc_en: Rav Bibi bar Rav Asi explains that 'clean white wool' refers to wool that is cleaned and used for the m'lath (a type of garment).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'clean white wool' (צֶמֶר לָבָן) refers to in the context of the appearance of a נגע צרעת (skin affliction).

sub.text: Rav Bibi bar Rav Asi in the name of Rav Asi
sub.text_en: Rav Bibi bar Rav Asi in the name of Rav Asi
sub.desc_en: Rav Bibi bar Rav Asi explains that 'clean white wool' refers to clean wool of a one-day-old lamb, which is used for a מֵילָת (a type of fine garment).

items.text: Mashal of the kings and governors for the shades of white
items.text_en: Mashal of the kings and governors for the shades of white
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina gives a mashal of two kings and two governors to illustrate the relationship between the shades of white. The Gemara refines the mashal, and various Amoraim offer alternative comparisons, including Rav Adda bar Abba, Rava, and Ravina, to clarify the hierarchy of whiteness.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina introduces a mashal (parable) of two kings and two governors to illustrate the hierarchy of white shades in negaim.
The Gemara objects that the mashal as stated is redundant, since it describes each king above his own governor but not the relative hierarchy between the two kings.
The Gemara corrects the mashal: each king is above his own governor, establishing a clear hierarchy within each pair.

Rav Adda bar Abba offers an alternative comparison: the king and the alkapta (a high official), and the rufila (another official) and the exilarch, but the Gemara objects that this still implies a redundant hierarchy.
Rava gives a different comparison: King Shapur and the Roman Caesar, representing two distinct high authorities.
Rav Pappa asks Rava which of the two (King Shapur or Caesar) is superior.

Rava answers that Caesar is superior, as his coinage circulates throughout the world, citing the verse about the beast that devours and tramples all the earth, and Rabbi Yochanan identifies this as wicked Rome.
Ravina offers a final comparison: a woolen cloak and its worn-out lining, and a linen sheet and its worn-out state, illustrating the gradation of whiteness.

items.text: Derivation that the Torah speaks only of tum'at mikdash vekodashav
items.text_en: Derivation that the Torah speaks only of tum'at mikdash vekodashav
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from a kal vachomer that the Torah's discussion of a sliding-scale offering applies only to impurity of the Temple and its holy things, not to terumah. The Gemara questions whether terumah could be included, but concludes that no sin of terumah carries a fixed offering.

sub.desc_en: A baraita derives from a kal vachomer (קל וחומר) that the Torah's discussion of a sliding-scale offering applies only to impurity of the Temple and its holy things, not to terumah.
The Gemara questions whether terumah could be included, since it also carries warning and punishment, but concludes that no sin of terumah carries a fixed offering.
The Gemara resolves that the kal vachomer applies only to a fixed offering (קרבן קבוע), not to a sliding-scale offering, thus excluding terumah.

items.text: Opening question: Why not bring a sliding-scale offering for utterance of lips?
items.text_en: Opening question: Why not bring a sliding-scale offering for utterance of lips?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the sliding-scale offering should not apply to the case of utterance of lips (Shevuot), given that it is a type of speech. This sets up the need to exclude terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the sliding-scale offering (עולה ויורד) should not apply to the case of utterance of lips (ביטוי שפתיים), since it involves speech.

items.text: Answer: The verse says 'in it' to exclude terumah
items.text_en: Answer: The verse says 'in it' to exclude terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the verse uses the word 'בהה' (in it) to exclude terumah from the sliding-scale offering. This is the initial derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the verse uses 'בָּהּ' (in it) to exclude terumah from the sliding-scale offering.

items.text: Challenge: Perhaps 'in it' excludes the Temple, and Rabbi's derivation
items.text_en: Challenge: Perhaps 'in it' excludes the Temple, and Rabbi's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that 'בהה' might exclude the Temple (Mikdash) instead, since one cannot bring a sliding-scale offering for Temple impurity. Rava praises Rabbi for his deep insight, citing a baraitha where Rabbi derives that the verse 'בהמה טמאה' refers to impurity of sacred food (Tum'at Kodesh) through a gezerah shavah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the word 'בָּהּ' (in it) might exclude the Temple (Mikdash) instead of Terumah, since one cannot bring a sliding-scale offering for Temple impurity.
Rava praises Rabbi for drawing deep insight, comparing him to one who draws water from deep wells.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi derives from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) that the verse 'בְּהֵמָה טְמֵאָה' refers to impurity of sacred food (Tum'at Kodesh).

items.text: Derivation of Temple impurity from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation of Temple impurity from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found impurity of sacred food, but from where do we derive impurity of the Temple? The answer is from the verse 'בכל קדש לא תגע ואל המקדש לא תבא', which juxtaposes the Temple to sacred food.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found impurity of sacred food, but from where do we derive impurity of the Temple?
The Gemara answers: the verse 'בכל קדש לא תגע ואל המקדש לא תבא' juxtaposes the Temple to sacred food, deriving Temple impurity from the same source.

items.text: Counter-challenge: Terumah also included, and the logical debate
items.text_en: Counter-challenge: Terumah also included, and the logical debate
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that terumah should also be included, as the Master said the verse 'בכל קדש לא תגע' includes terumah. The Gemara responds that the Torah excluded terumah with 'בהה'. But then why not exclude the Temple? The Gemara argues that Temple impurity is more similar because it carries karet like the impurity of sacred food, while terumah only involves eating. The counter-argument is that terumah also involves eating like the impurity of sacred food.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the verse 'בכל קדש לא תגע' includes the Temple, it should also include תרומה (priestly portion), as the Master said that verse includes תרומה.

The Gemara responds that the Torah already excluded תרומה with the word 'בָּהּ', and argues that the Temple should not be excluded because it shares the penalty of כרת (excision) with sacred food impurity, unlike תרומה which only involves eating.
The Gemara counters that on the contrary, תרומה should not be excluded because it also involves eating, just like the impurity of sacred food.

items.text: Rava's first answer: Three karets in peace-offering
items.text_en: Rava's first answer: Three karets in peace-offering
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the three mentions of karet in the peace-offering (Shelamim) serve: one for a general rule, one for a specific detail, and one for the unspecified impurity in the Torah, which is Tum'at Kodesh. If that is not needed for Tum'at Kodesh (since derived from Rabbi), apply it to Tum'at Mikdash. The Gemara objects that this is needed for Rabbi Avahu's derivation (things not eaten). For Rabbi Shimon, it brings inner sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks why the Torah wrote three mentions of karet in the peace-offering, proposing that one is for a general rule, one for a specific detail, and one for the unspecified impurity in the Torah.

Rava identifies the unspecified impurity as טומאת קודש (impurity of sacred food) and says that if that is already derived from Rabbi's teaching, apply the verse to טומאת מקדש (impurity of the Temple).
The Gemara objects that this third mention is needed for Rabbi Avahu's derivation regarding things that are not eaten.
For Rabbi Shimon, who exempts from karet for things not eaten, the third mention brings the inner sin-offering, teaching that one is liable despite the exemption for piggul.

items.text: Nehardeans' version: Three impurities in peace-offering
items.text_en: Nehardeans' version: Three impurities in peace-offering
items.desc_en: The Nehardeans say in Rava's name that the three mentions of impurity (not karet) in the peace-offering serve the same purpose. The Gemara objects that these are needed for Rabbi Avahu's derivation, but answers that since the Torah needed to write karet for Rabbi Avahu, it also wrote impurities, as it cannot do otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Nehardeans, citing Rava, ask why the Torah wrote three mentions of impurity (not karet) in the peace-offering, and propose that one is for a general rule, one for a specific detail, and one for an unspecified impurity in the Torah.
They explain that the unspecified impurity refers to טומאת קודש (impurity of sacred food), and if that is already derived from Rabbi's teaching, apply it to טומאת מקדש (impurity of the Temple).

The Gemara objects that these impurity mentions are needed for Rabbi Avahu's derivation, but the Nehardeans answer that since the Torah had to write karet for Rabbi Avahu, it also wrote the impurities, as it cannot do otherwise.

items.text: Rava's final answer: Gezerah shavah from 'tumato'
items.text_en: Rava's final answer: Gezerah shavah from 'tumato'
items.desc_en: Rava concludes with a gezerah shavah: the word 'טומאתו' written here (in the context of the sliding-scale offering) and elsewhere teaches the inclusion of Temple impurity.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by invoking a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'טומאתו' (his impurity) written here to the same word elsewhere, thereby including Temple impurity in the sliding-scale offering.

items.text: Derivation from "בָּהּ" to include נבלת עוף טהור
items.text_en: Derivation from "בָּהּ" to include נבלת עוף טהור
items.desc_en: The Gemara connects the verse "טָמֵא יִהְיֶה עוֹד טֻמְאָתוֹ בּוֹ" to the context of tum'at mikdash, and questions the purpose of the word "בָּהּ". It answers that "בָּהּ" comes to include the carcass of a clean bird, and explains that since "בָּהּ" is a מיעוט, and it appears after another מיעוט from "אוֹ כִּי יִגַּע", the two מיעוטים together teach an inclusion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'טָמֵא יִהְיֶה עוֹד טֻמְאָתוֹ בּוֹ' and establishes a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) that the context of טומאה (impurity) here is the same as there — טומאת מקדש (impurity of the Sanctuary).
The Gemara asks: if the analogy is already established, what is the purpose of the word 'בָּהּ' (in it) in the verse?
The Gemara answers: the word 'בָּהּ' comes to include the carcass of a clean bird (נבלת עוף טהור) in the category of טומאת מקדש.
The Gemara objects: but you said earlier that 'בָּהּ' is a מיעוט (restrictive term), not an inclusion!
The Gemara resolves: because 'בָּהּ' is a מיעוט, it is superfluous after another מיעוט from 'אוֹ כִּי יִגַּע', and the rule is that two consecutive מיעוטים (restrictions) come to include (לרבות).

items.text: Introduction of the baraita on the inner goat
items.text_en: Introduction of the baraita on the inner goat
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that discusses the verse "וְכִפֶּר עַל הַקֹּדֶשׁ מִטֻּמְאֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל" and the three types of tum'ah that might be included.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that cites the verse about the inner goat's atonement for tum'ah.

items.text: Three tum'ot and their exclusion
items.text_en: Three tum'ot and their exclusion
items.desc_en: The baraita specifies the three tum'ot: idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and bloodshed, each supported by a verse. It then concludes that the goat does not atone for these, as the verse says "מִטֻּמְאֹת" and not all tum'ot.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces three tum'ot (ritual impurities) that could be included: idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and bloodshed.
The baraita cites verses for each tum'ah: idolatry (Leviticus 20:3), forbidden sexual relations (Leviticus 18:30), and bloodshed (Numbers 35:34).

The baraita rejects the possibility that the goat atones for these three tum'ot, citing the verse 'מִטֻּמְאֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל' (from the tum'ot of the children of Israel) to exclude all tum'ot except those of the Temple and its sanctified items.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's derivation for tum'at mikdash v'kadashav
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's derivation for tum'at mikdash v'kadashav
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda argues that just as the verse distinguishes these three tum'ot from all others, so too here the goat atones only for tum'at mikdash v'kadashav.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda argues that just as the verse distinguishes these three tum'ot from all others, so too here the goat atones only for טומאת מקדש וקדשיו (impurity of the Temple and its holy things).

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's derivation and the scope of the goat's atonement
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's derivation and the scope of the goat's atonement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse itself that the goat atones for tum'ot of the mikdash, and then limits it to sins that are not subject to a korban, and includes cases of ידיעה בתחילה without ידיעה בסוף for which the goat provides תלייה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that the goat's atonement is derived from its own context, applying only to טומאת מקדש (impurity of the Sanctuary).
The Gemara raises a possibility that the goat might atone for any impurity related to sacred items.
Rabbi Shimon limits the goat's atonement to sins that are not subject to a korban (offering), by analogy to intentional sins (פשעים).
The Gemara asks for the source that the goat provides תלייה (suspension of punishment) for cases of initial knowledge without final knowledge.

Rabbi Shimon derives from the phrase 'לכל חטאתם' (for all their sins) that the goat includes those liable for a חטאת (sin-offering) in the general category, meaning it suspends punishment for cases lacking final knowledge.

items.text: Analysis of the case of idolatry
items.text_en: Analysis of the case of idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the case of idolatry listed among the three tum'ot: if done intentionally, it is a capital offense; if unintentionally, it requires a korban. The Gemara resolves that it refers to an intentional act without warning, or an unintentional act without knowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita listing the three tum'ot (idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, bloodshed) that the inner goat atones for.
The Gemara questions the case of idolatry: if done במזיד (intentionally) it is a capital offense, and if done בשוגג (unintentionally) it requires a korban, so how does the goat apply?
The Gemara resolves that the case is either intentional without warning (so no capital punishment) or unintentional without knowledge (so no korban), thus the goat atones.

items.text: Gemara's question on gilui arayot and shefichut damim
items.text_en: Gemara's question on gilui arayot and shefichut damim
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how cases of forbidden relations (gilui arayot) and bloodshed (shefichut damim) can be relevant to the se'ir's atonement, since intentional acts are capital and unintentional acts require a sacrifice or exile. It resolves that the cases involve no warning (for intentional) or no knowledge (for unintentional).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how forbidden relations (גילוי עריות) and bloodshed (שפיכות דמים) can be relevant to the se'ir's atonement, since intentional acts are capital and unintentional acts require a sacrifice or exile.
The Gemara resolves that the cases involve no warning (for intentional) or no knowledge (for unintentional), or that the bloodshed involves those not subject to exile.

items.text: Mar's statement: exclusion of three tum'ot
items.text_en: Mar's statement: exclusion of three tum'ot
items.desc_en: Mar states that one might think the se'ir atones for all three tum'ot, but the verse 'mitum'ot' excludes some, limiting it to tum'at mikdash vekodashav, according to Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that one might think the se'ir atones for all three tum'ot, but the verse 'mitum'ot' excludes some, limiting it to tum'at mikdash vekodashav, according to Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Challenge: avodah zarah as a 'divided' offering
items.text_en: Challenge: avodah zarah as a 'divided' offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that avodah zarah is a 'divided' offering (oleh veyored) and thus should be excluded. It notes that avodah zarah brings a se'irah, not a kisbah, indicating a different division.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'divided' means, explaining that it refers to a sliding-scale offering (עולה ויורד), and proposes that avodah zarah (idolatry) might be such a case.
A mnemonic note lists the cases to be discussed: avodah zarah, a woman after childbirth, a leper, a nazirite, etc.
The Gemara answers that avodah zarah is 'divided' because it requires a female goat (שעירה) rather than a lamb (כשבה), showing a different division of the offering.

items.text: Rav Kahana's distinction: lenient vs. stringent division
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's distinction: lenient vs. stringent division
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana clarifies that the division in avodah zarah is a leniency (bringing a se'irah instead of a kisbah), whereas the se'ir's exclusion is a stringency (not atoning for certain tum'ot).

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana resolves the objection by distinguishing that the division in avodah zarah is a leniency (bringing a se'irah instead of a kisbah), whereas the se'ir's exclusion is a stringency (not atoning for certain tum'ot).

items.text: Challenges from yoledet, metzora, and nazir tamei
items.text_en: Challenges from yoledet, metzora, and nazir tamei
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges with yoledet, metzora, and nazir tamei, each of which brings an oleh veyored offering. Rav Hosha'ya answers each with the verse 'lechol chatotam' – not for all tum'ot. For Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, the Gemara notes their own reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that a yoledet (woman after childbirth), who brings an oleh veyored (sliding-scale) offering, undermines the exclusion of all tum'ot (impurities) from the inner sin-offering.
Rav Hosha'ya answers with the verse 'ולא לכל חטאתם' — the goat atones for tum'ot defined by the verse, excluding the tum'ah of yoledet.
The Gemara asks what can be said according to Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, who holds that a yoledet is a sinner and thus her offering fits the exclusion.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Shimon follows his own reasoning — the verse itself resolves the contradiction locally (ממקומו הוא מוכרע).
The Gemara challenges with a metzora (leper), who also brings an oleh veyored offering.
Rav Hosha'ya again invokes the verse limiting the atonement to tum'ot of the sanctuary, excluding metzora.

sub.text: Gemara's question regarding Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
sub.text_en: Gemara's question regarding Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what can be said according to Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, who holds that leprosy comes for seven specific sins, making his offering a חטאת (sin-offering).
The Gemara answers that for the metzora, his affliction itself serves as atonement, and his offering is only to permit him to enter the camp.
The Gemara challenges with a nazir tamei (contaminated nazirite), who brings doves as an oleh veyored offering.
Rav Hosha'ya gives the same verse-based answer excluding nazir tamei from the inner sin-offering.

sub.text: Gemara's question regarding Rabbi Elazar HaKappar
sub.text_en: Gemara's question regarding Rabbi Elazar HaKappar
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what can be said according to Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, who holds that a nazir is a sinner.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Elazar HaKappar holds like Rabbi Shimon — the word 'ממקומו' resolves the contradiction.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda on 'mimkomo hu muchra'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda on 'mimkomo hu muchra'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon argues that the verse 'vechipper al hakodesh mitum'ot' implies atonement only for tum'at kodesh, which Rabbi Yehuda counters is needed for the comparison between the Holy of Holies and the Heikhal. Rabbi Shimon derives this from 'vechen ya'aseh'.

sub.desc_en: Mar introduces Rabbi Shimon's position that the verse 'וְכִפֶּר עַל הַקֹּדֶשׁ מִטֻּמְאוֹת' implies atonement only for טומאת קודש (impurity of sacred items).
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon's derivation seems sound.
Rabbi Yehuda counters that the verse is needed to teach that the same atonement procedure performed in the Holy of Holies is performed in the Heikhal.
Rabbi Shimon responds that the comparison between the Holy of Holies and the Heikhal is derived from the verse 'וְכֵן יַעֲשֶׂה' (and thus he shall do), not from the verse about טומאה.
Rabbi Yehuda objects that without the verse, one might think a separate bull and goat are brought for the Heikhal, so the verse teaches that the same animals suffice.
Rabbi Shimon resolves that the verse 'וְכֵן יַעֲשֶׂה לְאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד' itself implies that the same animals are used, so no additional verse is needed.

items.text: Mar's second statement: exclusion of tum'ot with knowledge
items.text_en: Mar's second statement: exclusion of tum'ot with knowledge
items.desc_en: Mar states that one might think the se'ir atones for all tum'ot of the sanctuary, but the verse excludes those with knowledge at the beginning and end, which require a sacrifice. The Gemara clarifies a case of knowledge close to sunset.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that one might think the se'ir atones for all tum'ot of the sanctuary, but the verse excludes those with knowledge at the beginning and end, which require a sacrifice.
The Gemara clarifies that the case involves knowledge close to sunset, where one might think the se'ir atones before a sacrifice could be brought.

items.text: Conclusion of previous discussion
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the verse teaches that the goat suspends punishment even in cases where there is initial awareness but no final awareness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the verse teaches that the goat suspends punishment even in cases where there is initial awareness but no final awareness.

items.text: Derivation that the goat suspends in cases of initial awareness without final awareness
items.text_en: Derivation that the goat suspends in cases of initial awareness without final awareness
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the derivation: just as intentional sins are not subject to a sacrifice, so too unintentional sins that are not subject to a sacrifice might be thought to never be suspended. The verse 'for all their sins' teaches that the goat only suspends for those sins that are eligible for a sacrifice when discovered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where is it derived that the goat suspends in cases of initial awareness without final awareness, and what is the difficulty?

The Gemara explains the difficulty: if intentional sins (פשעים) are never subject to a sacrifice, then unintentional sins (חטאים) that are never subject to a sacrifice might be thought to never be suspended, but cases of initial awareness without final awareness, which become eligible for a sacrifice upon discovery, might be thought not to be suspended.
The Gemara objects: one might say that cases of no initial awareness but final awareness are atoned for by the goat made outside and Yom Kippur.

The Gemara resolves: one might have thought to reverse the cases, but the verse 'for all their sins' (לכל חטאתם) teaches that the goat only suspends for those sins that are eligible for a sacrifice when discovered.

items.text: Why the goat suspends if it does not atone
items.text_en: Why the goat suspends if it does not atone
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the goat suspends punishment if it does not provide complete atonement. Rabbi Zeira answers that it ensures one dies without sin, but Rava objects that death itself atones. Rava instead explains that the goat protects from suffering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since the goat does not provide complete atonement (כפרה גמורה), why does it suspend punishment at all?
Rabbi Zeira answers that the goat's suspension ensures that if one dies, he dies without sin (בלא עון).
Rava objects that death itself atones (מיתה ממרקת), so the goat's suspension is unnecessary for that purpose.
Rava resolves that the goat's suspension protects the person from suffering (יסורין) in this world.

items.text: The outer goat's atonement and the limitation of one atonement
items.text_en: The outer goat's atonement and the limitation of one atonement
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the outer goat's atonement for impurity that occurred between the two goats. It derives from the verse 'one' that the inner goat atones only for its own designated sins, not for those of the outer goat, and from 'once a year' that the outer goat's atonement is limited to one atonement per year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule: for cases with no initial awareness but final awareness, the external goat and Yom Kippur atone.
The Gemara asks: since the inner and outer goats are juxtaposed, why not let the inner goat atone for both its own sins and those of the outer goat, even where the outer goat was not performed?
The Gemara answers: the verse says 'אַחַת' (one) — it atones for one atonement, not two.
The Gemara asks: let the outer goat atone for its own sins, and why does the inner goat affect it — this would apply to impurity that occurred between the two services.
The Gemara answers: the verse says 'אַחַת בַּשָּׁנָה' (once a year) — this atonement shall not be [for more than one purpose].

items.text: Question on Rabbi Yishmael's view
items.text_en: Question on Rabbi Yishmael's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yishmael's position that the outer goat atones for sins with no initial knowledge but eventual knowledge, asking why it would atone for sins with no knowledge at all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yishmael's view: if the outer goat atones for sins with initial ignorance but eventual knowledge, why would it atone for sins with no knowledge at all?

items.text: Answer: Rabbi Yishmael follows Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Answer: Rabbi Yishmael follows Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yishmael holds like Rabbi Meir, who says all goats have equal atonement for Temple impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yishmael holds like Rabbi Meir, who says all goats have equal atonement for Temple impurity.

items.text: Purpose of the comparison
items.text_en: Purpose of the comparison
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the comparison of the outer goat to the inner goat teaches that the outer goat does not atone for other sins.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For what halachic purpose was the outer goat compared to the inner goat?
The Gemara answers: Just as the inner goat does not atone for other sins, so too the outer goat does not atone for other sins.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's view and its derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's view and its derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that the goats of festivals and new moons atone for sins with no knowledge at all. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains the scriptural basis: the verse 'a goat for a sin-offering to the Lord' indicates atonement for a sin known only to God.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that the goats of festivals and new moons atone for sins with no knowledge at all.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains the scriptural basis: the verse 'a goat for a sin-offering to the Lord' indicates atonement for a sin known only to God.

items.text: Objection and resolution: Resh Lakish's teaching
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: Resh Lakish's teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse is needed for Resh Lakish's teaching that the goat of the new moon atones for the diminution of the moon. It resolves that the verse implies both meanings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse 'לַה׳' is needed for Resh Lakish's teaching that the goat of the new moon atones for the diminution of the moon.
The Gemara resolves that if the verse only meant Resh Lakish's teaching, it would have said 'עַל ה׳', so the extra wording 'לַה׳' implies both meanings.

The Gemara further resolves that if the entire verse were for Resh Lakish, it would have said 'חַטָּאת ה׳', so the wording 'לַה׳' teaches both the atonement for the moon's diminution and the atonement for unknown sin.

items.text: Limitation to Temple impurity
items.text_en: Limitation to Temple impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the goat should not atone for other sins, and answers via the school of Rabbi Yishmael that since both the new moon goat and the outer goat come at fixed times, the new moon goat is limited to Temple impurity like the outer goat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the new moon goat should not also atone for other sins beyond Temple impurity.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael answers that since both the new moon goat and the outer goat come at fixed times, the new moon goat is limited to atoning for Temple impurity like the outer goat.

items.text: Derivation for festival goats
items.text_en: Derivation for festival goats
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks to derive the same limitation for the festival goats, noting that a simple analogy from the new moon goat is flawed because the new moon is more frequent, and from Yom Kippur because its atonement is greater.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to derive the limitation for festival goats, noting that an analogy from the new moon goat is flawed because the new moon is more frequent, and from Yom Kippur because its atonement is greater.

items.text: Rejecting the initial analogy from Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Rejecting the initial analogy from Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the earlier attempt to derive the law of Rosh Chodesh from Yom Kippur, arguing that Yom Kippur's atonement is explicitly written, whereas here the entire matter is not derived.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the initial analogy from Yom Kippur, arguing that Yom Kippur's atonement is explicitly written, whereas here the entire matter cannot be derived.

items.text: Rabbi Chama's derivation via verbal analogy
items.text_en: Rabbi Chama's derivation via verbal analogy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina establishes a verbal analogy between the goats of the Festivals and those of New Moons, teaching that both only atone for sins committed without any knowledge at the outset or end.

sub.text: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina derives the law through a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'שעיר'–'ושעיר', linking the goats of festivals to those of Rosh Chodesh, establishing that both only atone for sins without any knowledge at the beginning or end.

items.text: Query regarding Rabbi Yehuda's position on eventual knowledge
items.text_en: Query regarding Rabbi Yehuda's position on eventual knowledge
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: does Rabbi Yehuda limit his ruling to sins that will never become known, or does he include sins that will eventually become known, considering them as having knowledge at the end?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does Rabbi Yehuda's ruling apply only to a sin whose end is unknown, or even to a sin whose end will eventually become known, since at present only God knows it?

items.text: Baraita resolving the query: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Baraita resolving the query: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda rules that Festival and New Moon goats atone even for sins that will eventually become known, while Rabbi Shimon limits atonement to Festival goats only, excluding New Moon goats.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda rules that Festival and New Moon goats atone for sins without awareness at the outset or end, and even for sins that will eventually become known.
Rabbi Shimon limits atonement to Festival goats only, excluding New Moon goats.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Oshaya explain Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Oshaya explain Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Oshaya explains Rabbi Shimon's view: a verbal analogy between the New Moon goat and the ציץ (frontlet) teaches that the goat only atones for impurity of the flesh (eating sacred meat while impure), not for other sins. Further derivations limit each to one sin and prevent overlap.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Oshaya introduces Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between the word 'עָוֹן' in the New Moon goat verse and in the ציץ (frontlet) verse teaches that the goat only atones for טומאת בשר (impurity of the flesh — eating sacred meat while impure).

The Gemara objects: if the analogy is complete, the goat should also atone for impurity of the sacrificial animal itself (עולין), like the ציץ does; the verse answers by specifying 'עֲוֹן הָעֵדָה' (sin of the congregation), limiting the atonement.

The Gemara asks: since the goat and the ציץ derive atonement from each other, why can't the goat atone for its own sin and the ציץ's sin simultaneously? The verse 'עֲוֹן' teaches it bears only one sin, not two.
The Gemara further asks: why can't the ציץ atone for its own sin and the goat's sin simultaneously? The verse 'אוֹתָהּ' teaches that it bears only its own sin, not another's.

Rav Ashi resolves the derivation: the verse here says 'עֲוֹן הָעֵדָה' (sin of the congregation) — atoning for the congregation, not for sacred items; the verse there says 'עֲוֹן הַקֳּדָשִׁים' (sin of the sacred items) — atoning for sacred items, not for the congregation.

items.text: Deriving the atonement of Festival goats
items.text_en: Deriving the atonement of Festival goats
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found that New Moon goats atone for a pure person who ate impure sacred meat; from where do we derive that Festival goats atone for sins without any knowledge? It answers by reapplying Rabbi Chama's verbal analogy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found that New Moon goats atone for a pure person who ate impure sacred meat; from where do we derive that Festival goats atone for sins without any knowledge?

sub.text: Gemara's answer via Rabbi Chama bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer via Rabbi Chama bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers by reapplying Rabbi Chama bar Chanina's verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'שעיר'–'ושעיר' to derive the atonement of Festival goats from New Moon goats.

items.text: Initial derivation and limitation of festival goats' atonement
items.text_en: Initial derivation and limitation of festival goats' atonement
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by linking festival goats to new moon goats via a verbal analogy (היקש), establishing that they atone for matters of the sacred. It then rejects the possibility that they atone for new moon or Yom Kippur sins, citing the verses 'אותה' and 'אחת בשנה' which limit each goat to its own sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes a verbal analogy (היקש) linking festival goats to new moon goats, concluding that festival goats also atone for matters of the sacred.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that festival goats atone for new moon sins, citing the verse 'אותה' which limits each goat to its own sin.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that festival goats atone for Yom Kippur sins, citing the verse 'אחת בשנה' which limits atonement to once a year.

items.text: Determining the specific sin for which festival goats atone
items.text_en: Determining the specific sin for which festival goats atone
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for what sin do these goats atone? It systematically eliminates cases involving initial or final knowledge (which require a personal offering or the outer goat), concluding that they must atone only for cases with no knowledge at all, neither at the beginning nor the end.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for what sin do the festival goats atone?
The Gemara eliminates cases involving initial or final knowledge, which require a personal offering, the inner goat, or the outer goat.
The Gemara concludes that the festival goats atone only for cases with no knowledge at all, neither at the beginning nor the end.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's view and the derivation from 'שעיר' and 'ושעיר'
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's view and the derivation from 'שעיר' and 'ושעיר'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir states that all goats have equal atonement.
