Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina explains his reasoning: the Torah uses 'שעיר' and 'ושעיר' to equate all goats via a verbal analogy, with the vav adding to the first matter. The Gemara initially objects based on Rabbi Yochanan's principle that in sacred matters one cannot learn from a derived case, but resolves that all goats learn from the first one.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir states that all goats have equal atonement.

sub.text: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina's explanation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina's explanation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina explains Rabbi Meir's reasoning: the Torah uses 'שעיר' and 'ושעיר' to equate all goats via a verbal analogy, with the vav adding to the first matter.
The Gemara objects based on Rabbi Yochanan's principle that in sacred matters one cannot learn a derived case from another derived case.
The Gemara resolves that all goats learn from the first one, not from each other, thus avoiding the problem.

items.text: Extending the equation to Shavuot and Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Extending the equation to Shavuot and Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how to include Shavuot and Yom Kippur, which lack the word 'ושעיר'. Rabbi Yona answers that the verse 'אלה תעשו לה' במועדיכם' equates all festivals. The Gemara objects that Rosh Chodesh is not a festival, but Abaye resolves that it is indeed called a 'מועד', citing a verse from Lamentations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for Shavuot and Yom Kippur, which lack the word 'ושעיר' (and a goat), from where do we derive that their goats are included in the analogy?
Rabbi Yona answers that the verse 'אלה תעשו לה' במועדיכם' (these you shall do for the Lord on your appointed times) equates all festivals, including Shavuot and Yom Kippur.
The Gemara objects that Rosh Chodesh (the New Moon) is not called a 'מועד' (appointed time), so the verse cannot include it.

Abaye resolves that Rosh Chodesh is indeed called a 'מועד' (appointed time), citing the verse 'קרא עלי מועד לשבור בחורי' (He called an appointed time against me to crush my young men) from Lamentations.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's limitation: the inner goat does not share atonement
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's limitation: the inner goat does not share atonement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Meir concedes that the inner goat (שעיר הנעשה בפנים) does not atone for the same sins as the other goats, nor do they atone for its sin. The inner goat atones only one atonement (for Yom Kippur), and the other goats cannot atone for its unique sin due to the verse 'אחת בשנה'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Meir concedes that the inner goat (שעיר הנעשה בפנים) does not atone for the same sins as the other goats, nor do they atone for its sin.
The Gemara explains that the inner goat atones only one atonement (for Yom Kippur), and the other goats cannot atone for its unique sin due to the verse 'אחת בשנה'.

items.text: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Meir's view
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Meir's view
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Meir: the festival goats, new moon goats, and the outer goat atone for cases without knowledge, for cases with only final knowledge, and for a pure person who ate impure food. The inner goat is excluded from this list, and its atonement is also excluded.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Meir: the festival goats, new moon goats, and the outer goat atone for cases without knowledge, for cases with only final knowledge, and for a pure person who ate impure food.
The baraita notes that the inner goat is excluded from this list, and its atonement is also excluded.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's view and the limitations between goats
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's view and the limitations between goats
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that new moon goats atone only for a pure person who ate impure food. The Gemara explains why new moon goats cannot atone for festival sins (due to 'עון' – one sin), and festival goats cannot atone for new moon sins (due to 'אותה'). Similarly, festival goats cannot atone for Yom Kippur sins (due to 'אחת בשנה'), and Yom Kippur cannot atone for festival sins (due to 'אחת' – one atonement). The Gemara notes that 'אחת' is written regarding the inner goat, but the verse 'מלבד' is cited to extend the limitation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that the new moon goats atone only for a pure person who ate impure food.
The Gemara explains why new moon goats cannot atone for festival sins (due to 'עון' – one sin) and why festival goats cannot atone for new moon sins (due to 'אותה' – that one bears sin).
The Gemara explains why festival goats cannot atone for Yom Kippur sins (due to 'אחת בשנה' – one atonement per year) and why Yom Kippur cannot atone for festival sins (due to 'אחת' – one atonement).
The Gemara objects that 'אחת' is written regarding the inner goat, not the festival goats, and cites the verse 'מלבד' to extend the limitation.

items.text: Introduction: linking outer and inner goats
items.text_en: Introduction: linking outer and inner goats
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the outer goat is linked to the inner goat through the phrase 'sin-offering of atonements'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that the outer goat is linked to the inner goat through the phrase 'sin-offering of atonements'.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of his teacher that the outer goat does not atone for the inner goat's sins.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda states in the name of his teacher that the outer goat does not atone for the inner goat's sins.

items.text: Why New Moons don't atone for Festivals
items.text_en: Why New Moons don't atone for Festivals
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that New Moon offerings do not atone for Festival sins because the verse says 'iniquity' (singular), meaning it bears only one iniquity. Conversely, Festivals do not atone for New Moon sins because the verse says 'it' (אותה), implying that only that specific offering bears iniquity. The Gemara notes that the word 'it' is not understood by some.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why New Moon offerings do not atone for Festival sins, and answers that the verse says 'עֲוֹן' (iniquity), meaning it bears only one iniquity.
The Gemara further explains that Festivals do not atone for New Moon sins because the verse says 'אוֹתָהּ' (it), implying that only that specific offering bears iniquity.
The Gemara notes that the word 'אוֹתָהּ' (it) is not understood by some, implying a potential objection to the previous reasoning.

items.text: Why Festivals don't atone for Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Why Festivals don't atone for Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Festival offerings do not atone for Yom Kippur sins, answering that the verse says 'once a year' (אחת בשנה), meaning this atonement occurs only once a year. Conversely, Yom Kippur does not atone for Festival sins because the verse says 'one' (אחת), implying it atones for one atonement, not two. The Gemara notes that the word 'one' is not understood by some.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Festival offerings do not atone for sins of Yom Kippur.
The Gemara answers that the verse says 'once a year' (אחת בשנה), meaning this atonement occurs only once a year.
The Gemara objects that if so, Yom Kippur should not atone for Festival sins either, because the verse says 'one' (אחת), implying it atones for one atonement, not two.
The Gemara notes that the word 'one' (אחת) is not understood by some as limiting atonement.

items.text: Objection: 'one' refers to inner goat
items.text_en: Objection: 'one' refers to inner goat
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not say that 'one' is written only regarding the inner goat, so Festivals could atone for Yom Kippur?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not say that 'אחת' (one) is written only regarding the inner goat, so Festivals could atone for Yom Kippur?

items.text: Resolution: 'one' applies to outer goat too
items.text_en: Resolution: 'one' applies to outer goat too
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that 'one' is indeed understood, but the verse 'and Aaron shall make atonement upon its horns once a year' teaches that only the inner altar's horns have one atonement, but the outer altar can have even two atonements.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that 'אחת' (one) is understood literally, but the verse 'וְכִפֶּר אַהֲרֹן עַל קַרְנֹתָיו אַחַת בַּשָּׁנָה' (and Aaron shall make atonement upon its horns once a year) teaches that only the inner altar's horns have one atonement per year, while the outer altar can have even two atonements.

items.text: Ulla's ruling on unneeded daily offerings
items.text_en: Ulla's ruling on unneeded daily offerings
items.desc_en: Ulla says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that daily offerings (תמידין) that were not needed for the community can be redeemed while still unblemished.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that daily offerings (תמידין) not needed for the community may be redeemed while still unblemished.

items.text: Rav Chisda's objection: where did the sanctity go?
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's objection: where did the sanctity go?
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda challenges Rabba, who was teaching Ulla's statement, asking who would listen to him and Rabbi Yochanan, since the sanctity of the offerings cannot simply disappear.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda objects to Rabba's teaching of Ulla's statement, questioning who would listen to him and Rabbi Yochanan, since the sanctity of the offerings cannot simply disappear.

items.text: Rabba's proof from leftover incense
items.text_en: Rabba's proof from leftover incense
items.desc_en: Rabba responds by citing a mishnah about leftover incense (קטורת) that was redeemed and given to artisans as payment, showing that sanctity can be transferred. He asks why not say 'where did the sanctity go?' there as well.

sub.desc_en: Rabba challenges Rav Chisda by asking whether he does not accept the principle that we do not ask 'where did the sanctity go?' and cites the mishnah about leftover incense (קטורת) that was redeemed and given to artisans as payment, showing that sanctity can be transferred without such a question.

items.text: Rav Chisda's distinction: incense is different
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's distinction: incense is different
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda responds that incense is different (שאני קטורת), implying a distinction that allows its redemption unlike daily offerings.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda responds that the case of incense (קטורת) is different, implying a distinction that allows its redemption unlike daily offerings.

items.text: Initial assumption: sanctity is monetary
items.text_en: Initial assumption: sanctity is monetary
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by assuming that the sanctity of the items in question is monetary (kedushat damim), based on a previous context.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by assuming that the sanctity involved is monetary (קדושת דמים), based on the previous context.

items.text: Challenge from tevul yom disqualification
items.text_en: Challenge from tevul yom disqualification
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption of monetary sanctity by citing a baraita that a meal-offering placed in a mortar is disqualified by tevul yom, and notes that only items sanctified in a vessel are susceptible to such disqualification, implying intrinsic sanctity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption of monetary sanctity by citing a baraita that a meal-offering placed in a mortar is disqualified by טבול יום (one who immersed but awaits sunset), implying intrinsic sanctity.

The Gemara anticipates and rejects the possible answer that all monetary sanctity items are disqualified by טבול יום, citing a Mishnah that only items sanctified in a vessel become susceptible to such disqualification.
The Gemara concludes that only items sanctified in a vessel are susceptible to disqualification by טבול יום, so the baraita's disqualification implies intrinsic sanctity, not monetary sanctity.

items.text: Challenge from linah disqualification
items.text_en: Challenge from linah disqualification
items.desc_en: The Gemara then considers the possibility of intrinsic sanctity (kedushat haguf) and challenges it by noting that linah disqualification also applies only after sanctification in a vessel, citing a mishnah about various offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the possibility of intrinsic sanctity (קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף) by noting that if it were intrinsic, the offering should be disqualified by לִינָה (overnight stay) even without sanctification in a vessel.

The Gemara cites a mishnah listing offerings (קומץ, לבונה, קטורת, etc.) that become eligible for disqualification by לִינָה only after sanctification in a vessel, proving that לִינָה disqualification depends on vessel sanctification.

items.text: Distinction for incense regarding linah
items.text_en: Distinction for incense regarding linah
items.desc_en: An anonymous answer distinguishes incense from other offerings regarding linah, because its form is consistent throughout the year, but the challenge remains.

sub.desc_en: The anonymous answer distinguishes incense from other offerings regarding לינה (overnight invalidation), because its form is consistent throughout the year.

items.text: Rabbah's resolution: conditional court intent
items.text_en: Rabbah's resolution: conditional court intent
items.desc_en: Rabbah resolves the contradiction by stating that the court conditions the sanctity: if the items are needed, they are used; if not, they revert to their monetary value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In any case, the difficulty remains — where did the sanctity of these items go?
Rabbah resolves the difficulty by stating that the court conditions the sanctity: if the items are needed, they are used; if not, they revert to their monetary value.

items.text: Abaye's objection and distinction
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and distinction
items.desc_en: Abaye objects based on a ruling that dedicating a male animal for its blood creates intrinsic sanctity, but Rabbah distinguishes between dedicating for 'blood of a burnt-offering' and 'blood of libations'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rabbah's position by citing Rabbah's own earlier ruling that dedicating a male animal for its blood creates intrinsic sanctity (קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף).

Rabbah distinguishes between dedicating an animal for 'blood of a burnt-offering' (לִדְמֵי עוֹלָה), which creates intrinsic sanctity, and dedicating for 'blood of libations' (לִדְמֵי נְסָכִים), which does not.

items.text: Further challenge from Yom Kippur offerings
items.text_en: Further challenge from Yom Kippur offerings
items.desc_en: Abaye raises another challenge from the law of the bull and goat of Yom Kippur that were lost and replaced, setting up the next discussion.

sub.desc_en: Abaye raises a challenge from the law of the bull and goat of Yom Kippur that were lost and replaced, setting up the next discussion.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Lost or replaced idolatry sin-offerings
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Lost or replaced idolatry sin-offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if sin-offerings for idolatry are lost and others substituted, all must die per Rabbi Yehuda, but Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say they graze until blemished then sold with proceeds to donation, because communal sin-offerings never die.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if sin-offerings for idolatry are lost and others substituted, all must die per Rabbi Yehuda, but Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say they graze until blemished then sold with proceeds to donation, because communal sin-offerings never die.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Why not let the court stipulate?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Why not let the court stipulate?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah doesn't allow the court to stipulate that the substituted animals should be treated like the lost ones, given that the court can impose conditions on dedicated property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Why not say the court imposes a condition on them (that if lost, they must die)?

items.text: First answer: Distinguish lost vs. not found
items.text_en: First answer: Distinguish lost vs. not found
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the case involves 'lost' animals which are not commonly found, so the court cannot stipulate about them; but for commonly found items like a cow, the court can stipulate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: You speak of lost items; lost items are uncommon, so the court cannot impose a standard condition.

items.text: Objection: Cow is uncommon yet redeemable
items.text_en: Objection: Cow is uncommon yet redeemable
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a cow (para) is also uncommon, yet the Mishnah says it can be redeemed if slaughtered on the altar. The Gemara distinguishes: the cow is for bedek habayit (Temple maintenance), not a sin-offering, so its redemption rules differ.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Consider the red heifer, which is also uncommon, yet the Mishnah teaches it can be redeemed for any blemish — if it dies or is slaughtered, it is redeemed; if a nicer one is found, it is redeemed; if slaughtered on its pyre, it has no permanent redemption. The distinction is that the red heifer is Temple property (קדשי בדק הבית).
The Gemara answers that the red heifer is different because it is consecrated for Temple maintenance (קדשי בדק הבית), not for the altar, so its redemption rules are more lenient.

items.text: Clarification: Redemption of dead/slaughtered cow
items.text_en: Clarification: Redemption of dead/slaughtered cow
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that if a cow dedicated to Temple maintenance dies or is slaughtered, it can be redeemed, but if slaughtered on the altar it has no permanent redemption. This is because it is bedek habayit, not a sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: If so, why does the Mishnah say a dead or slaughtered red heifer is redeemed? We require standing and valuation! This must be Rabbi Shimon's view, who says: Temple offerings (קדשי מזבח) are subject to standing and valuation, but Temple property (קדשי בדק הבית) is not.
The Gemara answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that the requirement of העמדה והערכה applies only to קדשי מזבח, not to קדשי בדק הבית.

items.text: Further objection: Rabbi Shimon's view on cow redemption
items.text_en: Further objection: Rabbi Shimon's view on cow redemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if it's Rabbi Shimon who says bedek habayit animals aren't subject to standing and valuation, then why does the Mishnah say a cow slaughtered on the altar has no redemption? Rabbi Shimon would allow redemption. The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling aligns with Rabbi Shimon's earlier statement that a cow slaughtered on the altar has no redemption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites supporting evidence: If it is Rabbi Shimon, consider the end of the Mishnah: 'slaughtered on its pyre — no permanent redemption.' That matches Rabbi Shimon's position.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Shimon's consistent ruling
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Shimon's consistent ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves by citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon explicitly says a cow slaughtered on the altar has no redemption, consistent with the Mishnah. This shows the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, not the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: But a baraita says Rabbi Shimon states: The red heifer imparts food impurity because it had a 'hour of fitness' (when it could be eaten). And Resh Lakish said: Rabbi Shimon would say the red heifer is redeemed on its pyre! That contradicts the Mishnah's end.

items.text: Alternative explanation: Cow's expensive blood
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Cow's expensive blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another reason: the cow's blood is expensive, so it's not redeemed because the blood would be wasted. This contrasts with sin-offerings whose blood is less costly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: The red heifer is different because its blood is precious (valuable for purification).

items.text: Gemara's question: Redeeming dead offerings for dogs?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Redeeming dead offerings for dogs?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if a cow dies, it can be redeemed, but why redeem it to feed to dogs? The answer: because of its hide. The court would stipulate about the hide.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's ruling that a dead red heifer may be redeemed, asking why one would redeem consecrated items to feed them to dogs.
Rav Mesharshiya answers that the redemption is for the sake of the hide, not the meat.
The Gemara objects: does the court really stipulate with the hide in mind, given its relatively low value?
Rav Kahana answers with a proverb: from a camel, even its ear is valuable, so the hide of a red heifer is worth redeeming.
Abaye raises an objection from the mishna where Rabbi Shimon rules that goats consecrated for different days may be sacrificed interchangeably, without invoking the court's stipulation.

items.text: Return to main argument: Rabbi Shimon vs. Sages on Temple offerings
items.text_en: Return to main argument: Rabbi Shimon vs. Sages on Temple offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages about whether Temple offerings not needed for the community can be redeemed intact. Rabbi Shimon says no, the Sages say yes. The Gemara cites a supporting baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Shimon did not simply invoke the principle that the court tacitly stipulates concerning the offerings.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Shimon does not accept the principle of the court tacitly stipulating.

sub.text: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Amram citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Amram citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: A tradition from Rabbi Yochanan is cited to support that Rabbi Shimon holds that unblemished daily offerings not needed by the public cannot be redeemed, while the Sages permit it.

items.text: Final question: Who are the Sages disagreeing with Rabbi Shimon?
items.text_en: Final question: Who are the Sages disagreeing with Rabbi Shimon?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: who are the Sages that disagree with Rabbi Shimon? If they are the Sages of the incense (ketoret) dispute, that would be a different group. The Gemara leaves this open.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana answers: People say: From a camel, its hump (the hide is valuable).

items.text: Distinction for incense
items.text_en: Distinction for incense
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes incense from other offerings because it is not subject to grazing (not a potential sacrifice).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes incense from other offerings because it is not subject to grazing (not a potential sacrifice).

items.text: Distinction for the red heifer
items.text_en: Distinction for the red heifer
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the red heifer might be different because its blood is precious, but this is rejected.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Rabbis regarding the red heifer (פרה) might also be distinguished because its blood is precious.

items.text: Analysis of the 'They said to him' Mishnah
items.text_en: Analysis of the 'They said to him' Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes whether the Mishnah's 'They said to him' reflects Rabbi Yehuda's view (with לב בית דין מתנה עליהם) or Rabbi Meir's view (all goats have equal atonement).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's 'They said to him' reflects Rabbi Yehuda's view, who holds לב בית דין מתנה עליהם (the court's intention conditions the goats), and presents the argument: according to Rabbi Yehuda, the goats are offered; according to the opponent, why should they be offered?

The Gemara alternatively suggests the Mishnah reflects Rabbi Meir's view, who holds all goats have equal atonement, and presents the parallel argument: according to Rabbi Meir, the goats are offered; according to the opponent, why should they be offered?

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's tradition
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's tradition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states a tradition: according to Rabbi Shimon, leftover goats are not redeemed; according to the Sages, they are redeemed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves that according to Rabbi Shimon the animals are not redeemed, but according to the Sages they are redeemed.

items.text: What to do with leftovers according to Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: What to do with leftovers according to Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak says in Rabbi Yochanan's name that they are used to chip the altar. Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak adds that Rabbi Shimon agrees that for sin-offering goats, only their money is used, not their bodies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is done with leftover communal offerings according to Rabbi Shimon, who rejects the principle that the court can stipulate their use in advance.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak reports in Rabbi Yochanan's name that the leftover animals are used to chip the altar (i.e., their bodies are used as fuel for the altar fire).
Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak adds that Rabbi Shimon concedes regarding sin-offering goats that only their monetary value is used for the altar, not their bodies.

items.text: Distinction between here and there
items.text_en: Distinction between here and there
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between the case of leftover goats (originally burnt-offering, now burnt-offering) and the case of sin-offering goats (originally sin-offering, now burnt-offering), where a decree is made after atonement due to before atonement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that here (the current case) the animal was originally designated as a burnt-offering (עולה) and remains so, but there (the case of sin-offerings) it was originally a sin-offering and now would be a burnt-offering, so a decree is made to prevent confusion between after-atonement and before-atonement.

items.text: Supporting baraitot for the decree
items.text_en: Supporting baraitot for the decree
items.desc_en: Abaye, Rava, and Ravina each cite a baraita (Yom Kippur bull and goat, idolatry goats, second animal, guilt-offering) to prove that a decree is made after atonement due to before atonement, preventing leftover sin-offerings from being offered as burnt-offerings.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita about the bull and goat of Yom Kippur and idolatry goats that were lost and replaced, where Rabbi Yehuda says they die and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say they graze and their proceeds go to gift offerings.
Abaye asks why the animals themselves cannot be offered as burnt-offerings, concluding that this proves a decree after atonement due to before atonement.
Rava cites a mishna about the second Yom Kippur goat that grazes until unfit and its proceeds go to gift offerings.
Rava asks why the animal itself cannot be offered as a burnt-offering, concluding that this proves a decree after atonement due to before atonement.

Ravina cites a mishna about a guilt-offering whose owner died or achieved atonement, where it grazes until unfit and its proceeds go to gift offerings, with dissenting opinions from Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua.
Ravina asks why the animal itself cannot be offered as a burnt-offering, concluding that this proves a decree after atonement due to before atonement, and the Gemara affirms the conclusion.

items.text: Question about what is brought from leftovers
items.text_en: Question about what is brought from leftovers
items.desc_en: A baraita asks what is brought from the leftover funds, introducing the next topic.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited, asking what offerings are brought from the leftover funds.

items.text: Clarification of the verse about the altar
items.text_en: Clarification of the verse about the altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a contradiction regarding the verse 'For every leaven and every honey' and resolves it by citing Rav Chanina's teaching that the verse refers to human consumption, not the altar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the verse says 'summer fruit for the altar,' but another verse forbids leaven and honey on the altar.
Rav Chanina resolves the contradiction by explaining that the verse refers to human consumption, not the altar.

items.text: Dispute about leftover bird offerings
items.text_en: Dispute about leftover bird offerings
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda rules that one does not use leftover wood for bird burnt offerings. Rava questions this, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains the ruling in the name of Rav Shimi of Nehardea, citing that leftovers go to communal donations and there are no bird burnt offerings in the community. Shmuel agrees with Rabbi Yochanan's principle that communal offerings are determined by the knife's slaughter.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda rules that one does not use leftover wood for bird burnt offerings.
Rava questions the ruling, calling it a 'blessing' (i.e., a surprising leniency).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains to Rava that the ruling comes from Rav Shimi of Nehardea: leftover wood goes to communal donations, and there are no bird burnt offerings in the community.
Shmuel agrees with Rabbi Yochanan's principle that communal offerings are determined by the knife's slaughter.

items.text: Supporting baraita about the goat's atonement
items.text_en: Supporting baraita about the goat's atonement
items.desc_en: A baraita supports the principle that a goat designated for Yom Kippur can be brought on other festivals if missed, because its sole purpose is to atone for the outer altar. Another Tanna states it was only sanctified for that purpose.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports the principle that a goat designated for Yom Kippur can be brought on other festivals if missed, because its sole purpose is to atone for the outer altar.
Another Tanna states that the goat was only sanctified for the purpose of atoning for the outer altar.

items.text: Source for the inner goat's atonement for intentional impurity
items.text_en: Source for the inner goat's atonement for intentional impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the inner goat atones for intentional impurity of the Temple and its holy things. It cites a baraita that interprets 'pesha'im' as rebellious acts and 'chata'ot' as unintentional sins, with supporting verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the inner goat atones for intentional impurity of the Temple and its holy things.
The baraita interprets 'pesha'im' as rebellious acts and 'chata'ot' as unintentional sins, citing supporting verses.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's categories of sins
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's categories of sins
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's listing of 'light and severe, intentional and unintentional' sins, noting redundancy. Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah means all sins, whether light (positive or negative commandments) or severe (karet or court-imposed death), whether done intentionally or unintentionally, and whether known or unknown.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's list of sin categories: light and severe, intentional and unintentional.
The Gemara points out redundancy: 'light' equals positive/negative commandments, 'severe' equals karet/death penalties, 'known' equals intentional, 'unknown' equals unintentional.

Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah means all sins, whether light (positive/negative commandments) or severe (karet/death penalties), whether intentional or unintentional, and for unintentional ones, whether known or unknown.

items.text: Question about the atonement for a positive commandment
items.text_en: Question about the atonement for a positive commandment
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a positive commandment can be atoned for by a sacrifice, since if one does not repent it is an abomination, and if one repents, forgiveness is immediate. Rabbi Zeira begins to address this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a positive commandment can be atoned for by a sacrifice, since if one does not repent it is an abomination, and if one repents, forgiveness is immediate.
Rabbi Zeira begins to address the question.

items.text: Rabbi's view on Yom Kippur atonement
items.text_en: Rabbi's view on Yom Kippur atonement
items.desc_en: Rabbi holds that Yom Kippur atones for all sins whether or not one repents, except for three sins: one who throws off the yoke, reveals faces in the Torah, and violates the covenant of circumcision. For these, atonement depends on repentance, as derived from the verse 'כי דבר ה' בזה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that the baraita deals with one who persists in rebellion, and it follows Rabbi's view.
A baraita cites Rabbi's position that Yom Kippur atones for all sins regardless of repentance, except for three sins where repentance is required.
The Gemara explains Rabbi's reasoning by citing a baraita that derives from the verse 'כי דבר ה' בזה' that the three sins are subject to excision before and after Yom Kippur.
The baraita resolves that if one repented, the verse 'עֲוֹנָהּ בָּהּ' teaches that atonement is withheld only when the sin remains.

items.text: Rabbis' alternative interpretation
items.text_en: Rabbis' alternative interpretation
items.desc_en: The Rabbis interpret the verses differently: 'הכרת' refers to this world, 'תכרת' to the world to come, and 'עונה בה' teaches that if one repents and dies, death completes the atonement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the Rabbis' alternative interpretation: 'הכרת' refers to this world, 'תכרת' to the World to Come, and 'עונה בה' indicates that death purges the sin if one repented.

items.text: Challenge: Is the Mishnah really Rabbi?
items.text_en: Challenge: Is the Mishnah really Rabbi?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that the Mishnah follows Rabbi, noting that the latter clause follows Rabbi Yehuda, implying the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita cannot be attributed to Rabbi, because the latter clause follows Rabbi Yehuda, implying the entire baraita is Rabbi Yehuda's.

items.text: Rav Yosef and Abaye's discussion on Rabbi and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rav Yosef and Abaye's discussion on Rabbi and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef suggests that the Mishnah is Rabbi, but he holds like Rabbi Yehuda. Abaye questions whether this means Rabbi Yehuda does not hold like Rabbi, and Rav Yosef confirms that Rabbi Yehuda does not hold like Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asserts that the Mishnah is according to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who holds like Rabbi Yehuda on this point.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether he means specifically that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds like Rabbi Yehuda but not vice versa, or that both hold like each other.
Rav Yosef confirms that he means specifically that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds like Rabbi Yehuda, but Rabbi Yehuda does not hold like Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that argues Yom Kippur only atones for penitents, using a logical comparison to sin-offerings and guilt-offerings. The baraita concludes with the word 'אך' to indicate a distinction. The Gemara notes that this anonymous baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a logical inference: since sin-offerings and guilt-offerings only atone for penitents, one might think Yom Kippur also only atones for penitents, but it notes that Yom Kippur atones for intentional sins like unwitting ones, so the comparison is flawed.
The baraita resolves the inference by citing the verse with the word 'אך' (yet), which divides and limits Yom Kippur's atonement to penitents only.
The Gemara notes that this anonymous baraita in the Sifra follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that Yom Kippur atones only for those who repent.

items.text: Contradictory baraita on Yom Kippur atonement
items.text_en: Contradictory baraita on Yom Kippur atonement
items.desc_en: Another anonymous baraita states that Yom Kippur atones even for one who did not fast or observe its sanctity, based on the verse 'יום כפורים הוא'. This contradicts the previous baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two unattributed baraitot in the Sifra: one limits atonement to penitents, while another teaches that Yom Kippur atones even without fasting or observing its sanctity.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction between baraitot
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction between baraitot
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by attributing one baraita to Rabbi and the other to Rabbi Yehuda. Rava offers an alternative: both are Rabbi, but Rabbi concedes that Yom Kippur itself imposes karet for its violation, so one who violates Yom Kippur without repentance is not atoned. The Gemara then suggests a case where this applies.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction between the two baraitot by attributing one to Rabbi and the other to Rabbi Yehuda.

Rava offers an alternative resolution: both baraitot are Rabbi, but Rabbi concedes that Yom Kippur itself imposes karet (excision) for its violation, so one who violates Yom Kippur without repentance is not atoned.
The Gemara suggests a case where this applies: one who violated Yom Kippur at night and died before daytime, so the day itself never came to atone for him.

items.text: Question about Rabbi's view on karet for Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Question about Rabbi's view on karet for Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi holds that there is no karet for Yom Kippur, and suggests cases where one might die before atonement, such as eating a half-olive bulk or close to sunset.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi holds that there is no karet (divine excision) for Yom Kippur.
The Gemara answers that one can find cases where karet applies, such as eating a half-olive bulk and choking to death, or eating close to sunset with no time for atonement.

items.text: Contradiction in the Mishnah about equality of atonement
items.text_en: Contradiction in the Mishnah about equality of atonement
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah first says Israelites, priests, and anointed priest are alike, then asks what distinguishes them. Rav Yehuda resolves this by explaining that they are alike in being atoned by the scapegoat for other transgressions, but differ regarding the bull for Temple impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Israelites, priests, and the anointed priest are alike in atonement.
The Gemara points out an internal contradiction: the Mishnah first says they are alike, then asks what distinguishes them.
Rav Yehuda resolves the contradiction: they are alike in being atoned by the scapegoat for other transgressions, but differ regarding the bull for Temple impurity.

items.text: Attribution to Rabbi Yehuda and his baraita
items.text_en: Attribution to Rabbi Yehuda and his baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Yehuda, citing a baraita where he derives from verses that all groups are equal in being atoned by the scapegoat for other transgressions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Yehuda, citing a baraita where he derives from verses that all groups are equal in being atoned by the scapegoat for other transgressions.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's view and the meaning of 'equal'
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's view and the meaning of 'equal'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon argues that the inner goat atones for Israelites' Temple impurity, and the bull for priests, while the scapegoat atones for Israelites' other transgressions and the bull's confession for priests. The Gemara clarifies that for Rabbi Shimon, 'equal' means they are all eligible for atonement, but each has its own mechanism.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that the inner goat's blood atones for Israelites' Temple impurity and the bull's blood for priests, and the scapegoat's confession atones for Israelites' other transgressions and the bull's confession for priests.
The Gemara asks: According to Rabbi Shimon, they are surely 'equal' — what does 'equal' mean?
The Gemara answers: 'Equal' means they are all eligible for atonement, but each atones in its own way.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's scriptural basis and Rabbi Yehuda's response
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's scriptural basis and Rabbi Yehuda's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon derives from the juxtaposition of the two goats that the scapegoat does not atone for priests, just as the inner goat does not. Rabbi Yehuda counters that the juxtaposition is only for physical similarity (appearance, height, value).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural basis of Rabbi Shimon's position that the scapegoat does not atone for priests.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon derives from the juxtaposition of the two goats (שְׂעִירִם) that the scapegoat, like the inner goat, does not atone for priests.
Rabbi Yehuda objects that the juxtaposition is only to require the two goats to be similar in appearance, height, and value, not to extend the atonement limitation.

items.text: Baraita on priests' atonement and its reasoning
items.text_en: Baraita on priests' atonement and its reasoning
items.desc_en: A baraita states that priests are not atoned by the inner goat but by Aaron's bull. It considers the possibility that they might not be atoned at all, but a verse shows they are. It then argues that Aaron's bull is preferable because it was permitted for his household, unlike the inner goat.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'וְשָׁחַט אֶת שְׂעִיר הַחַטָּאת אֲשֶׁר לָעָם' to show that priests are not atoned by the inner goat but by Aaron's bull.
The baraita raises the possibility that priests might not be atoned by Aaron's bull either, since the verse says 'אֲשֶׁר לוֹ' (which is for him), leaving them without atonement.
The baraita resolves that the verse 'יְכַפֵּר עַל הַכֹּהֲנִים' (he shall atone for the priests) provides them with atonement.
The baraita argues that Aaron's bull is preferable for atonement because it was permitted for his household, unlike the inner goat which was not permitted for his household.
The baraita cites the verse 'בֵּית אַהֲרֹן בָּרְכוּ אֶת ה׳, בֵּית הַלֵּוִי בָּרְכוּ אֶת ה׳, יִרְאֵי ה׳ בָּרְכוּ אֶת ה׳' as additional support.

items.text: Attribution of the baraita to Rabbi Shimon or Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Attribution of the baraita to Rabbi Shimon or Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya says the baraita is not like Rabbi Yehuda, who holds priests have atonement via the scapegoat. Rava says it is Rabbi Shimon. Abaye argues it could even be Rabbi Yehuda, interpreting the baraita as referring to Temple impurity, not other transgressions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the baraita.
Rabbi Yirmeya says the baraita is not like Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that priests have atonement via the scapegoat.
Rava says the baraita is Rabbi Shimon, who holds that priests have no atonement via the scapegoat.
Abaye argues that the baraita could even be Rabbi Yehuda, interpreting it as referring to Temple impurity, not other transgressions.

items.text: Opening baraita: why the bull of Aaron atones for all, not the inner goat
items.text_en: Opening baraita: why the bull of Aaron atones for all, not the inner goat
items.desc_en: The baraita states that for impurity of the Temple and its sancta, it is better that they be atoned by the bull of Aaron, which was permitted in part for his household, rather than by the inner goat, which was not permitted at all. The Gemara then explains the phrase 'if you wish to say' by citing a verse that all Israel are called 'his household'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by asking how impurity of the Temple and its sancta is atoned, and answers that it is better to atone with Aaron's bull, which was partially permitted for his household, than with the inner goat, which was not permitted at all.
The baraita cites a verse (Psalms 135:19) to support the claim that all Israel are called Aaron's household.

The Gemara explains the baraita's phrase 'if you wish to say' by clarifying that although the verse says 'his household,' all Israel are called 'his household,' as the verse includes 'fearers of the Lord.'

items.text: Derivation of 'which is for the people' and 'which is for him'
items.text_en: Derivation of 'which is for the people' and 'which is for him'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the necessity of the phrase 'which is for the people' (אשר לעם), and answers that it teaches the goat must come from the people. It then questions 'which is for him' (אשר לו), and explains through a baraita that it teaches the high priest brings from his own property, not from the community or his fellow priests, and that if he brought from others it is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the phrase 'אשר לעם' (which is for the people) is needed only to teach that the goat comes from the people.
The Gemara answers that this requirement is already derived from the verse 'ומאת עדת בני ישראל' (and from the congregation of the children of Israel).
The Gemara questions whether the phrase 'אשר לו' (which is for him) is needed only for that purpose.

The Gemara cites a baraita that teaches 'אשר לו' indicates the high priest brings from his own property, not from the community or his fellow priests, and that if he brought from others it is invalid.

items.text: The Tanna's difficulty: why the bull atones for all
items.text_en: The Tanna's difficulty: why the bull atones for all
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the Tanna's underlying question: why is the bull of Aaron different from the inner goat? Both involve no monetary loss to the people, yet the bull atones for all. The answer is that all are called 'his household'.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna raises a difficulty: why does the bull of Aaron atone for all, when the inner goat does not, given that both involve no monetary loss to the people?
The Gemara answers that all Israelites are called 'his household' (ביתו), so the bull atones for all.

items.text: The two confessions of the bull: Rabbi Shimon vs. Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: The two confessions of the bull: Rabbi Shimon vs. Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Shimon, the two confessions and blood of the bull correspond to the inner goat, outer goat, and the scapegoat. But according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds the bull atones only for the high priest and his household, why are two confessions needed? One is for him and one for his household, as per the school of Rabbi Yishmael: it is better that a meritorious person atone for a guilty one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Shimon, the two confessions and blood of the bull correspond to the inner goat, outer goat, and scapegoat.
The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehuda, who holds the bull atones only for the high priest and his household, needs two confessions and blood of the bull.

The Gemara answers that one confession is for the high priest himself and one for his household, citing the school of Rabbi Yishmael that it is better for a meritorious person to atone for a guilty one.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter: 'We return to you, Shevuot two'
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter: 'We return to you, Shevuot two'
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous chapter with the standard formula 'Hadran alach Shevuot shtayim' (we return to you, two oaths).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous chapter with the standard formula 'Hadran alach Shevuot shtayim' (we return to you, two oaths).

items.text: Mishnah: The four cases of awareness of impurity
items.text_en: Mishnah: The four cases of awareness of impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins a new chapter: 'Awarenesses of impurity are two which are four.' It lists the cases: one who became impure and knew, then forgot the impurity but remembered the sanctity; forgot the sanctity but remembered the impurity; forgot both; and then ate sanctified food or entered the Temple. It also discusses the addition to the city and courtyards, requiring a king, prophet, Urim and Thummim, and Sanhedrin.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that awarenesses of impurity are two which are four, and lists the first case: one who became impure and knew, then forgot the impurity but remembered the sanctity.
The Mishnah lists the second case: one who forgot the sanctity but remembered the impurity.
The Mishnah lists the third case: one who forgot both the impurity and the sanctity.
The Mishnah states that in these cases, if one ate sanctified food without knowing and later knew, he brings a sliding-scale offering (עולה ויורד).
The Mishnah lists the parallel cases for entering the Temple: one who became impure and knew, then forgot the impurity but remembered the Temple.
The Mishnah lists the second Temple case: one who forgot the Temple but remembered the impurity.
The Mishnah lists the third Temple case: one who forgot both the impurity and the Temple.
The Mishnah states that in these Temple cases, if one entered without knowing and later knew, he brings a sliding-scale offering.
The Mishnah rules that one who enters the Temple courtyard and one who enters its addition are treated alike.
The Mishnah explains that the addition to the city and courtyards requires a king, prophet, Urim and Thummim, Sanhedrin of seventy-one, two thanksgiving offerings, and song.
The Mishnah concludes by describing the procession: the court walks, the two thanksgiving offerings follow, and all of Israel follows them.

items.text: Conclusion of Mishnah: cases of entering the Temple in impurity
items.text_en: Conclusion of Mishnah: cases of entering the Temple in impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where one is liable for entering the Temple in impurity, and specifies that the positive commandment of the Temple (to build it) is not subject to liability for entering in impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes its list of cases of entering the Temple in impurity, stating that the positive commandment of the Temple is not subject to liability.

items.text: Positive commandment in Niddah
items.text_en: Positive commandment in Niddah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah asks which positive commandment in Niddah incurs liability, answering that if a man separates immediately when his wife says she became impure, he is liable because his departure is as pleasurable as his entry.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah asks which positive commandment in Niddah incurs liability.
The Mishnah answers that if a man separates immediately when his wife says she became impure, he is liable because his departure is as pleasurable as his entry.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on liability for forgetfulness of Temple vs. impurity
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on liability for forgetfulness of Temple vs. impurity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Yishmael debate which forgetfulness (of impurity or of the Temple) renders one liable for a sin-offering, based on the verse's repetition of 'ונעלם'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer derives from the verse that one is liable only for forgetfulness of the carcass (שרץ), not for forgetfulness of the Temple.
Rabbi Akiva derives from the verse that one is liable only for forgetfulness of impurity, not for forgetfulness of the Temple.
Rabbi Yishmael derives from the double occurrence of 'ונעלם' that one is liable for forgetfulness of both impurity and the Temple.

items.text: Gemara's question on the number of 'awarenesses' (ידיעות)
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the number of 'awarenesses' (ידיעות)
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Abaye that the Mishnah's 'two that are four' should be 'two that are six', counting awarenesses of impurity, sacred food, and the Temple. The Gemara resolves that only awarenesses that lead to a sacrifice are counted, with two versions of Rav Pappa's answer.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Abaye that the Mishnah's 'two that are four' should be 'two that are six', counting awarenesses of impurity, sacred food, and the Temple.
Abaye objects that according to Rav Pappa's reasoning there should be eight awarenesses, since impurity regarding sacred food and impurity regarding the Temple are distinct.
Rav Pappa rejects the objection, arguing that impurity is a single category, so the count remains six.

sub.text: First version of Rav Pappa's answer
sub.text_en: First version of Rav Pappa's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves that there are eight awarenesses, but the Mishnah counts only the last four that lead to a sacrifice, not the first four.

sub.text: Second version of Rav Pappa's answer
sub.text_en: Second version of Rav Pappa's answer
sub.desc_en: An alternative version: Rav Pappa says the Mishnah counts the first four awarenesses, which are unique to this case, and does not count the last four, which are found throughout the Torah.

items.text: Rav Pappa's query: ignorance of halakhot of impurity
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's query: ignorance of halakhot of impurity
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether one who knows that a dead creeping animal is impure but does not know that a lentil-sized piece conveys impurity is considered aware or unaware. The Gemara leaves it unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa raises a dilemma: if the halakhot of impurity were hidden from a person, what is the law? The Gemara clarifies that if he does not know basic facts like whether a שרץ (creeping animal) is impure, that is not a valid case.
The Gemara refines the case: he knows that a שרץ (creeping animal) is impure but does not know that a lentil-sized piece conveys impurity. The dilemma is left unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's query: Babylonian who forgot the Temple's location
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's query: Babylonian who forgot the Temple's location
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks about a Babylonian who ascended to Israel and forgot the Temple's location. The Gemara clarifies the dispute is according to Rabbi (who requires initial awareness and holds that knowing of the Temple's existence suffices), but leaves the question unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks about a Babylonian who ascended to Israel and forgot the Temple's location, whether he is liable.
The Gemara objects that the query is irrelevant according to Rabbi Akiva (who does not hold one liable for forgetting the Temple) and Rabbi Yishmael (who does not require initial awareness).
The Gemara clarifies the query is according to Rabbi, who requires initial awareness and holds that knowing of the Temple's existence suffices, but leaves the question unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Source for the Mishnah's list of Temple areas
items.text_en: Source for the Mishnah's list of Temple areas
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Chiyya cites a verse to derive the Mishnah's ruling that one is liable for entering the Temple's courtyard and its vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's ruling that one is liable for entering the Temple courtyard and its vessels.
Rav Shimi bar Chiyya cites the verse 'כְּכׇל אֲשֶׁר אֲנִי מַרְאֶה אוֹתְךָ, אֵת תַּבְנִית הַמִּשְׁכָּן וְאֵת תַּבְנִית כׇּל כֵּלָיו' as the source for the Mishnah's list of Temple areas.

items.text: Dedication of vessels: anointing vs. service
items.text_en: Dedication of vessels: anointing vs. service
items.desc_en: Rava challenges the idea that 'and thus you shall do' applies for all generations, citing that Moses' vessels were sanctified by anointing, but later ones by service. The Gemara resolves with a verse limiting anointing to those vessels, and Rav Papa adds another verse linking sanctification to service.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the verse 'וְכֵן תַּעֲשׂוּ' (and so shall you do) to teach that the Tabernacle's construction applies for all generations.

Rava objects by citing a baraita that Moses' vessels were consecrated by anointing, but later ones by service, and questions why the phrase 'וְכֵן תַּעֲשׂוּ' (and so shall you do) does not require anointing for all generations.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'וַיִּמְשָׁחֵם וַיְקַדֵּשׁ אֹתָם' (and he anointed them and consecrated them) limits anointing to those vessels, not to future generations.
The Gemara questions why future generations could not be consecrated either through anointing or through service.
Rav Papa answers by citing the verse 'אֲשֶׁר יְשָׁרְתוּ בָם בַּקֹּדֶשׁ' (with which they will serve in the Sanctuary), which makes sanctification dependent on service.
The Gemara resolves that the term 'אוֹתָם' (them) excludes future generations from anointing, so they are consecrated only through service.

items.text: The two thanksgiving loaves: bread, not meat
items.text_en: The two thanksgiving loaves: bread, not meat
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the two thanksgiving loaves mentioned in Nehemiah were brought with their bread but not their meat. Rav Chisda derives this from the verse. The Gemara clarifies that 'great' refers to the largest type of thanksgiving offering, which is leavened bread, and details the quantities involved.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that the two thanks-offerings mentioned in the mishna refer to their loaves, not their flesh.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of this teaching.
Rav Chisda cites the verse from Nehemiah about two large thanks-offerings to derive the source.
The Gemara asks what 'large' means in the verse.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that 'large' means a large species like oxen, since the verse would have explicitly said 'oxen'.
The Gemara concludes that 'large' means the largest and finest of their species.
The Gemara objects that size is irrelevant before Heaven, citing a mishna that one who brings much or little is equal if his heart is directed to Heaven.
The Gemara resolves that 'large' refers to the larger element in the thanks-offering loaves, i.e., the leavened bread, and details the quantities of flour and types of loaves.

items.text: Sanctification of the courtyard: analogy to Jerusalem
items.text_en: Sanctification of the courtyard: analogy to Jerusalem
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama states that the courtyard is sanctified only by the remnants of meal offerings, drawing an analogy to Jerusalem: just as Jerusalem is sanctified by what is eaten within it and becomes invalid when removed, so too the courtyard. The Gemara questions whether leavened bread could be used, but notes that leavened meal offerings do not exist.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama states that the courtyard is sanctified only by the remnants of meal offerings, drawing an analogy to Jerusalem where what is eaten within sanctifies it.
The Gemara objects that the bread of the thanksgiving offering is also eaten in the courtyard, so the analogy must be refined: just as Jerusalem invalidates food that leaves it, so too the courtyard.
The Gemara questions whether leavened bread could be used for sanctification, but immediately rejects the possibility since there is no leavened meal offering.

items.text: Impossibility of building the hearth on Shavuot
items.text_en: Impossibility of building the hearth on Shavuot
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers various ways to build the hearth for the two loaves on Shavuot when it coincides with Shabbat, but each is rejected: leavening the remnants is forbidden, building on Yom Tov is not permitted, building beforehand and sanctifying later fails because sanctification must be at the time of building, and building at night is prohibited as derived from the verse about the Tabernacle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the possibility of leavening the remnants and sanctifying them, but rejects it based on the verse forbidding leavening even the priests' portion.
Reish Lakish states that even the priests' portion of the two loaves cannot be baked as leaven.
The Gemara asks why it is impossible, and answers that sanctification of the two loaves occurs at the time of the lamb slaughter, making prior sanctification ineffective.
The Gemara considers building the hearth yesterday and sanctifying yesterday, but notes that the two loaves are sanctified only at the slaughter of the accompanying lambs.
The Gemara suggests building yesterday and sanctifying today, but rejects it because sanctification must occur at the time of building.
The Gemara considers building on Yom Tov and sanctifying on Yom Tov, but notes that building the Temple does not override Yom Tov.
The Gemara suggests building and sanctifying later, but rejects it because the loaves would become invalid due to overnight stay (לינה).
The Gemara proposes building on the eve of the festival, leaving a small part, and completing it at nightfall, but this is rejected.
Abaye cites the verse 'וביום הקים את המשכן' (on the day the Tabernacle was erected) to prove that Temple building cannot be done at night.
The Gemara concludes that it is impossible to build the hearth for the two loaves on Shavuot when it coincides with Shabbat.

items.text: The song of thanksgiving and the song of plagues
items.text_en: The song of thanksgiving and the song of plagues
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the song of thanksgiving sung with instruments on every corner and great stone in Jerusalem, and mentions the song of plagues (or afflictions). The two opinions are explained: one derives 'plagues' from a verse about no plague approaching, the other derives 'afflictions' from a verse about a thousand falling. The verses recited are then listed.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the song of thanksgiving (שיר של תודה) and the song of plagues (שיר של פגעים) or afflictions (שיר של נגעים), listing the instruments and locations.

The first opinion derives 'afflictions' (נגעים) from the verse 'no plague shall come near your tent', while the second opinion derives 'plagues' (פגעים) from the verse 'a thousand shall fall at your side'.
The baraita lists the verses recited in the song: Psalm 91 and Psalm 3, concluding with 'to the Lord is salvation, upon Your people is Your blessing, Selah'.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi recites verses for protection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi recites verses for protection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi would recite these verses and sleep. The Gemara questions this because he himself said it is forbidden to heal with words of Torah. The answer distinguishes between healing (forbidden) and protection (permitted). The Gemara further clarifies that the prohibition applies only when spitting is involved, as per Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi would recite these verses and then sleep.
The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi could do this, since he himself said it is forbidden to heal with words of Torah.
The Gemara answers that protection (הגנה) is different from healing, and is permitted.
The Gemara objects that the prohibition applies only when there is a wound, citing a baraita that one who whispers over a wound has no share in the World to Come.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the prohibition applies only when spitting is involved, because one may not mention God's name over spittle.

items.text: The procession of the two loaves and their arrangement
items.text_en: The procession of the two loaves and their arrangement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the court walks with two loaves of thanksgiving behind them. The Gemara questions whether the court walks before the loaves, citing a verse that suggests otherwise, and clarifies that the court walks behind them. A dispute between Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi arises: one says the loaves are side by side, the other says one after the other. The Gemara then examines the implications for which loaf is eaten and which is burned, and resolves the difficulty by citing Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the court walks with two loaves of thanksgiving behind them.
The Gemara questions whether the court walks before the loaves, citing a verse that suggests otherwise.
The Gemara clarifies that the court walks behind the loaves, citing a verse where the leaders walk after the thanksgiving offerings.
The Gemara asks how the two loaves are arranged in the procession.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi dispute: one says the loaves are side by side, the other says one after the other, and each explains which loaf is called 'inner'.

The Gemara objects: according to the Mishnah, the inner loaf is eaten and the outer burned; according to the side-by-side view, both loaves sanctify each other simultaneously, so why is only one eaten?
The Gemara counters: even according to the one-after-the-other view, how can one loaf sanctify the other, since the Mishnah requires all the loaves for the rite, and both are part of one mitzvah?
Rabbi Yochanan begins to resolve the difficulty, though the resolution is cut off at the section boundary.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a burnt-offering is eaten or burned based on a prophet's instruction, and that any offering not prepared with all these elements is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a burnt-offering is eaten or burned based on a prophet's instruction.

items.text: Amoraic dispute on the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Amoraic dispute on the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Nachman dispute whether the Mishnah says 'with all these' or 'with any one of these', reflecting their views on whether the original sanctification sanctified for the future.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute: Rav Huna says the Mishnah reads 'with all these,' while Rav Nachman says it reads 'with any one of these.'
Rav Huna holds that the first sanctification sanctified both for its time and for the future, so Ezra's actions were merely a memorial.
Rav Nachman holds that the first sanctification sanctified only for its time, so Ezra truly sanctified even without Urim and Thummim.

items.text: Rava's objection to Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Rava's objection to Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Rava cites the Mishnah which explicitly says 'with all these', challenging Rav Nachman's version.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Rav Nachman by citing the Mishnah which reads 'with all these,' but Rav Nachman responds that it teaches 'with any one of these.'

items.text: Baraita of Abba Shaul on the two chambers
items.text_en: Baraita of Abba Shaul on the two chambers
items.desc_en: Abba Shaul describes two chambers on the Mount of Olives: the lower one sanctified with all these, the upper one only by the returnees from exile, without a king or Urim and Thummim. The Gemara questions why they sanctified the upper one if not fully sanctified, and answers it was for practical access to Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita of Abba Shaul describing two chambers on the Mount of Anointment, where the lower was sanctified with all these elements and the upper only with burnt-offerings of the exile, without a king or Urim and Thummim.

sub.text: Baraita details on the lower chamber
sub.text_en: Baraita details on the lower chamber
sub.desc_en: The baraita explains that in the lower chamber with complete sanctity, common people enter and eat lesser holy offerings but not second tithe, while associates eat both.

sub.text: Baraita details on the upper chamber
sub.text_en: Baraita details on the upper chamber
sub.desc_en: The baraita explains that in the upper chamber without complete sanctity, common people enter and eat lesser holy offerings but not second tithe, while associates eat neither; the reason they did not sanctify it is that additions to the city and courtyards require a king, prophet, Urim and Thummim, Sanhedrin, two thanks-offerings, and song.

The Gemara clarifies that the question is not why they sanctified it (since they did not), but why they included it in the city — because it was a slope of Jerusalem and convenient for conquest from there.
The Gemara answers that they included the upper chamber within the sanctified area because it was a strategic vantage point of Jerusalem, convenient for conquering the city from there.

items.text: Tannaic dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Tannaic dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer says they made curtains for the Temple and courtyards when building, while Rabbi Yehoshua says sacrifices and eating of holy things are permitted even without a building, because the first sanctification sanctified for the future. The Gemara infers that Rabbi Eliezer holds it did not sanctify for the future.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tannaic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says that when building the Temple, they made curtains for the sanctuary and courtyards, building the sanctuary from outside and the courtyards from inside.

Rabbi Yehoshua says that offerings are brought even without a Temple, holy of holies eaten without curtains, and lesser holy offerings and second tithe without a wall, because the first sanctification sanctified both for its time and for the future; the Gemara infers that Rabbi Eliezer holds it did not sanctify for the future.
The Gemara infers from Rabbi Yehoshua's statement that Rabbi Eliezer must hold that the first sanctification did not sanctify for the future.

items.text: Ravina's rejection of the inference
items.text_en: Ravina's rejection of the inference
items.desc_en: Ravina suggests that both Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua may agree that the first sanctification sanctified for the future, and each merely reports what he heard; the curtains were only for modesty.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects to Rav Ashi that perhaps everyone agrees the first sanctification sanctified for both times, and each Tanna merely reports what he heard; the curtains for Rabbi Eliezer are only for modesty.

items.text: Contradiction in Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei's statements
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei's statements
items.desc_en: Two baraitot attributed to Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei contradict each other: one says the first sanctification did not sanctify for the future, the other says it did. The Gemara resolves by suggesting two different Tannaim or that one is actually Rabbi Elazar bar Yosei.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei explains that the sages listed only certain cities because the returnees found and sanctified them, implying the first sanctification did not sanctify for the future.

The Gemara raises a contradiction by citing another baraita where Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei says the sages merely counted the cities, not sanctified them, implying the first sanctification did sanctify for the future.
The second baraita explicitly states that the first sanctification sanctified both for its time and for the future, sharpening the contradiction.
The Gemara explicitly states the contradiction: Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei's own statements conflict.
The Gemara offers a first resolution: the two baraitot represent two different Tannaim who both transmit in the name of Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei.

The Gemara offers a second resolution: one of the baraitot is actually from Rabbi Elazar bar Yosei, not Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei, as supported by a baraita where Rabbi Elazar bar Yosei interprets the verse 'which had no wall' to include cities that once had a wall.

items.text: Derivation of impurity in the courtyard
items.text_en: Derivation of impurity in the courtyard
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives the source for impurity in the Temple courtyard from the two verses 'et Mishkan Hashem time' and 'ki et Mikdash Hashem time', arguing that if the verse is not needed for impurity outside, apply it to impurity inside.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the case of one who became impure in the Temple courtyard and forgot about the impurity.
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive the source for impurity in the courtyard?
Rabbi Elazar answers: One verse says 'et Mishkan Hashem time' and another says 'ki et Mikdash Hashem time'; if the verse is not needed for impurity outside, apply it to impurity inside.

items.text: The necessity of both verses
items.text_en: The necessity of both verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verses are superfluous, citing a baraita where Rabbi Elazar explains that each verse is needed: 'Mishkan' teaches liability for the Tabernacle (anointed with oil), and 'Mikdash' for the Temple (eternal sanctity). The Gemara then clarifies that Rabbi Elazar's real difficulty is that since both terms are interchangeable, why write both? This teaches two things.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the two verses are superfluous, given that a baraita shows they are both needed.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Elazar explains that each verse is needed: 'Mishkan' teaches liability for the Tabernacle (anointed with oil), and 'Mikdash' for the Temple (eternal sanctity).
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Elazar's real difficulty is that since both terms are interchangeable, why write both? This teaches two things.

items.text: Proof that Mishkan is called Mikdash
items.text_en: Proof that Mishkan is called Mikdash
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks a source that the Tabernacle is called 'Mikdash', rejecting a proof from the Ark, and instead citing the verse 've'asu li Mikdash' alongside 'tavnit haMishkan'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: It is understandable that the Temple is called Mishkan (Tabernacle), but from where do we derive that the Mishkan is called Mikdash (Sanctuary)?
The Gemara rejects a proposed proof from the verse 'and the Kohathites carrying the Mikdash shall journey', noting that this refers specifically to the Ark, not the Mishkan.

The Gemara provides the correct proof: the verse 've'asu li Mikdash' (make Me a Sanctuary) is immediately followed by 'tavnit haMishkan' (the pattern of the Tabernacle), showing that the Mishkan is called Mikdash.

items.text: Rava's distinction: bowing inward vs. outward
items.text_en: Rava's distinction: bowing inward vs. outward
items.desc_en: Rava states that the Mishnah's ruling (liable for bowing or pausing) applies only when bowing toward the inside; if bowing outward, one is liable only if they paused.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one is liable for bowing or pausing the duration of bowing in the Temple.
Rava distinguishes: the Mishnah's liability for bowing applies only when bowing inward; bowing outward requires a pause to be liable.

items.text: Alternative version: bowing outward requires pause
items.text_en: Alternative version: bowing outward requires pause
items.desc_en: Some teach Rava's statement on the latter clause: bowing itself requires a pause; Rava says this applies when bowing outward, but inward bowing is liable even without pause.

sub.desc_en: Introduces an alternative version that teaches Rava's statement on the latter clause of the Mishnah, implying that bowing itself requires a pause.
Rava clarifies that the rule applies only when bowing outward, but inward bowing is liable even without a pause.

items.text: Definition of bowing with and without pause
items.text_en: Definition of bowing with and without pause
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies: bowing without pause is a mere bending, while bowing with pause is the spreading of hands and feet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what constitutes bowing with a pause and bowing without a pause?
The Gemara answers: bowing without a pause is mere bending, while bowing with a pause is the spreading of hands and feet.

items.text: Dispute on the measure of pause
items.text_en: Dispute on the measure of pause
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani and Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi (or variants) dispute the measure of the pause: one says like the recitation of a verse, the other says from 'vayichre'u' to the end of the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the measure of the pause (שהייה) required for liability?

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani and Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi (or variants)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani and Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi (or variants)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute between Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani and Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi (or variants) regarding the measure of the pause: one says it is like the recitation of a verse, the other says from 'וַיִכְרְעוּ' to the end of the verse.
The Gemara cites the full verse from Chronicles (II Chron. 7:3) that describes the prostration, providing the scriptural basis for the measure of the pause.

items.text: Definitions of kiddah, kri'ah, and hishtachava'ah
items.text_en: Definitions of kiddah, kri'ah, and hishtachava'ah
items.desc_en: A baraita defines: kiddah is on the face, kri'ah on the knees, and hishtachava'ah is the spreading of hands and feet, with scriptural proofs.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines three forms of prostration: קידה (kiddah) on the face, כריעה (kri'ah) on the knees, and השתחוואה (hishtachava'ah) with spread hands and feet, each with a scriptural proof.

items.text: Rava's query: pause required for lashes?
items.text_en: Rava's query: pause required for lashes?
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether a pause is required for lashes (as opposed to a sacrifice), and the Gemara leaves the question unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether a pause (שהייה) is required for lashes (מלקות) as it is for a sacrifice, and the Gemara leaves the question unresolved.

items.text: First inquiry: whether שהייה applies equally to korban and malkut
items.text_en: First inquiry: whether שהייה applies equally to korban and malkut
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether the tradition of שהייה (waiting) for liability applies only to cases involving a korban or also to cases involving malkut. The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether the tradition of שהייה (waiting) for liability applies equally to cases involving a korban and to cases involving malkut, and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Second inquiry: whether שהייה applies to one who hangs in the air of the azara
items.text_en: Second inquiry: whether שהייה applies to one who hangs in the air of the azara
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether the tradition of שהייה applies only to one who is capable of prostration (בת השתחוואה) or also to one who is not. The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether the tradition of שהייה applies to someone suspended in the air of the Temple courtyard, who is not capable of prostration, and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).
Rava raises the alternative possibility that the tradition of שהייה applies to anyone inside the azara, regardless of capacity for prostration.
The gemara declares the question unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Third inquiry: whether שהייה applies to one who defiles himself intentionally
