items.text_en: Third inquiry: whether שהייה applies to one who defiles himself intentionally
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether the tradition of שהייה applies only to an unintentional case (אונס) or also to an intentional case (מזיד). The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether the tradition of שהייה applies to one who deliberately defiles himself, or only to one who is forced, and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Fourth inquiry: whether a nazir in a grave requires שהייה for malkut
items.text_en: Fourth inquiry: whether a nazir in a grave requires שהייה for malkut
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether the tradition of שהייה applies only to the Temple (פנים) or also to outside (חוץ), such as a nazir who enters a grave. The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether a nazirite who enters a grave requires שהייה (waiting) for liability to malkut, or whether the tradition applies only inside the Temple, and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).
The Gemara presents the two sides of the question and concludes with תיקו (the question stands unresolved).

items.text: Definition of 'short path' (קצרה)
items.text_en: Definition of 'short path' (קצרה)
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the 'short path' (קצרה) mentioned in the Mishnah includes even a path as short as the length from heel to toe, and even if one takes the entire day to traverse it.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the Mishnah rule that one who enters via the long path is liable, via the short path is exempt, and Rava adds that 'short path' includes even the distance from heel to toe, even if it takes all day.

items.text: Inquiry: whether multiple שהיות combine
items.text_en: Inquiry: whether multiple שהיות combine
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether multiple separate instances of שהייה combine to form the required duration. The Gemara notes that this is not resolved by Rava's own earlier statement, since there he spoke of a case without any שהייה.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether multiple periods of שהייה (waiting) combine to form the required duration, and the gemara notes that the answer can be derived from Rava's own statement, but distinguishes that case where there was no waiting.
The Gemara objects that Rava could resolve his own question from his earlier statement.
The Gemara resolves that Rava's earlier statement dealt with a case without any שהייה, so it does not resolve the current question.

items.text: Inquiry: whether one who takes a long path of short duration is liable
items.text_en: Inquiry: whether one who takes a long path of short duration is liable
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabba whether one who takes a long path (ארכה) but traverses it in the time of a short path (קצרה) is liable. Rabba answers that the long path was not given to be set aside for him (i.e., it is considered a short path).

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah whether one who enters via the long path but only stays the short-path duration is liable, and Rabbah answers that the long path was not given to be dismissed for him, meaning he is liable.
Rabba answers that the long path was not given to be set aside for him, meaning it is considered a short path and he is liable.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding a tamei who serves
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding a tamei who serves
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges: how can a tamei person who serves be liable to death (מיתה) if he either did not wait (שהייה) and cannot serve, or waited and is liable to karet? The Gemara resolves that he can force himself into a short path and serve, thus being liable for the short duration.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects that if a tamei (ritually impure) priest serves, he is liable to death; but if he did not wait, how could he serve, and if he waited, he would be liable to karet; the gemara resolves that he forced himself into a short path and performed the service.
The Gemara resolves that the case is where he forces himself into a short path (קצרה) and serves, thus being liable for the short duration without waiting.

items.text: Gemara's question and Abaye's answer about a zar who performs service
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Abaye's answer about a zar who performs service
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a zar can be liable for service if the tradition requires precise performance. Abaye answers with a case where the zar turned the meat with a spit, citing Rav Huna that such an act is liable. The Gemara then clarifies that this applies only when the turning speeds up the cooking, teaching that any act that brings the service closer is considered service.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a zar can be liable for service if the tradition requires precise performance.
Abaye answers with a case where the zar turned the meat with a spit, citing Rav Huna that such an act is liable.

sub.text: Gemara's question on Rav Huna's statement
sub.text_en: Gemara's question on Rav Huna's statement
sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the circumstances of Rav Huna's ruling, asking what act is performed if the meat would cook anyway.
The Gemara clarifies that the ruling applies when the turning speeds up the cooking, teaching that any act that brings the service closer is considered service.

items.text: Rabbi Oshaya's teaching on entering a leprous house through the back
items.text_en: Rabbi Oshaya's teaching on entering a leprous house through the back
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya states that one who enters a leprous house through the back, even if only his nose enters, remains pure, as the Torah only forbids entry through the normal entrance. Rava objects that if so, even entering entirely through the back should be pure, but he argues that such entry is no worse than vessels in the house, which become impure.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya introduces his teaching with hesitation, stating that one who enters a leprous house (בית המנוגע) through the back, even if only his nose enters, remains pure, because the Torah only forbids entry דרך ביאה (through the normal entrance).
Rava objects: if the rule is that only entry through the normal entrance is forbidden, then even entering entirely through the back should be pure.

Rava answers that entering entirely through the back is no worse than vessels in the house (כלים שבבית), which become impure, as the verse says 'וְלֹא יִטְמָא כׇּל אֲשֶׁר בַּבָּיִת' (and everything in the house shall be impure).

items.text: Supporting baraita about roofs and entry to the Temple
items.text_en: Supporting baraita about roofs and entry to the Temple
items.desc_en: A baraita supports the principle that entry through an unusual path (like roofs) does not render one liable for entering the Temple, as the verse says 'to the Temple' implying the normal way of entry.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports the principle that entry through roofs does not render one liable for entering the Temple, citing the verse 'to the Temple' to show that only the normal way of entry is prohibited.

items.text: Mishnah analysis: positive commandment in the Temple vs. niddah
items.text_en: Mishnah analysis: positive commandment in the Temple vs. niddah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's statement 'this is the positive commandment in the Temple for which one is not liable,' contrasting it with the positive commandment in niddah for which one is liable. The example given is a man who was with a pure woman and she said she became impure; he must separate immediately, and his departure is as pleasurable as his entry, making him liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: to what context does the Mishnah's phrase 'this is the positive commandment in the Temple for which one is not liable' refer, and explains that it refers to the earlier statement that one is not liable for a positive or negative commandment in the Temple and does not bring a provisional guilt-offering.
The Mishnah contrasts the Temple case with niddah, where one is liable for a positive or negative commandment and brings a provisional guilt-offering.
The Mishnah provides the example of a man who was with a pure woman and she said she became impure; he must separate immediately, and his departure is as pleasurable as his entry, making him liable.

items.text: Debate on liability for two transgressions in niddah case
items.text_en: Debate on liability for two transgressions in niddah case
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava both rule that one is liable for two transgressions: one for entry and one for separation. Rabba questions this, arguing that if the woman was close to her expected period and the man is a Torah scholar, he might be liable for entry (thinking he can cohabit), but why should he be liable for separation if he deliberately withdraws?

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Abaye in the name of Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav, and likewise Rava in the name of Rav Shmuel bar Sheba in the name of Rav Huna, both rule that one is liable for two transgressions in the niddah case: one for entry and one for separation.

Rabba challenges the ruling: if the case involves a woman close to her expected period (סמוך לוסתה) and the man is a Torah scholar (תלמיד חכם), then liability for entry makes sense (he thought he could cohabit), but why should he be liable for separation if he deliberately withdraws (מזיד הוא)?

items.text: Rava's initial objection: if close to her period, both cases are one act
items.text_en: Rava's initial objection: if close to her period, both cases are one act
items.desc_en: Rava argues that if the case is close to the woman's expected period (samukh l'vestah), then both entering and withdrawing are part of a single act of eating two olive-sized portions of forbidden fat in one lapse of awareness, so the Mishnah's distinction is unnecessary. He then considers the alternative: if not close to her period, and the man is a Torah scholar, he is exempt for entering (due to duress) but liable for withdrawing (intentional); if an ignoramus, he is liable only for withdrawing.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that if the case is close to her period (סמוך לוסתה), both entering and withdrawing are a single act of eating two olive-sized portions of forbidden fat in one lapse of awareness, so the Mishnah's distinction is unnecessary; if not close to her period, a Torah scholar is exempt for entering (duress) and liable for withdrawing (intentional), while an ignoramus is liable only for withdrawing.

items.text: Rava's retraction: always close to her period, but a Torah scholar for one and not the other
items.text_en: Rava's retraction: always close to her period, but a Torah scholar for one and not the other
items.desc_en: Rava retracts and says the case is always close to her period, and the man is a Torah scholar regarding one act (entering) but not regarding the other (withdrawing), explaining the Mishnah's two separate liabilities.

sub.desc_en: Rava retracts and says: the case is always close to her period, but the man is a Torah scholar regarding one act and not a Torah scholar regarding the other.

items.text: Rava cites Mishnah support for both cases
items.text_en: Rava cites Mishnah support for both cases
items.desc_en: Rava claims that both cases (withdrawing and entering) are explicitly taught in the Mishnah: withdrawing is taught in the case of 'he was serving with a pure woman and she said I became impure, and he withdrew immediately – liable'; entering is taught in 'blood found on his garment – they are impure and liable for a sacrifice'. He asks whether this does not prove the case is close to her period and about entering.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites two Mishnah sources: one for withdrawal (the case of 'she said I became impure' and he withdrew immediately) and one for entry (the case of 'found on his garment'), arguing that both support his interpretation that the case is close to her period and liability is for entry.
Rava cites the Mishnah's case of blood found on his garment, which implies entering, and asks whether this does not prove the case is close to her period and about entering.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Mattana objects: not close to her period, and about withdrawing
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Mattana objects: not close to her period, and about withdrawing
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Mattana tells Rava that the Mishnah can be explained as not close to her period and about withdrawing. The case of 'found on his garment' teaches that they are impure with uncertainty and exempt from sacrifice, and the parallel case of 'found on hers' was taught incidentally.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Matna's objection to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Matna's objection to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Matna objects that the case is not close to her period and applies to withdrawal; the Mishnah needed to teach the case of 'found on her garment' (impure with doubt, exempt from sacrifice), and the case of 'found on his garment' was taught incidentally alongside it.

items.text: Ravina's objection: 'found' implies after the fact, not at withdrawal
items.text_en: Ravina's objection: 'found' implies after the fact, not at withdrawal
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rav Adda: the Mishnah says 'found' (nimtza), which implies after the act, but if it is about withdrawing, the knowledge would be at the outset, not after.

sub.text: Ravina's objection to Rav Adda bar Matna
sub.text_en: Ravina's objection to Rav Adda bar Matna
sub.desc_en: Ravina objects that the Mishnah uses the term 'נמצא' (found), which implies after the fact, but if it refers to withdrawal, the awareness would have occurred at the very beginning of withdrawal.

items.text: Rava's response and the baraita's correction
items.text_en: Rava's response and the baraita's correction
items.desc_en: Rava tells Rav Adda to listen to what his master said, citing a baraita that calls the case a positive commandment, but if it were about withdrawing it would be a negative commandment. Rav Adda responds that the baraita should be read as missing a clause: the first case is a negative commandment, the second a positive commandment.

sub.desc_en: Rava tells Rav Adda to listen to his master's teaching, citing a baraita that calls the case a positive commandment (מצות עשה), implying that if it were about withdrawal it would be a negative commandment (מצות לא תעשה).
Rav Adda responds that the baraita should be read as missing a clause: the first case is a negative commandment (מצות לא תעשה), the second a positive commandment (מצות עשה).

items.text: How to withdraw immediately: dig in nails
items.text_en: How to withdraw immediately: dig in nails
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how one withdraws immediately: he digs his ten nails into the ground until he dies, and good for him (i.e., it is praiseworthy).

sub.text: Gemara's question about the method of withdrawal
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about the method of withdrawal
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one should withdraw immediately, and Rav Huna in the name of Rava answers: he should dig his ten fingernails into the ground until he dies, and it is good for him.

sub.text: Rav Huna in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Huna in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna in the name of Rava answers that one digs his ten nails into the ground until he dies, and it is praiseworthy for him.

items.text: Rava and Abaye debate: one who has intercourse with a dead relative
items.text_en: Rava and Abaye debate: one who has intercourse with a dead relative
items.desc_en: Rava infers that one who has intercourse with a dead relative (i.e., a corpse) is exempt, because here the man is exempt due to duress; if he were liable, why would he be exempt? Abaye counters that he is liable, but here the man is exempt because he could have withdrawn with minimal pleasure but withdrew with maximal pleasure.

sub.desc_en: Rava infers from the earlier discussion that one who has intercourse with a corpse is exempt from liability.
Rava asks: if one were liable for intercourse with a corpse, why would the earlier case exempt the man due to duress?
Abaye objects that one who has intercourse with a corpse is indeed liable.

Abaye explains that in the earlier case the man is exempt because he is under duress, but the one who withdraws immediately is liable because he could have withdrawn with minimal pleasure but withdrew with maximal pleasure.

items.text: Rabba bar Chanan's question: a long and short path in niddah
items.text_en: Rabba bar Chanan's question: a long and short path in niddah
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Chanan asks Abaye: if so, we have found a 'long and short' in niddah (i.e., a distinction between minimal and maximal pleasure), implying a difficulty with Abaye's explanation.

sub.text: Rabba bar Chanan's question to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Chanan's question to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Chanan asks Abaye: if so, we have found a 'long and short' in niddah (a distinction between a long and short withdrawal), implying a problematic distinction.

items.text: Gemara's objection to Abaye's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to Abaye's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Abaye's statement about an 'ones' (forced situation) implies the case is not close to her expected period, but Abaye elsewhere said one is liable for two offerings, implying it is close to her period. This contradiction is resolved by saying Abaye's statement was made in a general context.

items.text: Rav Huna's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Huna's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Huna the son of Rav Nathan challenges the resolution, arguing that Abaye's statement about an 'ones' implies the case is not close to her period, but Abaye elsewhere said one is liable for two offerings, implying it is close. The Gemara resolves that Abaye's statement was made in a general context.

items.text: Source for warning a man who cohabits with a niddah
items.text_en: Source for warning a man who cohabits with a niddah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosei ben Lakonya asks Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei ben Lakonya for the Torah source for the warning against one who cohabits with a niddah. He is answered with the verse 'Do not approach a woman in her menstrual impurity.' Then the question shifts to the source for a man who was told by his pure wife that she became impure and must not separate immediately; Chizkiyah derives it from the verse 'And her impurity shall be upon him.'

items.text: Source for the negative commandment
items.text_en: Source for the negative commandment
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the negative commandment (not to separate immediately). Rav Pappa derives it from the verse 'Do not approach,' interpreting it as 'do not separate,' as in the verse 'Who say, Approach me not, for I am holy.'

items.text: Derashot on separating near the expected period
items.text_en: Derashot on separating near the expected period
items.desc_en: The Sages taught a baraita: 'And you shall separate the children of Israel from their impurity' – Rabbi Yoshiya derives from here a warning for Israel to separate from their wives near their expected period. Rabba defines the time as 'onah.' Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says that one who does not separate will have sons die like Aaron's sons. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says that one who separates will have male sons, citing the juxtaposition of verses. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that they will be sons fit for teaching.

items.text: Additional derashot on having male sons
items.text_en: Additional derashot on having male sons
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says that one who recites Havdalah over wine at the conclusion of Shabbat will have male sons, based on a verbal analogy. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says they will be sons fit for teaching. Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet in the name of Rabbi Elazar says that one who sanctifies himself at the time of intercourse will have male sons, citing the verse 'And you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy.'

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva about knowing the specific impurity
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva about knowing the specific impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Eliezer says 'the creeping thing and it was hidden from him' etc. The Gemara asks what is the difference between them. Chizkiyah says the difference is between a creeping thing and a carcass: Rabbi Eliezer requires knowing whether one became impure from a creeping thing or a carcass, while Rabbi Akiva does not require knowing the specific type. Ulla similarly says the difference is between a creeping thing and a carcass, and he raises a contradiction from Rabbi Eliezer's own statement about one who ate fat or leftover, etc., where he says one is liable without knowing the specific sin. The Gemara resolves that there the verse 'which he sinned and brought' implies any sin, but here the verse 'or with the carcass of an unclean creeping thing' teaches that one must know the specific source.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's position
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to explain Rabbi Akiva's position, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Explanation of the repetition of the section on creeping things
items.text_en: Explanation of the repetition of the section on creeping things
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Torah repeats the section about creeping things, citing Rabbi Yishmael's principle that a repeated section introduces a new element. It connects this to Rabbi Akiva's view that the word "bah" excludes one who is engaged in a permitted act.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Torah needed to write the section on creeping animals (שרץ) alongside the section on domesticated and wild animals (בהמה וחיה) because of a principle from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: any section that is repeated is repeated only for the sake of a new element introduced in it.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation of "bah"
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation of "bah"
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Eliezer does with the word "bah" and answers that he uses it to exclude one who is merely engaged in a permitted act (mit'asek).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Eliezer does with the word 'בה' (in it) from the verse, and answers that it excludes one who is engaged in a permitted act (מתעסק).
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Eliezer uses the word to exclude one who is merely engaged in a permitted act (מִתְעַסֵּק).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Sheshet on the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Sheshet on the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Sheshet state that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva is about the interpretation of the verses (mashma'ut dorshin). Rav Sheshet even swaps their positions.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Sheshet state that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva is about the interpretation of the word 'בה' (in it), and Rav Sheshet reverses their positions.
Rav Sheshet agrees with Rabbi Yochanan but swaps the positions of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva.

items.text: Rava's question about forgetfulness of both impurity and Temple
items.text_en: Rava's question about forgetfulness of both impurity and Temple
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman about a case where one forgot both the impurity and the Temple. Rav Nachman initially says he is liable due to forgetfulness of impurity, but Rava objects that he could be exempt due to forgetfulness of the Temple. Rav Ashi resolves the dilemma by examining which forgetfulness the person is distancing himself from, but Ravina challenges this, concluding that there is no difference.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman about a case where one forgot both the impurity and the Temple.
Rav Nachman rules that the person is liable because he forgot the impurity.
Rava objects that one could equally argue the person is exempt due to forgetfulness of the Temple.
Rav Ashi resolves the dilemma by examining which forgetfulness the person is distancing himself from.
Ravina challenges Rav Ashi, arguing that distancing from one necessarily involves the other.
The gemara concludes that there is no difference between the two forgetfulnesses.

items.text: Baraita about two paths and entering the Temple
items.text_en: Baraita about two paths and entering the Temple
items.desc_en: A baraita is presented discussing a case of two paths, one impure and one pure. If one walked on the first without entering, then on the second and entered, he is liable. If he walked on the first, entered, purified himself, then walked on the second and entered, he is liable according to the Sages, but Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda exempt him in all cases.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a case of two paths, one impure and one pure, and states that if one walked on the first without entering the Temple, then walked on the second and entered, he is liable.

The baraita continues with a second scenario: after walking on the first path and entering, then purifying himself, then walking on the second path and entering, he is still liable according to the Sages.
Rabbi Shimon exempts the person in this second scenario.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, citing Rabbi Shimon, exempts the person in all cases.

items.text: Rava's resolution of the contradiction about partial knowledge
items.text_en: Rava's resolution of the contradiction about partial knowledge
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the case involves someone who walked in the first path, forgot that he walked, and then walked in the second path. The dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon is whether מקצת ידיעה is considered like full ידיעה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: even in the first path, he is definitely impure from every angle.
Rava resolves the contradiction by positing a case where the person walked in the first path but forgot it when walking the second, creating only partial knowledge (מקצת ידיעה).
Rava explains the dispute: Tanna Kamma holds that partial knowledge (מקצת ידיעה) is considered like full knowledge, while Rabbi Shimon disagrees.

items.text: Dispute about uncertain knowledge (ספק ידיעה)
items.text_en: Dispute about uncertain knowledge (ספק ידיעה)
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one walked in the first path, entered, sprinkled, waited, immersed, and then walked in the second path and entered, he is liable, but Rabbi Shimon exempts. Rabbi Yochanan explains that here they treated ספק ידיעה as ידיעה, while Resh Lakish attributes the ruling to Rabbi Yishmael who does not require ידיעה בתחילה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one walked in the first path, entered, sprinkled, waited, immersed, then walked in the second path and entered — the first Tanna holds him liable, but Rabbi Shimon exempts him.
The Gemara asks: Why is he liable? This is a case of uncertain knowledge (ספק ידיעה), which should not trigger a sacrifice.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that in this case the Sages treated uncertain knowledge (ספק ידיעה) as definite knowledge (ידיעה), making him liable.
Resh Lakish attributes the Mishnah to Rabbi Yishmael, who holds that initial knowledge (ידיעה בתחילה) is not required for liability.

items.text: Contradiction between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish's statements
items.text_en: Contradiction between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish's statements
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraisa about eating uncertain chelev. Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi says one brings a chatat and an asham talui for each instance, while Rabbi Shimon's students say only one asham talui. Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan each explain the baraisa differently, leading to a contradiction with their earlier statements.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara announces a contradiction between Rabbi Yochanan's statements and between Resh Lakish's statements.

The Gemara cites a baraita about eating uncertain chelev (forbidden fat), where Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi requires a chatat and an asham talui for each instance, while Rabbi Shimon's students require only one asham talui.
Resh Lakish explains that Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi taught here that uncertain awarenesses (ידיעות ספקות) are divided for multiple chatat offerings.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that just as certain awarenesses (ידיעות ודאי) are divided for multiple chatat offerings, so too uncertain awarenesses are divided for multiple asham talui offerings.

items.text: Resolution of the contradictions
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradictions
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rabbi Yochanan's contradiction by distinguishing between this case, where ידיעה is not explicit in the verse, and the rest of the Torah where a full ידיעה is required. For Resh Lakish, the Gemara explains that his statement teaches that Rabbi Yishmael does not require ידיעה בתחילה, even though it is obvious from the verses, to counter the possibility that he might require it from tradition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's statements by distinguishing between this case, where 'ידיעה' is not explicit in the verse but derived from 'ונעלם', and the rest of the Torah, where a full 'ידיעה' is required from the verse 'או הודע אליו'.
The Gemara questions why Reish Lakish interprets the baraita according to Rabbi Yishmael rather than according to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
The Gemara explains that Reish Lakish's statement teaches that Rabbi Yishmael does not require 'ידיעה בתחילה' (awareness at the beginning).

The Gemara objects that it is obvious Rabbi Yishmael does not require 'ידיעה בתחילה' because he has no superfluous verses, as he uses 'ונעלם' to teach liability for a lapse of awareness of the Temple.

The Gemara resolves that Reish Lakish's teaching is necessary to counter the possibility that Rabbi Yishmael might require 'ידיעה בתחילה' from tradition, even though he does not derive it from verses.

items.text: Transition to the Mishnah on שבועות
items.text_en: Transition to the Mishnah on שבועות
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter on ידיעות הטומאה and begins the Mishnah on שבועות, which lists the four categories of oaths: 'that I will eat', 'that I will not eat', 'that I ate', and 'that I did not eat'. Rabbi Akiva rules that one who swears not to eat and eats any amount is liable, and he defends his position against the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter on ידיעות הטומאה (awareness of impurity) with the standard formula 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you).
The Mishnah introduces the four categories of oaths: 'that I will eat', 'that I will not eat', 'that I ate', and 'that I did not eat'.
Rabbi Akiva rules that one who swears not to eat and eats any amount is liable.
The Sages object to Rabbi Akiva, asking where we find that one who eats any amount is liable.
Rabbi Akiva defends his position by arguing that the oath itself is a speech act that brings a sacrifice, so any amount of eating violates it.

items.text: Gemara's question on the meaning of 'שאוכל'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the meaning of 'שאוכל'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'שאוכל' implies 'that I will eat', citing a contradiction from a baraisa where 'שבועה שאוכל לך' is prohibited, implying it means 'that I will not eat'. Abaye resolves that 'שאוכל' always means 'that I will eat', but the difference lies in whether the person is being urged to eat or not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'שאוכל' means 'that I will eat', citing a baraisa where 'שבועה שאוכל לך' is prohibited, implying it means 'that I will not eat'.
Abaye resolves that 'שאוכל' always means 'that I will eat', but the difference lies in whether the person is being urged to eat or not.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the Mishnah and Baraita contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the Mishnah and Baraita contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses the contradiction between the Mishnah, which implies no refusal to eat, and the Baraita, which involves refusal. Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah should be read as 'shevuah she'i ochel lakh' (an oath that I will not eat from you), and the Baraita's repetition of 'lo achelna' indicates an oath not to eat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes the contradiction between the Mishnah (which implies no refusal to eat) and the Baraita (which involves refusal), and proposes that the Mishnah refers to a case without refusal while the Baraita involves refusal and a repeated statement of 'I will not eat'.
Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by reading the Mishnah as 'shevuah she'i ochel lakh' (an oath that I will not eat from you), teaching that even though the wording is unusual, it is valid.

items.text: Abaye's interpretation of the Baraita on 'issar'
items.text_en: Abaye's interpretation of the Baraita on 'issar'
items.desc_en: The Baraita states that 'mivta' is an oath, 'issar' is an oath, and 'issur issar' depends on whether one considers 'mattpis bishvuah' as equivalent to uttering an oath. Abaye clarifies that 'issar' means being 'mattpis bishvuah', and liability depends on whether this is considered like uttering an oath.

sub.desc_en: The Baraita states that 'mivta' is an oath, 'issar' is an oath, and 'issur issar' depends on whether one considers 'issar' as an oath.
The Gemara questions the Baraita's phrasing, noting that if 'issar' is already an oath, the conditional statement is redundant.
Abaye clarifies that 'issar' means being 'mattpis bishvuah' (associating with an oath), and liability depends on whether this is considered like uttering an oath.

items.text: Scriptural proofs for 'mivta' and 'issar'
items.text_en: Scriptural proofs for 'mivta' and 'issar'
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks scriptural sources: 'mivta' is an oath from 'levatei bifatayim', 'issar' from 'shevu'at issar'. It questions whether 'issar' is 'mattpis bishvuah' from 'asrah issar al nafshah bishvuah'. Abaye then provides a different proof for 'mivta' from the verse 'o mivta sifateha' which implies an oath without explicitly saying 'shevuah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source that 'mivta' is an oath, citing the verse 'אוֹ נֶפֶשׁ כִּי תִשָּׁבַע לְבַטֵּא בִשְׂפָתַיִם' (or if a person swears to utter with lips), and that 'issar' is also an oath from the verse 'כׇּל נֵדֶר וְכׇל שְׁבֻעַת אִסָּר' (every vow and every oath of a bond).

The Gemara asks from where it is derived that 'issar' means an association with an oath (מִיתְּפֵס בִּשְׁבוּעָה), citing the verse 'אוֹ אָסְרָה אִסָּר עַל נַפְשָׁהּ בִּשְׁבֻעָה' (or bound her soul by a bond with an oath).

The Gemara objects that 'mivta' (clear utterance) is also associated with an oath in a verse, as it is written: 'לְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יְבַטֵּא הָאָדָם בִּשְׁבֻעָה' (whatever a man shall utter clearly with an oath).

Abaye provides a different proof for 'mivta' being an oath from the verse 'וְאִם הָיוֹ תִהְיֶה לְאִישׁ וּנְדָרֶיהָ עָלֶיהָ, אוֹ מִבְטָא שְׂפָתֶיהָ אֲשֶׁר אָסְרָה עַל נַפְשָׁהּ' (and if she be married to a husband, while her vows are upon her, or the clear utterance of her lips, with which she has bound her soul), which does not explicitly say 'shevuah', implying that 'mivta' itself is an oath.

items.text: Rava's alternative interpretation and the dispute between Abaye and Rava
items.text_en: Rava's alternative interpretation and the dispute between Abaye and Rava
items.desc_en: Rava argues that 'mattpis bishvuah' is not like uttering an oath; rather, 'issar' itself is an oath, and 'issur issar' means the Torah placed it between vow and oath, so it follows the language used. The Gemara notes that this reflects their known dispute: Abaye holds 'mattpis bishvuah' is like uttering an oath, Rava disagrees.

sub.desc_en: Rava asserts that 'mattpis bishvuah' is not like uttering an oath; rather, 'issar' itself is an oath, and 'issur issar' means the Torah placed it between vow and oath, so it follows the language used.
The Gemara cites the verse 'וְאִם בֵּית אִישָׁהּ נָדָרָה אוֹ אָסְרָה אִסָּר עַל נַפְשָׁהּ בִּשְׁבֻעָה' to show where the Torah placed 'issar' between vow and oath.
The Gemara notes that Rava's interpretation aligns with the known dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding whether 'mattpis bishvuah' is like uttering an oath.

items.text: Supporting Baraita and its analysis
items.text_en: Supporting Baraita and its analysis
items.desc_en: A Baraita is brought defining 'issar' as a vow to abstain from meat and wine like on a day of mourning. Shmuel adds that it must be a day already vowed from. The Gemara notes that this supports Abaye's view: being 'mattpis' in a vow makes it a vow, and similarly being 'mattpis' in an oath makes it an oath.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited defining 'issar' as a vow to abstain from meat and wine like on a day of mourning.
Shmuel adds that the vow is only valid if the day of mourning was already vowed upon.
The Gemara notes that this supports Abaye's view: being 'mattpis' in a vow makes it a vow, and similarly being 'mattpis' in an oath makes it an oath.

items.text: Rava's resolution of the difficulty
items.text_en: Rava's resolution of the difficulty
items.desc_en: Rava reinterprets the Mishnah's definition of 'issar neder' as a vow to abstain from meat and wine like a day of mourning, citing Shmuel's condition that it must be a new prohibition. The Gemara explains the scriptural basis: a neder must involve something already forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rava's position faces a difficulty from the Mishnah's wording.
Rava reinterprets the Mishnah's definition of 'issar neder' as a vow to abstain from meat and wine like a day of mourning, citing Shmuel's condition that it must be a new prohibition.
The Gemara explains the scriptural basis: a neder must involve something already forbidden.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's example
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's example
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah specifies 'the day Gedaliah ben Achikam was killed'—it might have been thought that since the day is already forbidden, a vow to abstain like that day is not a valid neder; the Mishnah teaches that it is.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to specify 'the day Gedaliah ben Achikam was killed,' since it is obvious that a vow abstaining like that day is valid.

The Gemara explains that the specification is necessary because one might have thought that since the day is already forbidden, a vow to abstain like it would not take effect; the Mishnah teaches that it does.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statements on oaths and vows
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statements on oaths and vows
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Rava's principle. He distinguishes between 'shevuah' (oath) and 'issar' (vow), and between 'sheker' (false oath about the future) and 'shav' (vain oath about the past), with scriptural warnings for each. 'Konamot' (vows) violate 'Lo yachel devaro'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Rava's principle, as reported by Ravin: the terms 'mivta' and 'issar' in the context of 'lo ochal lach' constitute a 'shevuah' (oath).

sub.text: Rav Dimi's report of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi's report of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports Rabbi Yochanan's distinction: 'ochal' and 'lo ochal' (future) are 'sheker' (false oath) with a warning from 'lo tishavu bishmi lashaker'; 'achalti' and 'lo achalti' (past) are 'shav' (vain oath) with a warning from 'lo tisa et shem Hashem Elohecha lashav'.
The Gemara concludes that 'konamot' (vows) violate the prohibition 'lo yachel devaro' (he shall not profane his word).

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that 'shav' and 'sheker' are one, implying that 'sheker' also applies to the past, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan. The Gemara resolves that they are not identical in content but were uttered in one divine utterance, like 'Zachor' and 'Shamor'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that equates 'shav' and 'sheker', arguing that since 'shav' applies to the past, 'sheker' must also apply to the past, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan's distinction.
The Gemara resolves that 'shav' and 'sheker' are not identical in content but were uttered in one divine utterance, analogous to 'Zachor' and 'Shamor' in the Decalogue.

items.text: Clarifying the halakhic implication of the baraita
items.text_en: Clarifying the halakhic implication of the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the practical halakha of the baraita's comparison. It first suggests that just as one is liable for 'shav', so too for 'sheker', but then corrects: just as one is liable for 'sheker', so too for 'shav', establishing that both carry lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the practical halakhic purpose of the baraita's comparison between 'shav' and 'sheker', noting that while the parallel of 'zachor' and 'shamor' has a halakhic application (via Rav Adda bar Ahava's derivation), here the comparison seems to lack a clear legal consequence.

The Gemara initially suggests that the baraita teaches that just as one is liable to lashes for a false oath about the past (שָׁוְא), so too one is liable to lashes for a false oath about the future (שֶׁקֶר).

The Gemara rejects the first formulation as backwards (כְּלַפֵּי לְיָיא) and corrects it: just as one is liable for lashes on a false future oath (שֶׁקֶר), so too one is liable for lashes on a false past oath (שָׁוְא), establishing that both carry lashes.

items.text: Rejecting a potential objection
items.text_en: Rejecting a potential objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the liability for both is obvious, but anticipates a possible objection from Rav Pappa to Abaye about 'Lo yinakeh', which is left incomplete.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the liability for both false and vain oaths is obvious, but anticipates a potential objection from Rav Pappa to Abaye regarding the phrase 'לא ינקה' (he will not be cleansed) as a general principle.

items.text: Alternative explanation for the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Alternative explanation for the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: just as one brings a sacrifice for a false oath (שקר), so too for a vain oath (שוא), and this aligns with Rabbi Akiva who holds one liable for the past like the future.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah teaches us according to the alternative explanation previously given.

The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: just as one brings a sacrifice for a false oath (שקר), so too for a vain oath (שוא), and this aligns with Rabbi Akiva who holds one liable for the past like the future.

items.text: Objection from a baraita defining vain and false oaths
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita defining vain and false oaths
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that defines a vain oath as swearing to change the known, and a false oath as swearing to exchange, implying a distinction that challenges the previous explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that defines a vain oath (שְׁבוּעַת שָׁוְא) as swearing to change the known, and a false oath (שְׁבוּעַת שֶׁקֶר) as swearing to exchange, implying a distinction that challenges the previous explanation.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction between past and future oaths
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction between past and future oaths
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan clarifies: 'I ate' and 'I did not eat' are false oaths (שקר) and one is warned from 'לא תשא', while 'I will eat' and 'I will not eat' violate 'לא יחל דברו'. A vain oath is swearing to change the known.

sub.text: Ravin's tradition in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Ravin's tradition in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes: 'I ate' and 'I did not eat' are false oaths (שקר) warned by 'לא תשא', while future oaths are governed by 'לא יחל דברו'.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's definition of a vain oath
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's definition of a vain oath
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan defines a vain oath (שבועת שוא) as swearing to change what is known to people.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's statement derived from a general principle
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's statement derived from a general principle
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu's statement was not explicit but inferred from a broader rule by Rabbi Yochanan: for any negative commandment without an action, one is not lashed, except for swearing, converting, and cursing a friend. The source for swearing is derived from 'לא תשא' implying lashes by an earthly court.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa clarifies that Rabbi Avahu's statement was not explicit but inferred from a general principle.

sub.text: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Amram citing Rav Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
sub.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Amram citing Rav Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin transmits the general rule: for any negative commandment without an action, one is not lashed, except for swearing, converting, and cursing a friend.
The gemara asks: from where do we derive that swearing is included in the exception?

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: the verse 'לֹא תִשָּׂא' implies that an earthly court lashes and purifies the swearer, while the heavenly court does not purify.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge to Abaye on the derivation
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge to Abaye on the derivation
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Abaye: perhaps 'לא ינקה' means no cleansing at all, but the verse says 'כי לא ינקה ה׳', implying only God does not cleanse, but an earthly court lashes and cleanses.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Abaye: perhaps 'לא ינקה' means no cleansing at all, but the verse says 'כי לא ינקה ה׳', implying only God does not cleanse, but an earthly court lashes and cleanses.

items.text: Derivation of false oath from vain oath via verbal analogy
items.text_en: Derivation of false oath from vain oath via verbal analogy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives the false oath from the vain oath using the repetition of 'לשוא' twice: if not needed for a vain oath, apply it to a false oath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found the source for a vain oath (שבועת שוא), but from where do we derive the false oath (שבועת שקר)?
Rabbi Yochanan answers: the Torah writes 'לשוא' (in vain) twice; if the second instance is not needed for the vain oath itself, apply it to the false oath via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy).

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's inquiry and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's inquiry and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu questions the nature of a false oath: if 'I will not eat' and he ate, it involves an action; if 'I will eat' and he did not eat, he is not lashed, as per the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan (no action) and Reish Lakish (uncertain warning).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu asks what constitutes a false oath (שבועת שקר), considering that if one swears not to eat and then eats, it involves an action, while if one swears to eat and fails to eat, Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish both rule he is not lashed.
The gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan rules no lashes because it is a negative command without action, while Reish Lakish rules no lashes because the warning is a doubtful warning (התראת ספק).

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's resolution: false oath is about the past
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's resolution: false oath is about the past
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu concludes that the false oath must be about the past ('I ate'/'I did not eat'), and Rava explains that the Torah explicitly equates false oath to vain oath: just as vain is about the past, so too false is about the past.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu resolves that the false oath (שבועת שקר) must be about the past, specifically 'I ate' or 'I did not eat'.
Rava explains that the Torah explicitly equates false oath to vain oath: just as vain oath (שבועת שוא) is about the past, so too false oath is about the past.

items.text: Objection from a Mishnah and resolution distinguishing lashes from sacrifice
items.text_en: Objection from a Mishnah and resolution distinguishing lashes from sacrifice
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects with a Mishnah stating that for 'I will not eat' and he ate, one is liable for lashes and a sacrifice, implying past oaths are excluded. The Gemara resolves: it excludes past oaths from a sacrifice, but lashes still apply, aligning with Rabbi Yishmael who holds liability only for the future regarding sacrifice, but lashes apply.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects to Rabbi Avahu by citing a Mishnah that states one who says 'I will not eat' and eats is liable only once, implying past oaths are excluded.
The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'this is' excludes, suggesting it excludes past oaths from lashes.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah excludes past oaths only from a sacrifice, not from lashes, aligning with Rabbi Yishmael who holds liability only for the future regarding sacrifice but lashes still apply.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction between the Mishnah's first and last clauses
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction between the Mishnah's first and last clauses
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's last clause, which implies that only a vain oath exempts from a sacrifice, but oaths about the past (e.g., 'I ate') would require a sacrifice. It resolves that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Akiva, and the first clause excludes 'I will eat' from lashes, not from a sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's last clause, which implies that only a vain oath exempts from a sacrifice, but oaths about the past (e.g., 'I ate') would require a sacrifice.
The Gemara answers that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Akiva, and the first clause excludes 'I will eat' from lashes, not from a sacrifice.
The Gemara objects that the first clause seems to be Rabbi Yishmael, but resolves that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Akiva, and the first clause excludes 'I will eat' from lashes, not from a sacrifice.

items.text: Clarifying the logic of the exclusion
items.text_en: Clarifying the logic of the exclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah excludes future-oriented oaths from lashes but not from a sacrifice: since the Mishnah deals with future oaths, it naturally excludes future oaths from lashes, not past ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah excludes past oaths from lashes but not from a sacrifice, given that it deals with future oaths.

items.text: The dilemma regarding Rabbi Akiva's general position on minimal amounts
items.text_en: The dilemma regarding Rabbi Akiva's general position on minimal amounts
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does Rabbi Akiva generally hold like Rabbi Shimon, who imposes lashes for any amount (כל שהוא), or like the Rabbis? The context is a Mishnah about an oath not to eat, where eating any amount incurs liability, and the Gemara considers whether this is due to Rabbi Akiva's general view or the specific logic of explicit versus general oaths.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does Rabbi Akiva generally hold like Rabbi Shimon, who imposes lashes for any amount (כל שהוא), citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon states that any amount suffices for lashes, and the measure of an olive-bulk is only for offerings?

The Gemara presents the first possibility: if Rabbi Akiva holds like Rabbi Shimon, the dispute should have been stated generally, but it is stated here to show the far-reaching nature of the Rabbis' opinion, that even though one who specifies any amount is liable, one who does not specify is exempt.

The Gemara presents the second possibility: perhaps Rabbi Akiva generally holds like the Rabbis, and here the reason he deems one liable for any amount is that since one who specifies any amount is liable, one who does not specify is also liable.

items.text: First attempted proof from the Sages' challenge to Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: First attempted proof from the Sages' challenge to Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that Rabbi Akiva holds like the Rabbis, because when the Sages challenged him about liability for any amount, he did not respond that he follows Rabbi Shimon. The Gemara explains that he was speaking to them according to their own reasoning, but they still rejected his argument.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that Rabbi Akiva holds like the Rabbis, because when the Sages challenged him about liability for any amount, he did not respond that he follows Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva was speaking to the Sages according to their own reasoning, but they still rejected his argument.

items.text: Second and third proofs from Nazir and the oath about forbidden foods
items.text_en: Second and third proofs from Nazir and the oath about forbidden foods
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings two proofs: from a Nazir who soaks bread in wine, where Rabbi Akiva requires a kezayit, contradicting Rabbi Shimon's view; and from an oath not to eat, where eating forbidden foods is liable only due to inclusion of permitted items, implying Rabbi Akiva holds like the Rabbis. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Akiva generally holds like the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Akiva rules that a Nazir who soaks bread in wine is liable only if there is a kezayit (olive's bulk) of wine, implying he does not hold like Rabbi Shimon who would require liability for any amount.

The Gemara cites a Mishnah where one who swears not to eat and then eats forbidden foods is liable, and Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan explain this is because the oath includes permitted items alongside forbidden ones, implying Rabbi Akiva holds like the Rabbis.

Reish Lakish explains that the Mishnah's liability is only found either in a case of explicit half-measure according to the Rabbis, or in a standard case according to Rabbi Akiva who holds that a person can prohibit himself with any amount.

The Gemara concludes that since Rabbi Akiva's position in the Mishnah would be redundant if he held like Rabbi Shimon, it must be that generally Rabbi Akiva holds like the Rabbis, and the proof is established.

items.text: Refuting the Sages' challenge with counterexamples
items.text_en: Refuting the Sages' challenge with counterexamples
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Sages' claim that there is no precedent for liability for any amount, citing an ant (a creature), consecrated property (requires a perutah), explicit oaths (like a creature), and dirt. The discussion is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Sages challenge Rabbi Akiva: where do we find liability for eating any amount, that this oath should be liable?
The Gemara objects: is there no precedent? What about an ant (a creature)? The Gemara answers that a creature is different.
The Gemara objects: what about consecrated property? The Gemara answers that consecration requires a perutah's worth.
The Gemara objects: what about explicit oaths? The Gemara answers that explicit oaths are like a creature (any amount counts).
The Gemara objects: what about dirt? The discussion is cut off.

items.text: Rava's question about eating dirt
items.text_en: Rava's question about eating dirt
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers Rava's question: if one swore not to eat and then ate dirt, what is the minimum measure? It suggests resolving it by requiring an olive's bulk, but notes that this applies only to items of eating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests resolving Rava's question about the minimum measure for eating dirt under a vow by requiring an olive's bulk, but notes this applies only to items of eating.

items.text: Objection from kunnamot
items.text_en: Objection from kunnamot
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that kunnamot (vows of consecration) are different because they are considered explicit, implying a different standard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that kunnamot (vows of consecration) are considered explicit, implying a different standard for the minimum measure.

items.text: Distinguishing kunnamot from other cases
items.text_en: Distinguishing kunnamot from other cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why kunnamot are not comparable to other cases like blasphemy, nazirite, or consecration: each has a unique feature. Kunnamot are considered as one who speaks and prohibits himself, and there is no misuse (me'ilah) in kunnamot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where we find a case of one who speaks and brings a sacrifice, as the speaker of kunnamot does.
An objection is raised: what about the blasphemer (מגדף), who speaks and brings a sacrifice? The Gemara rejects this, noting that the blasphemer is a speaker who sins, not one who prohibits himself.

Another objection: what about the nazirite (נזיר), who brings a sacrifice due to his speech? The Gemara distinguishes: the nazirite brings a sacrifice to permit himself wine, not as a penalty for speaking.

A third objection: what about consecration (הקדש), which prohibits an object? The Gemara distinguishes: consecration prohibits the object to everyone, whereas kunnamot prohibit only the speaker himself.
The Gemara resolves that kunnamot are unique because there is no מעילה (misuse of consecrated property) in kunnamot, distinguishing them from other cases.

items.text: Rava's distinction: explicit vs. implicit
items.text_en: Rava's distinction: explicit vs. implicit
items.desc_en: Rava states that the dispute (about minimum measure) applies only to implicit oaths, but for explicit ones, all agree that any amount suffices, because explicit is like a specific entity.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the dispute by distinguishing between implicit oaths (סתם), where the minimum measure is debated, and explicit oaths (מפורש), where all agree any amount suffices because explicit is like a specific entity (בריה).

items.text: Rava's second distinction: 'not eat' vs. 'not taste'
items.text_en: Rava's second distinction: 'not eat' vs. 'not taste'
items.desc_en: Rava further distinguishes: the dispute is only for 'not eat', but for 'not taste', all agree any amount suffices. The Gemara notes this is obvious, but Rava teaches that 'taste' in common parlance might be considered like eating.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish applies only to the phrase 'not eat', but for 'not taste', all agree that any amount suffices.
The Gemara objects that this distinction is obvious, since 'taste' implies any amount.
The Gemara explains that Rava's teaching is necessary because one might have thought that 'taste' in common parlance is considered like eating, so Rava teaches that it is not.

items.text: Rav Pappa's distinction: oaths vs. kunnamot
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's distinction: oaths vs. kunnamot
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that the dispute applies to oaths, but for kunnamot, all agree any amount suffices, because kunnamot do not mention the word 'eating', making them like explicit vows.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves that the dispute about minimum measure applies only to oaths, but for kunnamot (vow-offerings), all agree any amount suffices because kunnamot do not mention the word 'eating', making them like explicit vows.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita on combining kunnamot
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita on combining kunnamot
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that two kunnamot combine but two oaths do not. If any amount sufficed for kunnamot, why would they need to combine? The Gemara resolves by specifying that the case is where one said 'eating from this is konam' and 'eating from that is konam', but then explains that it actually refers to 'eating from both is konam'. Rabbi Meir equates kunnamot to oaths, but the Gemara reverses it: Rabbi Meir says oaths are like kunnamot, and he does not accept Rav Pinchas's reasoning.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that two kunnamot combine but two oaths do not, and Rabbi Meir equates kunnamot to oaths.
The Gemara challenges: if one is liable for any amount, why would kunnamot need to combine?
The Gemara initially explains that the case is where one said 'eating from this is konam' and 'eating from that is konam', but then objects that each lacks the minimum measure.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to one who said 'eating from both is konam', so the two combine to reach the minimum measure.
The Gemara asks: if the parallel case for oaths is 'I swear not to eat from both', why do oaths not combine?
Rav Pinchas explains that oaths are different because they are divided for sin-offerings, so they do not combine.
The Gemara objects: if Rabbi Meir says kunnamot are like oaths, why would kunnamot not combine? They are not divided for sin-offerings.
The Gemara reverses the statement: Rabbi Meir actually says oaths are like kunnamot, and he does not accept Rav Pinchas's reasoning.

items.text: Ravina's resolution: lashes vs. sacrifice
items.text_en: Ravina's resolution: lashes vs. sacrifice
items.desc_en: Ravina resolves the contradiction: Rav Pappa's statement applies to lashes, while the baraita deals with sacrifice, which requires a perutah's worth.

sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between Rav Pappa's statement about lashes and the baraita about sacrifice, which requires a perutah's worth (שוה פרוטה).

items.text: Question on me'ilah in kunnamot
items.text_en: Question on me'ilah in kunnamot
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Rabbis hold that there is me'ilah in kunnamot, citing a baraita that distinguishes between 'this loaf is consecrated' and 'this loaf is consecrated to me', where only the latter has me'ilah for the owner. This is the opinion of Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Rabbis hold that there is me'ilah in kunnamot, citing a baraita that distinguishes between 'this loaf is consecrated' and 'this loaf is consecrated to me', where only the latter has me'ilah for the owner, according to Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Dispute about me'ilah in konamot
items.text_en: Dispute about me'ilah in konamot
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies a tannaitic dispute about whether konamot (vows of consecration) have the law of me'ilah (misuse of sacred property). Rabbi Meir argues they are like oaths and have no me'ilah, while the Sages distinguish between the vow-maker and his friend. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining Rabbi Meir's statement as addressed to the Sages' position.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites the Sages' ruling that neither the vow-maker nor his friend commits me'ilah (misuse of sacred property) with konamot (vows of consecration).
The Gemara inverts the Mishnah's attributions: Rabbi Meir says neither commits me'ilah, and the Sages say the vow-maker commits me'ilah but his friend does not.
The Gemara objects: if Rabbi Meir says konamot are like oaths, then they should have me'ilah, but he explicitly says there is no me'ilah in konamot at all.

The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Meir was speaking to the Sages according to their own reasoning, saying 'for me there is no me'ilah in konamot at all, but for you, at least admit that konamot are like oaths.'
The Gemara explains the Sages' position: oaths have the leniency of Rabbi Pinchas (allowing partial atonement), but konamot do not, so the Sages distinguish between them.

items.text: Rava's query about eating dirt
items.text_en: Rava's query about eating dirt
items.desc_en: Rava asks: if one swears not to eat dirt, what is the minimum amount for liability? Since dirt is not normally eaten, perhaps any amount suffices, or perhaps the oath intends a kezayit (olive's bulk). The Gemara leaves it unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rava states that if one swears not to eat and then eats dirt, he is exempt from liability.
Rava asks: if one swears not to eat dirt, what is the minimum amount for liability?
The Gemara presents two possibilities: since he said 'not eat,' his intent is for a kezayit (olive's bulk), or since dirt is not normally eaten, any amount suffices.
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Rava's query about eating grape pits
items.text_en: Rava's query about eating grape pits
items.desc_en: Rava asks: if one swears not to eat grape pits (chartzan), what is the minimum amount? Since they are edible through mixture, perhaps a kezayit is required, or since they are not eaten alone, any amount suffices. The Gemara leaves it unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks: if one swears not to eat grape pits (חרצן), what is the minimum amount for liability? Since they are edible through mixture, perhaps a kezayit is required, or since they are not eaten alone, any amount suffices. The Gemara leaves it unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rav Ashi's query about a nazirite's oath
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's query about a nazirite's oath
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks: if a nazirite swears not to eat grape pits, what is the minimum amount? Since a kezayit of grape pits is a Torah prohibition for a nazirite, perhaps the oath is about permitted things and any amount suffices, or perhaps the general phrase 'not eat' implies a kezayit. The Gemara leaves it unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks: if a nazirite swears not to eat grape pits, what is the minimum amount — since a kezayit is a Torah prohibition, perhaps the oath is about permitted things and any amount suffices, or perhaps the general phrase 'not eat' implies a kezayit.

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah about eating forbidden foods
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah about eating forbidden foods
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve Rava's query from a Mishnah where one who swears not to eat and eats neveilot (carrion) is liable, and Rabbi Shimon exempts. The Gemara explains the dispute: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan say it is because the oath includes permitted items with forbidden ones; Resh Lakish says it applies only when specifying half-shiurim or according to Rabbi Akiva. The Gemara concludes that neveilot is like dirt, but rejects the proof because neveilot is edible while dirt is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to resolve Rava's query by citing a Mishnah where one who swears not to eat and eats forbidden meats is liable, and Rabbi Shimon exempts.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah holds one liable, given that he is already bound by the Torah prohibition against eating these forbidden items.

sub.text: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan's answer
sub.text_en: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan explain that the oath is liable because it includes permitted items along with forbidden ones, making the oath effective.

Resh Lakish offers an alternative explanation: the Mishnah's liability applies only when specifying half-shiurim according to the Sages, or in a general oath according to Rabbi Akiva who holds that one can prohibit oneself with any amount.

The Gemara infers that since neveilah is like dirt relative to a nazir, and the Mishnah's liability depends on specifying, it implies that without specification one intends a kezayit, thus resolving Rava's query.
The Gemara attempts to resolve Rava's query about eating dirt by analogy to neveilah, concluding that one intends a kezayit unless specified otherwise.
The Gemara rejects the proof, distinguishing dirt as completely inedible while neveilah is edible but prohibited, like a lion lying upon it.

items.text: Mishnah: General vs. specific oaths
items.text_en: Mishnah: General vs. specific oaths
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a general oath not to eat incurs only one liability for eating and drinking, but a specific oath for each item incurs multiple liabilities. Eating non-edible items is exempt, but eating forbidden foods like neveilot is liable according to the Sages, while Rabbi Shimon exempts. A konam (vow) that one's wife is forbidden if he ate such items is effective.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a general oath not to eat incurs only one liability for eating and drinking, while a specific oath for each item incurs multiple liabilities.
The Mishnah states that eating non-edible items under a general oath is exempt from liability.
The Mishnah rules that eating forbidden foods like neveilot under a general oath is liable according to the Sages.
Rabbi Shimon exempts one who eats forbidden foods under a general oath.
The Mishnah concludes that a konam (vow) forbidding one's wife if he ate such items is effective.

items.text: Gemara: Drinking is included in eating
items.text_en: Gemara: Drinking is included in eating
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin quotes Shmuel: if one swears not to eat and drinks, he is liable. This can be derived from common sense (people say 'let's taste something' and include drinking) or from a verse where 'eating' includes drinking, as Resh Lakish proves from Deuteronomy 14:23.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin reports in the name of Shmuel that one who swears not to eat and then drinks is liable.
The Gemara offers a common-sense proof: people say 'let's taste something' and then eat and drink, showing drinking is included in eating.
Resh Lakish provides a scriptural proof from Deuteronomy 14:23, where 'eating' includes wine (drink), showing drinking is subsumed under eating.

items.text: Initial scriptural derivation: wine is included in 'eating'
items.text_en: Initial scriptural derivation: wine is included in 'eating'
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by noting that wine is called 'תירוש' and the verse says 'ואכלת', implying drinking is included in eating. This is challenged by the possibility that it refers to wine mixed with water (אניגרון).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that תירוש (wine) is called wine, and the verse uses 'וְאָכַלְתָּ' (and you shall eat), implying drinking is included in eating.

items.text: Challenge: perhaps it refers to diluted wine (אניגרון)
items.text_en: Challenge: perhaps it refers to diluted wine (אניגרון)
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a possibility that the verse refers to wine mixed with water (אניגרון), citing Rabba bar Shmuel's definition of אניגרון as water from boiled vegetables.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a possibility that the verse refers to wine mixed with water (אניגרון).
Rabba bar Shmuel defines אניגרון as water from boiled vegetables and אכסיגרון as water from all types of beets.

items.text: Alternative derivation from 'שכר' and further challenge
items.text_en: Alternative derivation from 'שכר' and further challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov offers a new derivation from the verse 'ונתתה הכסף... ביין ובשכר', where 'שכר' indicates intoxicating drink. The Gemara challenges that this might also refer to diluted wine, and then suggests it could be a date-beer (דבילה קעילית), citing a baraita about such items.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov proposes a new derivation from the verse 'ונתתה הכסף... ביין ובשכר', arguing that since 'יין' is wine and the verse says 'ואכלת', drinking wine is included in eating.
The Gemara objects that perhaps here too the wine is consumed via an אניגרון (a mixture), not as pure wine.
The Gemara answers that the verse writes 'שכר', which indicates an intoxicating drink, not a diluted mixture.
The Gemara objects that 'שכר' might refer to a date-beer (דבילה קעילית), citing a baraita that one who eats such items and enters the Temple is liable.

items.text: Gezerah shavah from nazirite to establish wine
items.text_en: Gezerah shavah from nazirite to establish wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the derivation by using a gezerah shavah (verbal analogy) between 'שכר' here and in the nazirite context, concluding that just as there it means wine, so too here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the derivation by using a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between 'שכר' here and in the nazirite context, concluding that just as there it means wine, so too here.

items.text: Rava's proof from the Mishna: drinking is included in 'eating'
items.text_en: Rava's proof from the Mishna: drinking is included in 'eating'
items.desc_en: Rava argues from the Mishna that if one swore 'not to eat' and then ate and drank, he is only liable once, proving drinking is included in eating. He contrasts this with a case of eating and working, which would obviously be separate.

sub.desc_en: Rava argues from the Mishna that if one swore 'not to eat' and then ate and drank, he is only liable once, proving drinking is included in eating; he contrasts this with a case of eating and working, which would obviously be separate.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution: drinking is included in eating, but not vice versa
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution: drinking is included in eating, but not vice versa
items.desc_en: Abaye objects by citing the Mishna's seifa where one swears 'not to eat and not to drink' and is liable for two, arguing that if drinking were included, the second oath would be redundant. Rava resolves that the seifa refers to a case where 'not to drink' was said first, and drinking is included in eating but eating is not included in drinking.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rava's proof: if drinking is included in eating, then the Mishna's seifa where one swears 'not to eat and not to drink' and is liable for two would be redundant, as the second oath would add nothing.
Rava resolves that the seifa refers to a case where 'not to drink' was said first, so drinking is included in eating but eating is not included in drinking, explaining the two liabilities.

items.text: Further analysis: the order of oaths reveals intent
items.text_en: Further analysis: the order of oaths reveals intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishna didn't teach a case where one says 'not to eat and not to drink' and is only liable once, which would be a stronger proof. It concludes that the Mishna's wording is precise, and when one says 'not to eat' first and then 'not to drink', it reveals that the original 'eating' meant only eating, not drinking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishna did not teach the case of 'not to eat and not to drink' to prove that drinking is included in eating, which would be a stronger proof.
The Gemara answers that the Mishna's wording is precise: when one says 'not to eat' first and then 'not to drink', it reveals that the original 'eating' meant only eating, not drinking.

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof from the Mishna's details and final resolution
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof from the Mishna's details and final resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi brings a proof from the Mishna's case of eating unfit foods, where the Mishna implies that if the foods were fit, one would be liable even though only 'not to eat' was said. The Gemara considers and rejects alternative interpretations, concluding that the Mishna's wording is precise and supports the inclusion of drinking in eating.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi introduces a proof from the Mishna that eating fit foods triggers liability even under an explicit eating-only vow, implying drinking is included in eating.
The Gemara objects that the Mishna might be referring to someone who uttered two separate vows, one against eating and one against drinking.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's rejection of the objection
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's rejection of the objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi counters that the Mishna's structure, detailing specific types of bread, cannot be explained as merely exempting the person from other types of bread.
The Gemara objects that the Mishna's wording could be interpreted as referring to eating wheat bread and tasting barley and spelt bread, not to liability for drinking.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's rejection of the second objection
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's rejection of the second objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi rejects the objection by noting that if the intent were to distinguish eating from tasting, the Mishna should have used the wording 'bread of wheat' and 'bread of barley' instead of the actual formulation.

Rav Ashi concludes that the Mishna's precise wording demonstrates that the phrase 'not eat' inherently includes both eating and drinking, as the Mishna would otherwise have needed an explicit distinction.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution on תערובת
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution on תערובת
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the mishnah's case might involve a mixture (תערובת), and resolves that the repetition of 'פת' indicates a division into separate liabilities.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the mishnah's case might involve a mixture (תערובת) rather than separate liabilities.
The Gemara resolves that the repetition of 'פת' (bread) indicates a division into separate liabilities, not a mixture.

items.text: Challenge to the mishnah's ruling on drinks
items.text_en: Challenge to the mishnah's ruling on drinks
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the mishnah's ruling that one who swears not to drink and drinks many beverages is liable only once, questioning why the oath is not interpreted as excluding other drinks.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the mishnah's ruling that one who swears not to drink and drinks many beverages is liable only once, questioning why the oath is not interpreted as excluding other drinks.

items.text: Rav Pappa's resolution with specific formulations
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's resolution with specific formulations
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the case involves drinks placed before him, and the oath must be formulated in a way that includes all possibilities, leading to a series of refinements until the correct phrasing is found.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa opens by stating that the case involves drinks placed before him, and the oath should have been formulated as 'I will not drink these,' but the gemara objects that this would only exclude these drinks, not others.
The gemara refines the formulation to 'I will not drink like these,' but objects that this would still allow drinking smaller or larger amounts.
The gemara further refines to 'I will not drink from this type,' but objects that this would still allow drinking the very items themselves.
The gemara resolves that the correct formulation is 'I will not drink these and their type,' covering both the specific drinks and their category.

items.text: Rav Acha's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Acha's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika explains that the case involves a friend urging him to drink, and the listing of specific drinks serves to impose liability for each one individually.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika explains that the case involves a friend urging him to drink, and the listing of specific drinks serves to impose liability for each one individually.

items.text: Mishnah on claims and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
items.text_en: Mishnah on claims and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
