The Gemara cites a baraita that interprets the verse 'וְעָמְדוּ שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים' (And the two men shall stand) as referring to witnesses.
The baraita raises the possibility that the verse might refer to litigants rather than witnesses.
The baraita answers that since the verse already mentions litigants with 'אֲשֶׁר לָהֶם הָרִיב' (between whom the controversy is), the phrase 'וְעָמְדוּ שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים' must refer to witnesses.
The baraita provides an additional proof using a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'שְׁנֵי' (two) used elsewhere regarding witnesses.
The Gemara asks: What is the meaning of the baraita's phrase 'וְאִם נַפְשְׁךָ לוֹמַר' (And if it is your wish to say)?
The Gemara explains that the initial proof was inadequate because one might argue that the entire verse speaks of litigants, so the verbal analogy is needed to confirm it refers to witnesses.

items.text: Second Baraita: Exclusion of Women
items.text_en: Second Baraita: Exclusion of Women
items.desc_en: A second baraita is cited, which also interprets the verse as referring to witnesses. It argues that if the verse meant litigants, why would it say 'two men'? Women also come to court. The baraita then uses the same verbal analogy to confirm that it speaks of witnesses.

sub.desc_en: A second baraita is cited, opening with the claim that the verse 'then the two men shall stand' speaks of witnesses.
The baraita raises the objection that the verse might refer to litigants rather than witnesses.
The baraita rejects the litigant interpretation by arguing that if the verse meant litigants, it would not specify 'two', since three or more can also come to court.
The baraita provides a verbal analogy: just as 'two' in the later verse refers to witnesses, so too here it refers to witnesses.
The Gemara asks why the baraita needed the additional verbal analogy, implying the initial rejection was insufficient.
The Gemara explains that the initial rejection could be countered by saying the verse speaks of a plaintiff and defendant, so the verbal analogy is needed to confirm it refers to witnesses.
The Gemara concludes that the verbal analogy resolves the doubt, confirming the verse speaks of witnesses.

items.text: Third Baraita: Exclusion of Relatives and Disqualified
items.text_en: Third Baraita: Exclusion of Relatives and Disqualified
items.desc_en: A third baraita is cited, which again interprets the verse as referring to witnesses. It argues that if the verse meant litigants, why would it say 'two men'? Women also come to court. The baraita then uses the same verbal analogy to confirm that it speaks of witnesses.

sub.desc_en: A third baraita is cited, opening with the claim that the verse 'וְעָמְדוּ שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים' (then the two men shall stand) speaks of witnesses.
The baraita poses a rhetorical question: does the verse refer to witnesses or litigants?
The baraita objects: if the verse referred to litigants, why specify 'men'? Women also come to court.
The baraita provides a verbal analogy: just as 'two' elsewhere refers to witnesses, so too here.
The Gemara asks: what is the meaning of the baraita's phrase 'if it is your wish to say'?

The Gemara explains: the initial proof was inadequate because one might argue that women do not typically come to court due to 'כָּל כְּבוּדָּה בַת מֶלֶךְ פְּנִימָה' (all the glory of the king's daughter is within), so the verse speaks of litigants; the verbal analogy resolves this.

items.text: Baraita on Court Etiquette: Standing and Sitting
items.text_en: Baraita on Court Etiquette: Standing and Sitting
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'And the two men shall stand' is a mitzvah for litigants to stand. Rabbi Yehuda says he heard that if both litigants wish to sit, they may. The prohibition is that one should not stand while the other sits, or one speaks at length while the other is told to be brief.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that the verse 'וְעָמְדוּ שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים' (and the two men shall stand) establishes a mitzvah for litigants to stand during court proceedings.
רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) reports a tradition that if both litigants wish to sit, the court may seat them.
רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) asks: What then is prohibited?

רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) answers: The prohibition is that one litigant should not stand while the other sits, nor should one be allowed to speak at length while the other is told to curtail his words.

items.text: Derivation from 'In righteousness shall you judge your neighbor'
items.text_en: Derivation from 'In righteousness shall you judge your neighbor'
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse 'In righteousness shall you judge your neighbor' that a judge must not have one litigant standing and the other sitting, or one speaking at length while the other is told to be brief. Another interpretation: judge every person favorably.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the verse 'בְּצֶדֶק תִּשְׁפֹּט עֲמִיתֶךָ' (In righteousness shall you judge your neighbor) that a judge must not have one litigant sitting and the other standing, or one speaking at length while the other is told to be brief.
The baraita offers an alternative interpretation of the verse: judge every person favorably (לְכַף זְכוּת).

items.text: Rabbi Yosef's Teaching and the Case of Rav Ulla
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosef's Teaching and the Case of Rav Ulla
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef teaches that 'your neighbor' refers to one who is with you in Torah and mitzvot; strive to judge him favorably. The Gemara relates that Rav Ulla, a colleague of Rav Yosef, had a case before Rav Nachman. Rav Yosef sent a message to Rav Nachman that Ulla is a 'colleague' in Torah and mitzvot. Rav Nachman initially suspected flattery but then realized it was to resolve his case.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef teaches that the verse 'בצדק תשפוט עמיתך' (judge your neighbor righteously) refers to one who is with you in Torah and mitzvot, and one must strive to judge him favorably.
The Gemara relates that Rav Ulla had a case before Rav Nachman, and Rav Yosef sent a message to Rav Nachman that Ulla is a colleague in Torah and mitzvot.
Rav Nachman initially questions why Rav Yosef sent this message, suspecting it might be flattery.
Rav Nachman then realizes that Rav Yosef's message was intended to resolve Ulla's case favorably, not to flatter.

items.text: Alternative interpretation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation for the Mishnah's ruling about judges sitting and litigants standing, suggesting it might be for the sake of the judges' convenience.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative interpretation: the Mishnah's ruling about judges sitting and litigants standing is for the judges' convenience (שודא דדייני).

items.text: Dispute about witnesses and stages of judgment
items.text_en: Dispute about witnesses and stages of judgment
items.desc_en: Ulla and Rav Huna debate whether the dispute about standing applies to litigants or witnesses, and whether it applies during deliberation or the final verdict. A second version of Rav Huna's statement compares witnesses to the final verdict.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that the dispute about standing applies to litigants, but all agree witnesses must stand, citing the verse 'וְעָמְדוּ שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים'.
Rav Huna states that the dispute about standing applies during deliberation, but at the final verdict all agree judges sit and litigants stand, citing the verse about Moses.

sub.text: Second version of Rav Huna's statement
sub.text_en: Second version of Rav Huna's statement
sub.desc_en: A second version of Rav Huna's statement compares witnesses to the final verdict, requiring standing for both.

items.text: Rav Nachman's dilemma with Rav Huna's wife
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's dilemma with Rav Huna's wife
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman, faced with judging a case involving Rav Huna's wife, devises a plan to stand without disrespecting her or the litigant. The Gemara questions this against the earlier ruling, and explains he sat as if removing his shoes while delivering the verdict.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman, faced with judging a case involving Rav Huna's wife, devises a plan to stand without disrespecting her or the litigant.
The Gemara questions Rav Nachman's standing against the earlier ruling that during the final verdict judges sit and litigants stand.
The Gemara explains that Rav Nachman sat as if removing his shoes while delivering the verdict, thus not violating the rule.

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's ruling on a Torah scholar and an ignoramus
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's ruling on a Torah scholar and an ignoramus
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna rules that when a Torah scholar and an ignoramus have a case, the scholar is seated, and the ignoramus is told to sit; if he stands, we do not object.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna rules that when a Torah scholar (צורבא מרבנן) and an ignoramus (עם הארץ) have a case together, the scholar is seated, the ignoramus is told to sit, and if he stands we do not object.

items.text: Rav Pappa's case with Rav bar Sherevya
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's case with Rav bar Sherevya
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa initially seats both Rav bar Sherevya and his litigant, but when the court agent disturbs the seating, he does not reseat the ignoramus. He justifies this by assuming the scholar considered himself seated.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Rav bar Sherevya had a case before Rav Pappa, and Rav Pappa seated both him and his litigant.
The gemara questions how Rav Pappa could allow the court agent to disturb the seating, since this would silence the litigant's arguments.
Rav Pappa explains that the scholar likely considered himself seated, and it was only the agent who was not appeased by him.

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's caution against appearing to arrange the case
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's caution against appearing to arrange the case
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna warns that a Torah scholar should not sit first in a case with an ignoramus, as it appears he is arranging his arguments, unless he has a fixed study time.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna warns that a Torah scholar should not sit first in a case with an ignoramus, as it appears he is arranging his arguments, unless he has a fixed study time.

items.text: Testimony before an inferior court and the exception for Hillul Hashem
items.text_en: Testimony before an inferior court and the exception for Hillul Hashem
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna rules that a Torah scholar should not go to testify before a lesser judge if it is beneath his dignity, but Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi supports this with a Mishnah. However, in matters of prohibition or Hillul Hashem, honor is set aside.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna rules that a Torah scholar who knows testimony should not go to a lesser court if it is beneath his dignity.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's support
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's support
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi supports this with a Mishnah: one who finds a sack or basket that it is not his dignity to take should not take it.
The Gemara distinguishes: the honor rule applies only to monetary cases, but in matters of prohibition or Hillul Hashem (desecration of God's name), one does not defer to a rabbi's honor.

items.text: Ameimar seats witnesses despite Ulla's ruling
items.text_en: Ameimar seats witnesses despite Ulla's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Yeymar had testimony for Mar Zutra, and Ameimar seated all parties. Rav Ashi objects based on Ulla's ruling that witnesses must stand, but Ameimar explains that the honor of Torah overrides the requirement to stand.

sub.desc_en: The narrative opens: Rav Yeymar knew testimony for Mar Zutra, came before Ameimar, and Ameimar seated all of them.
Rav Ashi objects to Ameimar, citing Ulla's ruling that witnesses must stand.
Ameimar answers that both are positive commandments, and the commandment of honoring Torah takes precedence.
The Gemara provides a mnemonic for the upcoming discussion: advocacy, ignoramus, robbery, fraud.

items.text: Baraita on distancing from falsehood
items.text_en: Baraita on distancing from falsehood
items.desc_en: A Baraita derives from the verse 'Distance yourself from a false matter' that a judge must not act as an advocate for his own words, seat an ignorant student, or join with a known robber or a case he knows is fraudulent.

sub.desc_en: The Baraita opens by deriving from the verse 'Distance yourself from a false matter' that a judge must not act as an advocate for his own statements.
The Baraita derives from the same verse that a judge must not seat an ignorant student before him.
The Baraita derives from the same verse that a judge or witness who knows another is a robber must not join with him.
The Baraita begins to derive from the same verse that a judge who knows a case is fraudulent must not decide it based on the witnesses' testimony alone.

items.text: Opening rhetorical question and answer
items.text_en: Opening rhetorical question and answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a collar is hung around the neck of witnesses, and answers with the verse "Distance yourself from a false matter" as the source for the prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks rhetorically whether a collar is hung around the neck of witnesses, implying someone might think the only deterrent is physical.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'Distance yourself from a false matter' (משפטים) serves as the biblical source forbidding false testimony.

items.text: Siman (mnemonic) for the list
items.text_en: Siman (mnemonic) for the list
items.desc_en: A mnemonic lists the topics that follow: three cases of a student, three of creditors, and cases of a shabby garment, a listener, and one who prompts.

sub.desc_en: A mnemonic marker (סימן) is given to recall the upcoming list of examples.

items.text: Three prohibitions for a student
items.text_en: Three prohibitions for a student
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives three prohibitions for a student from the verse: not to remain silent when seeing a merit for the poor or a liability for the rich, not to wait for his teacher to err in judgment to later claim the ruling, and not to join as a witness when his teacher claims to have a single witness. The Gemara clarifies that the last case involves a scenario where the student merely stands there without testifying falsely, yet it is still prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where is it derived that a student sitting before his teacher who sees a merit for the poor or a liability for the rich may not remain silent? It answers: the verse 'מִדְּבַר שֶׁקֶר תִּרְחָק' (distance yourself from a false matter) teaches this.
The Gemara derives a second prohibition: a student who sees his teacher err in judgment may not wait for the ruling to be completed in order to later claim it as his own, from the same verse.
The Gemara derives a third prohibition: a student whose teacher claims to have a single witness may not join with him as a second witness, from the same verse.

The Gemara objects: does this third case really come from 'מִדְּבַר שֶׁקֶר תִּרְחָק'? The student is certainly lying, and the Torah already prohibits false testimony with 'לֹא תַעֲנֶה בְרֵעֲךָ עֵד שָׁקֶר' (do not bear false witness against your neighbor).

The Gemara resolves: the case is where the teacher says 'I definitely have one witness, come and stand there but say nothing, since you are not uttering a falsehood' — even so it is prohibited, because of the verse 'מִדְּבַר שֶׁקֶר תִּרְחָק' (distance yourself from a false matter).

items.text: Three prohibitions for creditors
items.text_en: Three prohibitions for creditors
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives three prohibitions for a creditor from the verse: not to claim double to extract an admission and then a oath, not to deny in court and admit outside to avoid an oath, and not to have three creditors act as two witnesses and one litigant to extract money and divide it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where is it derived that a creditor who is owed 100 dinars should not claim 200 to extract an admission and then an oath?
The Gemara answers: the verse 'Distance yourself from a false matter' teaches this prohibition.
The Gemara asks: from where is it derived that a debtor who is claimed 200 dinars should not deny in court and admit outside to avoid an oath?
The Gemara answers: the verse 'Distance yourself from a false matter' teaches this prohibition.
The Gemara asks: from where is it derived that three creditors should not act as one litigant and two witnesses to extract money and divide it?
The Gemara answers: the verse 'Distance yourself from a false matter' teaches this prohibition.

items.text: Prohibition regarding disparity in dress
items.text_en: Prohibition regarding disparity in dress
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that if one litigant is shabbily dressed and the other is finely dressed, the court must tell the wealthy one to dress like the poor one or clothe the poor one, citing the verse. Rava bar Rav Huna would tell litigants to remove their shoes before judgment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where is it derived that if two litigants come to court, one dressed in rags and one in a fine garment, the court must tell the wealthy one to dress like the poor one or clothe the poor one? It answers: The verse states: 'Distance yourself from a false matter.'
The Gemara relates that when litigants would come before רבא בר רב הונא (Rava bar Rav Huna), he would tell them: Remove your fine shoes and descend for judgment.

items.text: Prohibition for judge and litigant to hear or present before the other party arrives
items.text_en: Prohibition for judge and litigant to hear or present before the other party arrives
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that a judge must not hear the words of one litigant before the other arrives, and a litigant must not present his case to the judge before the other arrives. Rav Kahana teaches this from the verse "Do not bear" (Exodus 20:13) interpreted as "Do not cause to bear."

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where is it derived that a judge must not hear the words of one litigant before the other arrives, and answers: The verse 'מִדְּבַר שֶׁקֶר תִּרְחָק' (distance yourself from a false matter) teaches this.
The Gemara asks: From where is it derived that a litigant must not present his case to the judge before the other arrives, and answers: The same verse teaches this.
Rav Kahana teaches the same prohibition from the verse 'לֹא תִשָּׂא' (Do not bear), interpreting it as 'לֹא תַשִּׂיא' (Do not cause to bear).

items.text: Interpretation of "And who did not do good among his people"
items.text_en: Interpretation of "And who did not do good among his people"
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute the meaning of the verse: Rav says it refers to one who comes with authorization (to testify), and Shmuel says it refers to one who purchases a field with liens against it.

sub.desc_en: Rav explains the verse 'who did not do well among his people' (יחזקאל) as referring to one who accepts a transfer of debt in court (הרשאה); Shmuel explains it as one who buys a field that has claims attached (עסיקין).
Rav interprets the verse as referring to one who comes with authorization (to testify).
Shmuel interprets the verse as referring to one who purchases a field with liens against it.

items.text: Exclusion of a king and a dice player from testimony
items.text_en: Exclusion of a king and a dice player from testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the mishnah's statement that the oath of testimony applies only to those fit to testify excludes a king (Rav Pappa) or a dice player (Rav Acha bar Yaakov). The Gemara clarifies that the dice player is biblically fit but rabbinically disqualified, while the king is biblically unfit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the mishnah's phrase 'only those fit to testify' excludes.
Rav Pappa answers that it excludes a king from testimony.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that it excludes a dice player from testimony.
The Gemara resolves the dispute: the one who says dice player logically includes the king, but the one who says king holds that the dice player is biblically fit and only rabbinically disqualified.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis on the scope of the oath of testimony
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis on the scope of the oath of testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis regarding whether the oath of testimony applies only in court or also outside. Rabbi Meir derives from the analogy to the oath of deposit that it applies both in and out of court, while the Rabbis limit the oath administered by others to court, but the self-administered oath applies even outside.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: On what basis do Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis dispute regarding the oath of testimony applying both in and out of court?

The Rabbis before Rav Pappa explain that the dispute is between deriving from the oath of deposit by full analogy (דון מינה ומינה) versus deriving the rule but limiting it to its original context (דון מינה ואוקי באתרה).

Rabbi Meir holds the full analogy (דון מינה ומינה): just as the oath of deposit applies both when the defendant swears himself and when others administer it, and both in and out of court, so too the oath of testimony applies in all these cases.

The Rabbis hold the limited analogy (דון מינה ואוקי באתרה): they derive that a self-administered oath of testimony is liable, but restrict it to court only, just as an oath administered by others applies only in court.

items.text: Rav Pappa's explanation of the Sages' position
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's explanation of the Sages' position
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that the Sages do not derive the law of the oath of testimony from the oath of deposit via a direct analogy (דון מינה ומינה). Instead, they derive it via a kal vahomer: if one is liable when sworn by others, all the more so when sworn by oneself. Applying the principle 'dayo laba min hadin lihyot kanidon', the Sages limit the liability to before a court, just as the oath by others is only in court.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa opens by asserting that if the Sages derived the law of the oath of testimony from the oath of deposit, everyone agrees they would not derive it via a direct analogy (דון מינה ומינה).
Rav Pappa explains that the Sages' actual reasoning is a kal vahomer (a fortiori argument): if one is liable when sworn by others, all the more so when sworn by oneself.

Rav Pappa applies the principle 'dayo laba min hadin lihyot kanidon' (the derived case is limited to the source case), concluding that the Sages restrict liability to before a court, just as the oath by others is only in court.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Pappa from the Mishnah of deposit
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Pappa from the Mishnah of deposit
items.desc_en: The Sages challenge Rav Pappa, citing a Mishnah about the oath of deposit that shows a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding whether the oath by others applies only in court. They argue that this dispute must be based on a direct analogy (דון מינה ומינה) from the law of testimony. The Gemara concludes that the challenge is valid only from that Mishnah, not from the earlier kal vahomer.

sub.desc_en: The Sages challenge Rav Pappa, arguing that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages in the Mishnah of deposit must be based on a direct analogy (דון מינה ומינה) from the law of testimony.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from the Mishnah of deposit
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from the Mishnah of deposit
sub.desc_en: The Sages cite the Mishnah of deposit, which states that Rabbi Meir requires the oath by others to be in court, while the Sages hold that both in and out of court are liable.
The Gemara asks: from where do the Sages derive that the oath by others in deposit is liable — is it not from the law of testimony, proving that the dispute is based on a direct analogy?
The Gemara resolves that the challenge is valid only from that Mishnah (of deposit), not from the earlier kal vahomer argument.

items.text: Source for liability for intentional violation of the oath
items.text_en: Source for liability for intentional violation of the oath
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that one is liable for intentional violation of the oath of testimony. It cites a baraita: in all other oaths, the Torah uses the term 'וְנֶעְלַם' (unwitting), but here it does not, thereby teaching that one is liable for intentional violation as for unwitting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that one is liable for intentional violation of the oath of testimony.
The Gemara cites a baraita: in all other oaths the Torah uses the term 'וְנֶעְלַם' (unwitting), but here it does not, thereby teaching that one is liable for intentional violation as for unwitting.

items.text: Definition of unwitting violation with intentional false testimony
items.text_en: Definition of unwitting violation with intentional false testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the case of unwitting violation of the oath combined with intentional false testimony. Rav Yehuda quoting Rav defines it as one who says, 'I know this oath is forbidden, but I do not know if one is liable to bring a korban for it.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to define the case of unwitting violation of the oath combined with intentional false testimony.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav defines the case as one who says, 'I know this oath is forbidden, but I do not know if one is liable to bring a korban for it.'

items.text: No liability for pure unwitting violation
items.text_en: No liability for pure unwitting violation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that there is no liability for a purely unwitting violation (without intentional false testimony). It questions whether this is already taught by the statements of Rav Kahana and Rav Asi, but concludes that it was necessary to teach it explicitly, lest one think that since the Torah omitted 'וְנֶעְלַם' here, any unwitting act would be exempt; the Mishnah teaches that this is not the case.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that there is no liability for a purely unwitting violation (without intentional false testimony).
The Gemara asks whether this ruling is already taught by the statements of Rav Kahana and Rav Asi.
The Gemara answers that it was necessary to teach it explicitly, even though it was already implied.

The Gemara explains that without this explicit teaching, one might think that since the Torah omitted 'וְנֶעְלַם' here, any unwitting act would be exempt; the Mishnah teaches that this is not the case.

items.text: Mishnah: The oath of testimony
items.text_en: Mishnah: The oath of testimony
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the oath of testimony: if one says to two witnesses 'Come and testify for me,' and they swear that they know no testimony, or they say 'We swear we know no testimony,' or he administers an oath and they say 'Amen,' they are liable. It details cases of multiple oaths outside and inside court, and the opinions of Rabbi Shimon. It also covers cases where witnesses deny one after another, and where there are two groups of witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking how the oath of testimony works, then lists cases where witnesses swear falsely and are liable.
The Mishnah details cases of multiple oaths outside and inside court, and Rabbi Shimon explains the reason for the difference.
The Mishnah rules on cases where witnesses deny together or one after another, and where one denies and the other admits.

sub.text: Mishnah's case of two groups of witnesses
sub.text_en: Mishnah's case of two groups of witnesses
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that when two groups of witnesses both deny, both are liable because testimony can be established through either group.

items.text: Gemara: Shmuel's ruling on witnesses who initiate an oath
items.text_en: Gemara: Shmuel's ruling on witnesses who initiate an oath
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that if witnesses see a litigant running after them and they say 'What are you running after us? We swear we know no testimony for you,' they are exempt unless they heard the oath from his mouth. The Gemara notes that this is already taught in a Mishnah about sending a message via a slave, but Shmuel's ruling is still necessary.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that witnesses who initiate an oath without hearing it from the litigant's mouth are exempt.
The Gemara asks what novel point Shmuel is teaching, since the Mishnah already covers a similar case.
The Gemara cites a baraita that already teaches that witnesses who receive an oath via a messenger or from the defendant are exempt.

items.text: Gemara's question about running after witnesses
items.text_en: Gemara's question about running after witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the mishnah's phrase 'until they hear from the claimant' is necessary to counter a possible assumption: if a claimant runs after witnesses, one might think it is as if he explicitly told them to testify. The mishnah teaches that this is not sufficient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the mishnah's phrase 'עַד שֶׁיִּשְׁמְעוּ מִפִּי הַתּוֹבֵעַ' (until they hear from the claimant) as the basis for its question.

The Gemara explains that the phrase is necessary to counter a possible assumption: if a claimant runs after witnesses, one might think it is as if he explicitly told them to testify, so the mishnah teaches that this is not sufficient.

items.text: The word 'said' is not precise
items.text_en: The word 'said' is not precise
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that in the mishnah about the oath of testimony, the word 'said' is not meant literally. It proves this from the parallel mishnah about the oath of deposit, where 'said' cannot be literal because liability applies even without explicit speech. Therefore, 'said' in both contexts is not precise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah about the oath of testimony, which uses the word 'אמר' (said), and questions whether this implies that liability requires explicit speech.
The Gemara asserts that the word 'אמר' (said) in the mishnah is not precise (לאו דווקא) and does not require literal speech.

sub.text: Supporting argument from the oath of deposit
sub.text_en: Supporting argument from the oath of deposit
sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports this by noting that in the parallel mishnah about the oath of deposit (שבועת הפקדון), the word 'אמר' cannot be literal because liability applies even without explicit speech, as the verse 'וכחש בעמיתו' (and he denied to his fellow) includes any denial.
The Gemara concludes that just as in the oath of deposit the word 'אמר' is not precise, so too in the oath of testimony it is not precise.

items.text: Alternative explanation: teaching the common way
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: teaching the common way
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers an alternative: perhaps the word 'said' is precise in both mishnayos, but the Tanna uses it to teach the common way of speaking. This resolves the redundancy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the word 'אמר' (said) is precise in the mishnah of Shevuot haPikadon but not in Shevuot haEidut, why does the Tanna bother to teach it in both places?
The Gemara answers: perhaps the Tanna uses the word 'אמר' (said) merely to teach the common way of speaking, not to indicate precision.

items.text: Supporting baraita for Shmuel
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for Shmuel
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Shmuel's view: if witnesses are seen coming after the claimant and they swear they don't know, they are exempt; but if it's about a deposit, they are liable.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Shmuel's view: witnesses seen coming after the claimant who swear they don't know are exempt, but if it's about a deposit they are liable.

items.text: Liability for denial in court vs. outside court
items.text_en: Liability for denial in court vs. outside court
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a verse that liability for false testimony applies only in court, where the denial could lead to monetary loss. Rav Papa questions whether the oath itself is also limited to court, but a baraita shows that multiple oaths outside court are liable individually, while in court only one liability applies. Thus, the oath can be outside court, but the denial must be in court.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that if one administered an oath to witnesses five times outside court and they denied, they are liable for each oath.
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that liability is specifically for denial in court, not outside court?

Abaye derives from the verse 'אִם לוֹא יַגִּיד וְנָשָׂא עֲוֹנוֹ' (If he does not utter it, he shall bear his iniquity) that liability applies only where the testimony would render another liable for monetary payment, i.e., in court.
Rav Papa objects: If so, one might say that the oath itself must be taken in court, not outside court.

Abaye rejects this, citing a baraita that the verse 'לְאַחַת' (for any one of these) makes one liable for each oath individually, and the mishnah shows that for oaths in court only one liability applies; thus the oath can be outside court but the denial must be in court.

items.text: Simultaneous denial by two witnesses
items.text_en: Simultaneous denial by two witnesses
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that if two witnesses deny together, they are liable. Rav Chisda explains this follows Rabbi Yossi HaGelili, who holds that simultaneous action is possible. Rabbi Yochanan says even the Rabbis agree, if they deny within 'toch kedei dibur' (the time it takes to greet a teacher). Rav Acha from Difti questions the length of this interval, and Ravina answers that each witness speaks within the other's speech.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that if two witnesses deny together, they are liable, and the Gemara questions how simultaneous denial is possible.
Rav Chisda explains that the mishnah follows Rabbi Yossi HaGelili, who holds that simultaneous action is possible.
Rabbi Yochanan says that even the Rabbis agree if the denials occur within 'toch kedei dibur' (the time it takes to greet a teacher), which is considered like simultaneous speech.
Rav Acha from Difti questions the length of 'toch kedei dibur', noting that the time to say the oath is longer than the greeting interval.
Ravina answers that each witness speaks within the other's speech, so the interval is measured from the end of the previous speaker's words.

items.text: Liability for a single witness
items.text_en: Liability for a single witness
items.desc_en: The mishnah says if witnesses testify one after another, the first is liable and the second exempt. A baraita disputes this: Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon holds a single witness is liable. The Gemara initially suggests they argue whether a single witness comes for an oath or for money, but Abaye's statement shows all agree a single witness comes for an oath. The real dispute is whether 'davar hagarim lemamon' (a matter that leads to money) is considered like money itself.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that when witnesses testify one after another, the first is liable and the second exempt.
The Gemara notes that the mishnah disagrees with a baraita where Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon holds a single witness liable.
The Gemara suggests the dispute is whether a single witness comes for an oath or for money.
The Gemara rejects this, citing Abaye's statement that all agree a single witness comes for an oath.
The Gemara resolves that all agree a single witness comes for an oath; the dispute is whether a matter that leads to money (דבר הגורם לממון) is considered like money itself.

items.text: Abaye's principle on witnesses for a sotah
items.text_en: Abaye's principle on witnesses for a sotah
items.desc_en: Abaye clarifies his earlier statement: all agree that a single witness for sotah (testifying to impurity) is liable because the Torah believed him; all agree that witnesses of kinuy (jealousy warning) are exempt because it is a 'gerama d'gerama' (indirect cause). The dispute is about witnesses of sotah (testifying to impurity) themselves.

sub.desc_en: Abaye introduces his principle: all agree on the liability of a single witness for sotah (טומאה) and on the exemption of witnesses for kinuy (jealousy warning), while the dispute concerns witnesses for sotah themselves.

Abaye explains that all agree a single witness for sotah (testifying to impurity) is liable because the Torah believed him, as derived from the verse 'וְעֵד אֵין בָּהּ' (and there is no witness against her).
Abaye explains that all agree witnesses for kinuy (jealousy warning) are exempt because their testimony is a גּוֹרֵם דְּגוֹרֵם (indirect cause) of the sotah's punishment.

items.text: Dispute about witnesses of a sotah
items.text_en: Dispute about witnesses of a sotah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between the two opinions in the Mishnah regarding witnesses of a sotah. One opinion holds that a matter that causes monetary loss is considered like money itself, so the witness is liable; the other holds it is not like money, so the witness is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute about witnesses of a sotah (סוטה), explaining that Mar holds that a matter causing monetary loss is considered like money itself (דבר הגורם לממון כממון דמי) and the witness is liable, while the other Mar holds it is not like money and the witness is exempt.

items.text: All agree in the case where the opposing party is suspected regarding an oath
items.text_en: All agree in the case where the opposing party is suspected regarding an oath
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the case where all agree that the witness is liable: when the opposing party (the borrower) is suspected of swearing falsely. The Gemara explains that this refers to a situation where both parties are suspected, and the oath returns to the one obligated to pay, who cannot swear and therefore must pay.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that all agree in the case where the opposing party is suspected regarding an oath, and also in the case of a single witness of Rabbi Abba.

The Gemara asks who is suspected: if the borrower is suspected, the lender could say 'if you had testified, I would have sworn and collected,' but the witness can retort 'who says you would have sworn?'
The Gemara answers that the case is where both parties are suspected, so the oath returns to the one obligated to pay, and since he cannot swear, he pays.

items.text: All agree in the case of a single witness of Rabbi Abba
items.text_en: All agree in the case of a single witness of Rabbi Abba
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the incident of a man who snatched a basket from another. A single witness testified, and the defendant admitted. Rabbi Ami was unsure how to judge, but Rabbi Abba ruled that since the defendant is obligated to take an oath but cannot (because he is a robber), he must pay.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of a single witness (עד אחד) associated with Rabbi Abba, describing a man who snatched a basket from his fellow.

Rabbi Ami questions how to judge the case: the defendant cannot be ordered to pay (only one witness), cannot be acquitted (one witness testifies), and cannot take an oath (he admitted to theft, making him a robber).
Rabbi Abba rules that the defendant is obligated to take an oath but cannot, and therefore must pay.

items.text: All agree in the case of a witness of death
items.text_en: All agree in the case of a witness of death
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that all agree there is a case where a witness of death is liable and a case where he is exempt. The exempt case is when the witness told the woman directly (not the court), as per the Mishnah that a woman who says 'my husband died' may remarry. The liable case is when he did not tell her or the court.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that all agree there is a case where a witness of death is liable and a case where he is exempt.
The Gemara explains the exempt case: when the witness told the woman directly and not the court, citing the Mishnah that a woman who says 'my husband died' may remarry.
The Gemara explains the liable case: when the witness did not tell the woman or the court.

items.text: Inference about land testimony
items.text_en: Inference about land testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the previous discussion that one who administers an oath to witnesses about land is liable. It deflects this by suggesting the case involved movable property that the woman had seized.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the previous discussion that one who administers an oath to witnesses about land is liable.
The Gemara deflects the inference by suggesting the case involved movable property that the woman had seized.

items.text: One denied and one admitted
items.text_en: One denied and one admitted
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case: if when both deny sequentially the first is liable, why mention the case where one admits? It answers that the case is where both denied and then one admitted within 'toch kedei dibbur', teaching that within that time it is considered like speech. It then resolves a difficulty between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Yochanan regarding the need for two teachings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to teach the case where one witness denied and one admitted, given that the earlier case of sequential denials already implies the first is liable.
The Gemara answers that the case is where both denied and then one admitted within 'toch kedei dibbur', teaching that within that time it is considered like speech.
The Gemara questions why according to Rabbi Yochanan, who already learns 'toch kedei dibbur' from the first clause, the second clause is also needed.
The Gemara resolves that the second clause is necessary to teach that 'toch kedei dibbur' applies even when the first statement is a denial and the second is an admission.

items.text: Two sets of witnesses: first set denied, then second set denied
items.text_en: Two sets of witnesses: first set denied, then second set denied
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if there are two sets of witnesses, and the first set denied, then the second set denied, the second set is liable because the first set already denied (so the second set's denial is false). But why is the first set liable?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if there are two sets of witnesses, and the first set denied, then the second set denied, the second set is liable because the first set already denied, but why is the first set liable?

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about the second wife
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about the second wife
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that the case involves a second wife whose husband was dying at the time of the first wife's denial, and her relatives were near death. The Gemara teaches that despite the presumption that most dying people die, she is not considered dead yet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the second wife is still alive, so why treat her as dead?

Ravina explains that the case involves a second wife whose husband was dying at the time of the first wife's denial, and her relatives were near death; the Gemara teaches that despite the presumption that most dying people die, she is not considered dead yet.

items.text: Mishnah: Different formulations of the oath and liability
items.text_en: Mishnah: Different formulations of the oath and liability
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where an oath is administered to witnesses. If the oath is general ('I adjure you...'), they are liable only once; if it specifies each item, they are liable for each. It lists various claims including deposits, theft, damages, fines, and personal injuries.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a case where a general oath formulation ('I adjure you...') leads to only one liability for the witnesses.
The Mishnah contrasts with a specific oath formulation that enumerates each claim, making the witnesses liable for each item separately.
The Mishnah presents another general oath case involving multiple types of grain, where witnesses are liable only once.
The Mishnah contrasts with a specific oath listing each grain type, making witnesses liable for each.
The Mishnah concludes with a list of diverse claims including damages, fines, and personal injuries, all under a general oath, and rules the witnesses liable.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry: Swearing witnesses to a fine
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry: Swearing witnesses to a fine
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one who swears witnesses to a fine (קנס) is liable. It distinguishes between Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's view (that a cause of money is like money) and the Rabbis' view (that it is not). The question is whether, since admitting to a fine exempts one, the denial is not of actual money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: what is the law regarding one who administers an oath to witnesses concerning a fine (קנס)?
The Gemara clarifies that according to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who holds that a cause of money is like money, there is no question — the witnesses are liable.
The Gemara states that the question arises according to the Rabbis, who hold that one who admits to a fine and then witnesses come is exempt.
The Gemara questions which view the Rabbis of that other sugya follow, concluding they align with the Rabbis here who hold that a cause of money is not like money.
The Gemara presents the dilemma: since admitting to a fine exempts one, is the denial not of actual money, or perhaps now he has not admitted and it is still money?

items.text: First attempted proof: Half-damage as a fine
items.text_en: First attempted proof: Half-damage as a fine
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's mention of 'half-damage' (חצי נזק) which is a fine. It explains that this follows the view that half-damage is monetary, or alternatively refers to half-damage from pebbles (צרורות) which is halachically monetary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's mention of 'half-damage' (חצי נזק) as evidence that an oath on fines is valid, noting that this follows the view that half-damage is monetary.

The Gemara first answers that the proof works only for the view that half-damage is monetary, then offers a second answer that the Mishnah refers to half-damage from pebbles (צרורות), which is halachically monetary.

items.text: Further analysis of the Mishnah's list
items.text_en: Further analysis of the Mishnah's list
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that double payment and four/five-fold payment are due to the principal, and seduction/rape cases involve shame and degradation (monetary). The Mishnah teaches two things: that half-damage from pebbles is monetary, and that setting fire on Yom Kippur excludes Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana's view that Yom Kippur is like Shabbat for payment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's mention of double payment (תשלומי כפל) to argue that it is due to the principal (קרנא) and thus monetary.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah's mention of four/five-fold payment (תשלומי ארבעה וחמישה) to argue that it is also due to the principal (קרנא) and thus monetary.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah's mention of seduction and rape cases (אנס ופתה) to argue that they involve shame and degradation (בושת ופגם), which are monetary.
The Gemara asks what the Mishnah teaches by listing these items, and answers that it teaches that all of them are monetary (ממונא).
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah teaches two things: the first part teaches that half-damage from pebbles (חצי נזק צרורות) is monetary.
The Gemara resolves that the second part teaches that setting fire on Yom Kippur (הדליק גדישי ביום הכיפורים) excludes Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana's view that Yom Kippur is like Shabbat for payment.

items.text: Incomplete continuation
items.text_en: Incomplete continuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins another attempted proof from the Mishnah's text but is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins another attempted proof from the Mishnah's text but is cut off.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's first clause
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's first clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the first clause of the Mishnah as following Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who requires witnesses to testify even without a prior claim. It then resolves an apparent contradiction with the second clause by explaining that the exemption for admission applies only when there are no witnesses at all.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that witnesses who testify about a bad name are liable, but one who admits on his own is exempt.
The Gemara identifies the first clause as following Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who requires witnesses to testify even without a prior claim.
The Gemara objects that the second clause, which exempts one who admits on his own, seems to follow the Rabbis, not Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara resolves that the entire Mishnah follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, and the exemption for admission applies only when there are no witnesses at all.

items.text: Mishnah: list of exempt testimonies
items.text_en: Mishnah: list of exempt testimonies
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists various testimonies about personal status and torts for which witnesses are exempt from the oath of testimony, including claims about being a priest, a Levite, or about certain damages.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists testimonies about personal status and torts for which witnesses are exempt from the oath of testimony.

items.text: Gemara's inference and Shmuel's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's inference and Shmuel's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that only non-monetary claims are exempt, but monetary claims would be liable. It notes a contradiction with a later Mishnah requiring the witnesses to hear from the claimant. Shmuel resolves this by saying the case involves a formal authorization (harsha'ah), and the Nehardeans' objection about movables is addressed by distinguishing whether the defendant denied the claim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that only non-monetary claims (like 'so-and-so is a priest') are exempt, implying that monetary claims would make the witnesses liable.
The Gemara objects that a later Mishnah explicitly requires witnesses to hear the claim from the plaintiff, contradicting the inference that monetary claims would be liable.
Shmuel resolves the contradiction by explaining that the case involves a formal authorization (הרשאה) where the claimant authorizes the witnesses to act on his behalf.
The Nehardeans object that they do not write a power of attorney (אורכתא) for movable property, which would undermine Shmuel's explanation.
The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing: the Nehardeans' rule applies only when the defendant denies the claim, but if he does not deny it, a power of attorney is written.

items.text: Tosefta: Rabbi Eliezer's gezerah shavah and objections
items.text_en: Tosefta: Rabbi Eliezer's gezerah shavah and objections
items.desc_en: A Tosefta cites Rabbi Eliezer who uses a gezerah shavah from 'or' in the oath of testimony to 'or' in the law of deposits to limit the oath to monetary claims. Objections are raised from the 'or' in murder and the 'or' in the sotah, but they are rejected because murder lacks an oath and sotah involves a priest.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta opens with a question: from where do we know that the verse speaks only of a monetary claim? Rabbi Eliezer answers with a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'אוֹ' (or) used in the oath of testimony to 'אוֹ' in the law of deposits, concluding that both are limited to monetary claims.
An objection is raised: the 'אוֹ' (or) in the law of murder should prove the analogy wrong, since it uses 'אוֹ' but does not involve a monetary claim.
The objection is rejected: the analogy is drawn only between cases that include an oath (שבועה), and murder lacks an oath, so it is excluded.
A second objection is raised: the 'אוֹ' (or) in the law of the sotah (suspected adulteress) should prove the analogy wrong, since it includes an oath but does not involve a monetary claim.
The second objection is rejected: the analogy is drawn only between cases that include an oath and do not involve a priest (כֹּהֵן), and the sotah involves a priest, so it is excluded.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva derives from the verse 'vehayah ki ye'asham le'achat me'eleh' that some cases are liable and some exempt: monetary claims are liable, other matters are exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva derives from the verse 'וְהָיָה כִּי יֶאְשַׁם לְאַחַת מֵאֵלֶּה' that some cases are liable (monetary claims) and some exempt (other matters).

items.text: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili explains that the verse 'vehu ed o ra'ah o yada' refers to testimony that can be established by sight without knowledge or knowledge without sight, giving examples of each.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili opens by citing the verse 'וְהוּא עֵד אוֹ רָאָה אוֹ יָדָע' and states that it speaks of testimony that can be established by sight without knowledge or knowledge without sight.

Rabbi Yosei HaGelili provides an example of sight without knowledge: a claimant says 'I counted a maneh for you in the presence of so-and-so' and calls witnesses who saw the transaction but did not know it was a loan.

Rabbi Yosei HaGelili provides an example of knowledge without sight: a claimant says 'You admitted to me that you owe a maneh in the presence of so-and-so' and calls witnesses who heard the admission but did not see the loan.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's kal vachomer
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon argues from a comparison to the law of deposits and a kal vachomer: since deposits, which include women, relatives, and disqualified witnesses, are limited to monetary claims, the oath of testimony is certainly limited to monetary claims.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon opens with a comparison: the oath of testimony (here) and the oath of deposits (there) both use the same language, so both are limited to monetary claims.

Rabbi Shimon adds a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): since the law of deposits, which includes women, relatives, and disqualified witnesses, is limited to monetary claims, the oath of testimony is certainly limited to monetary claims.

items.text: Gezeirah Shavah from deposit to testimony
items.text_en: Gezeirah Shavah from deposit to testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that just as the oath of deposit (פיקדון) applies only to monetary claims, so too the oath of testimony should be limited to monetary claims, using a gezeirah shavah from the word 'תֶּחֱטָא'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita argues that since the oath of deposit (פיקדון) applies only to monetary claims, the oath of testimony should also be limited to monetary claims, using a kal vachomer (a fortiori) inference.

The Gemara objects that the kal vachomer is flawed: the oath of deposit has leniencies (no liability for one who was adjured or for intentional false oaths), while the oath of testimony has stringencies (liability for both), so the inference is invalid.

The Gemara resolves by citing a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'תֶּחֱטָא' (shall sin) in both contexts, establishing that the oath of testimony, like the oath of deposit, applies only to monetary claims.

items.text: Rabba bar Ulla's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rabba bar Ulla's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Ulla challenges the gezeirah shavah by pointing to the 'or' (אוֹ) cases in the Torah, which include non-monetary claims. The Gemara then debates which analogy is stronger—deposit or 'or'—and concludes that deposit is more fitting due to multiple shared features.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Ulla objects to the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) by pointing to the 'אוֹ' (or) cases in the Torah, which include non-monetary claims.
The Gemara answers that it is more reasonable to derive from the case of a deposit (פיקדון) due to the verbal analogy of 'תֶּחֱטָא' (shall sin).
The Gemara objects that one could derive from the case of an utterance (ביטוי) since both involve a חטאת (sin-offering).
The Gemara answers again that deriving from deposit is more fitting due to multiple shared features: sin, intentionality, claim, denial, and past event.
The Gemara objects again that deriving from utterance is more fitting due to shared features of sin-offering and sliding scale, but concludes that the features of deposit are more numerous.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's derivation from 'מֵאֵלֶּה'
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's derivation from 'מֵאֵלֶּה'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva derives from the verse 'וְהָיָה כִי יֶאְשַׁם לְאַחַת מֵאֵלֶּה' that liability for false testimony applies only to monetary claims, not other matters. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Akiva relies on Rabbi Eliezer's 'or' cases.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva states his derivation from the verse 'וְהָיָה כִי יֶאְשַׁם לְאַחַת מֵאֵלֶּה' that liability for false testimony applies only to monetary claims, not other matters.
The Gemara objects: one could invert the derivation and conclude the opposite.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Akiva relies on Rabbi Eliezer's 'or' cases to support his interpretation.

items.text: Difference between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Difference between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva. One difference is witnesses to land (קרקע) or fines (קנס), with Rabbi Eliezer holding them liable and Rabbi Akiva exempting them, though Rabbi Yochanan disputes the land case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the positions of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva.
One difference is the case of one who administers an oath to witnesses regarding land (קרקע): Rabbi Eliezer holds them liable, Rabbi Akiva exempts them.
Rabbi Yochanan objects, stating that even according to Rabbi Eliezer, one who administers an oath to witnesses regarding land is exempt, so this cannot be the difference.
The Gemara provides an alternative difference: witnesses to fines (קנס), where Rabbi Eliezer holds them liable and Rabbi Akiva exempts them.

items.text: Rabbi Yose HaGlili's view and its implications
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose HaGlili's view and its implications
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yose HaGlili interprets the verse 'וְהוּא עֵד אוֹ רָאָה אוֹ יָדָע' to refer to testimony that can be established by sight without knowledge or knowledge without sight. The Gemara discusses whether this implies he rejects Rabbi Acha's principle and concludes that he holds witnesses to fines are exempt, as otherwise sight without knowledge would be impossible.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yose HaGlili interprets the verse 'וְהוּא עֵד אוֹ רָאָה אוֹ יָדָע' to refer to testimony that can be established by sight without knowledge or knowledge without sight.

Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether Rabbi Yose HaGlili rejects Rabbi Acha's principle, since if he accepted it, he would also find a case of sight without knowledge in capital cases, like Rabbi Shimon ben Shatach's story.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Shatach describes a case of circumstantial evidence in a capital case, where he saw a man with a bloody sword next to a dying victim but could not execute him due to the requirement of two witnesses.

The Gemara answers that even if Rabbi Yose HaGlili accepts Rabbi Acha's principle, knowledge without sight is possible, but sight without knowledge is impossible because one must know if the killer was a gentile or a Jew, or if the victim was a טריפה (mortally wounded) or healthy.

The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yose HaGlili holds that one who administers an oath to witnesses of a fine (קנס) is exempt from the oath of testimony, because if he were liable, sight without knowledge would be possible in cases of fines where one must know if a gentile or Jew, or a virgin or non-virgin, was involved.

items.text: Beginning of a new case: 'Maneh' deposit
items.text_en: Beginning of a new case: 'Maneh' deposit
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna sits before Rav Yehuda, who raises a question about a case where one says 'I deposited a maneh with you in the presence of so-and-so.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna sits before Rav Yehuda, who raises a question about a case where one says 'I deposited a maneh with you in the presence of so-and-so.'

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Hamnuna's response about witnesses outside
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Hamnuna's response about witnesses outside
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a case where witnesses see the defendant from outside. Rav Hamnuna explains that if the defendant says 'it never happened,' he is deemed a confirmed liar; if he says 'yes, I took it, but it's mine,' the witnesses are irrelevant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the law is when witnesses see the defendant from outside the house.

Rav Hamnuna explains that the outcome depends on the defendant's claim: if he denies the event entirely, he is a confirmed liar; if he admits taking but claims ownership, the witnesses are irrelevant.

items.text: Case of a claim near a pillar and Reish Lakish's ruling
items.text_en: Case of a claim near a pillar and Reish Lakish's ruling
items.desc_en: A man claims he lent money to another near a pillar; the defendant says he never passed that pillar. Witnesses testify he urinated there. Reish Lakish rules he is a confirmed liar.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case where a claimant says he lent money near a pillar, the defendant denies ever passing that pillar, witnesses testify he urinated there, and Reish Lakish rules he is a confirmed liar.

items.text: Rav Nachman's objection to Reish Lakish's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's objection to Reish Lakish's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects that this is a Persian judgment; the defendant only denied the specific incident, not that he never passed the pillar at all.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects that Reish Lakish's ruling is a Persian judgment, since the defendant only denied the specific incident, not that he never passed the pillar at all.

items.text: Alternative version of the case and Rava's explanation
items.text_en: Alternative version of the case and Rava's explanation
items.desc_en: An alternative version has the defendant saying 'I never passed that pillar at all,' and Rav Nachman rules him a confirmed liar. Rava explains that a person may do something without it being on his mind.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version presents the case where the defendant says 'I never passed that pillar at all,' witnesses testify he urinated there, and Rav Nachman rules him a confirmed liar.
Rava explains to Rav Nachman that a person may do something without it being on his mind, justifying the ruling.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon's statement
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon's statement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah quotes Rabbi Shimon who says he is liable here (for the oath of testimony) and liable for the oath of deposit, etc.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Shimon's statement that one is liable here (for the oath of testimony) and liable for the oath of deposit, etc.

items.text: First question about the joke in the West
items.text_en: First question about the joke in the West
items.desc_en: The Gemara reports that they laughed about this in the West. The first explanation is that the Mishnah states: 'What is true of deposit? That it did not make the one sworn by others like the one sworn by himself, nor the intentional like the unintentional.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that they laughed about this in the West and asks: what is the joke?

The Gemara explains that the joke is in the Mishnah's statement: 'What is true of deposit? That it did not make the one sworn by others like the one sworn by himself, nor the intentional like the unintentional.'

items.text: Objection: Rabbi Shimon derives 'sworn by himself' from deposit
items.text_en: Objection: Rabbi Shimon derives 'sworn by himself' from deposit
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Since Rabbi Shimon derives 'sworn by himself' in testimony from deposit via a gezerah shavah, why does he need to say that deposit did not make 'sworn by others' like 'sworn by himself'? He could derive it from testimony!

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Since Rabbi Shimon derives 'sworn by himself' in testimony from deposit via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), why does he need to say that deposit did not make 'sworn by others' like 'sworn by himself'? He could derive it from testimony!

items.text: Rejection: Rabbi Shimon uses a kal vachomer
items.text_en: Rejection: Rabbi Shimon uses a kal vachomer
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the objection: Perhaps Rabbi Shimon derives it via a kal vachomer – if one is liable when sworn by others, all the more so when sworn by himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the objection: perhaps Rabbi Shimon derives the liability for a self-administered oath in testimony via a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from an oath administered by others.

items.text: Second question: the intentional like the unintentional
items.text_en: Second question: the intentional like the unintentional
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the joke is about the phrase 'intentional like unintentional' in deposit. It objects: In testimony, the intentional is derived from the absence of 'and it was hidden'; here too there is no 'and it was hidden'!

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the joke is about the phrase 'intentional like unintentional' in the deposit case.
The Gemara objects: In testimony, the intentional is derived from the absence of 'and it was hidden'; here too there is no 'and it was hidden'!

items.text: Rav Huna's suggestion and the joke about deriving from me'ilah
items.text_en: Rav Huna's suggestion and the joke about deriving from me'ilah
items.desc_en: Rav Huna suggests that Rabbi Shimon derives the intentional in deposit from me'ilah (sacrilege). The joke is: why derive from me'ilah when he could derive from testimony?

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna asks what the joke is, suggesting that Rabbi Shimon derives the intentional case in deposit from me'ilah (sacrilege).
The gemara objects that the joke is precisely this: why derive from me'ilah when he could derive from testimony?

items.text: Debate over which derivation is more appropriate
items.text_en: Debate over which derivation is more appropriate
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates whether it is more logical to derive from me'ilah (because of common features like 'everything,' 'benefit,' 'fixed,' 'principal,' 'guilt-offering') or from testimony (because of 'sin,' 'layman,' 'oath,' 'claim and denial,' 'yes/no'). The latter has more points of similarity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that it is more logical to derive the law from me'ilah (מעילה) because the derivation is from a similar case of me'ilah.
The Gemara counters that deriving from testimony (עדות) is more appropriate because both use the term 'תֶּחֱטָא' (shall sin).
The Gemara argues that me'ilah is more fitting because it shares multiple features: 'everything,' 'benefit,' 'fixed,' 'principal,' and 'guilt-offering.'
The Gemara concludes that testimony has more points of similarity: 'sin,' 'layman,' 'oath,' 'claim and denial,' and 'yes/no,' so it is the more appropriate derivation.

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna's final explanation of the joke
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna's final explanation of the joke
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua explain that the joke is: since Rabbi Shimon learns via a gezerah shavah, why does he need to object that deposit did not make 'sworn by others' like 'sworn by himself'? The Gemara suggests he only objects before the gezerah shavah is established.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the joke actually is, given that Rabbi Shimon learns from a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) and could have objected to the comparison before it was established.

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua explain that the joke is that Rabbi Shimon's objection about 'sworn by others' and 'sworn by himself' was made before the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) was established, but after it was established he no longer objects.

items.text: Rava bar Ittai's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rava bar Ittai's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava bar Ittai challenges: But Rabbi Shimon is the one who says the oath of deposit is not subject to atonement for intentional violation! The Gemara resolves: He only objects about 'intentional like unintentional' (derived from me'ilah), but not about 'sworn by others like sworn by himself.' The Gemara then suggests that testimony could derive from deposit that intentional is not like unintentional, just as deposit derives from me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Ittai objects: But Rabbi Shimon is the one who taught that the oath of deposit is not subject to atonement for intentional violation, contradicting the earlier resolution.
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Shimon only objects about 'intentional like unintentional' (derived from me'ilah), but not about 'sworn by others like sworn by himself.'
The Gemara then suggests that testimony could derive from deposit that intentional is not like unintentional, just as deposit derives from me'ilah.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Torah's juxtaposition
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Torah's juxtaposition
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Torah wrote the law of testimony alongside the laws of oath of utterance and impurity of the Temple and its sancta: to teach that in all those cases the word 've-ne'elam' (and it was hidden) is stated, but here it is not stated, thereby making one liable for intentional transgression like an unintentional one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Torah juxtaposed the law of testimony with oath of utterance and impurity of the Temple and its sancta to teach that in all those cases the word 've-ne'elam' (and it was hidden) is stated, but here it is not stated, thereby making one liable for intentional transgression like an unintentional one.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of exemption from the oath of testimony
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of exemption from the oath of testimony
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists several cases where witnesses are exempt from liability for an oath of testimony: when the claim is not a monetary claim like a deposit, when the oath precedes the knowledge of testimony, when the oath is given in a general assembly without specifying the witnesses, when the witnesses are invalid (e.g., relatives or disqualified), and when the oath is delivered through a messenger or by the defendant.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the first case of exemption: when the claim is not a monetary claim like a deposit, the witnesses are exempt.
The Mishnah states the second case: if the oath precedes the knowledge of testimony, the witnesses are exempt.
The Mishnah states the third case: if the oath is given in a general assembly without specifying the witnesses, they are exempt.
The Mishnah states the fourth case: if the witnesses are invalid (e.g., relatives or disqualified), they are exempt.
The Mishnah states the fifth case: if the oath is delivered through a messenger or by the defendant, the witnesses are exempt.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation for monetary claim requirement
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation for monetary claim requirement
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from a verbal analogy (gezeirah shavah) between the word 'techeta' (shall sin) stated here and in the case of a deposit, that the oath of testimony only applies to a monetary claim where the claimant has a right to the money.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the case and states that a verbal analogy (גזירה שוה) from the word 'תֶּחֱטָא' is needed to derive the requirement of a monetary claim.
The Gemara completes the verbal analogy: just as the word 'תֶּחֱטָא' in the deposit case refers to a monetary claim where the claimant has a right, so too here it requires a monetary claim.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation that oath must follow knowledge
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation that oath must follow knowledge
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 've-sham'ah kol alah ve-hu ed o ra'ah o yada' that the oath must come after the witnesses have knowledge, not before.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse to derive that the oath must follow knowledge, not precede it.
The Gemara concludes that the verse teaches liability only when knowledge precedes the oath, not when the oath precedes knowledge.

items.text: Gemara: Analysis of the case of standing in the synagogue
items.text_en: Gemara: Analysis of the case of standing in the synagogue
items.desc_en: Shmuel comments that even if the witnesses are among the crowd, the oath is not binding unless the oath-taker specifically addresses them. The Gemara clarifies that this is necessary only when he is standing over them, lest one think it is as if he addressed them. A baraita supports this, deriving from 've-hu ed' that the witnesses must be designated.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of one who stood in the synagogue and said 'I adjure you'.
Shmuel rules that even if the witnesses are among the crowd, the oath is not binding unless specifically addressed.
The Gemara questions why Shmuel's statement is necessary, as it seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that Shmuel's statement is needed when the speaker stands over them, lest one think it is as if he addressed them.
A baraita supports Shmuel, deriving from 've-hu ed' that the witnesses must be designated.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation for invalid witnesses
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation for invalid witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'im lo yagid ve-nasa avono' that the oath only applies to those who are fit to give testimony, excluding those who know only from hearsay or are relatives or disqualified.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the verse 'אִם לוֹא יַגִּיד וְנָשָׂא עֲוֹנוֹ' that the oath only applies to those fit to give testimony (not those who know only from hearsay or are relatives/disqualified).

items.text: Gemara: Derivation for oath via messenger or defendant
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation for oath via messenger or defendant
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'im lo yagid' that the oath must be heard from the claimant himself, not from a messenger or the defendant. Rabbi Elazar explains: 'im lo yagid' – if he (the witness) does not tell him (the claimant), he bears sin, but if he does not tell another, he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that if the oath is sent via a slave or spoken by the defendant, the witnesses are exempt; Rabbi Elazar explains from the verse 'אִם לוֹא יַגִּיד' — if he does not testify for HIM (the plaintiff) he bears iniquity, but if for another he is exempt.
Rabbi Elazar explains the derivation: the verse 'im lo yagid' implies that only if the witness does not tell the claimant himself does he bear sin, but if he does not tell another, he is exempt.

items.text: Mishnah: Types of oath formulations and divine names
items.text_en: Mishnah: Types of oath formulations and divine names
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses which formulations of an oath are binding: using the words 'mashbi'a', 'metzaveh', 'oser', or 'koveil' are effective. Swearing by heaven and earth is not binding, but swearing by various divine names (e.g., 'El', 'Elohim', 'Shaddai', 'Tzeva'ot', 'Channun ve-Rachum') is binding. It also discusses the laws of cursing using these names, with disputes between Rabbi Meir and the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists effective oath formulations: 'mashbi'a', 'metzaveh', 'oser', and 'koveil' all render the witnesses liable.
The Mishnah states that swearing by heaven and earth is not binding.
The Mishnah lists divine names (e.g., 'El', 'Elohim', 'Shaddai', 'Tzeva'ot', 'Channun ve-Rachum') that render an oath binding.
Rabbi Meir holds that one who curses using any of these names is liable.
The Sages exempt one who curses using these names.
Rabbi Meir holds that one who curses his father or mother using these names is liable.
The Sages exempt one who curses his father or mother using these names.
The Mishnah states that one who curses himself or his friend using these names violates a negative commandment, and defines the Torah's curse formula.
Rabbi Meir holds that euphemistic curse formulations like 'Al yakekha' render one liable.
The Sages exempt one who uses euphemistic curse formulations.

items.text: Gemara: Interpretation of the oath formulations
items.text_en: Gemara: Interpretation of the oath formulations
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that 'mashbi'a' means 'I adjure you by the oath stated in the Torah', and similarly for 'metzaveh' and 'oser'. Abaye objects based on a baraita that includes 'koveil' (I bind you), which is not a Torah term. Abaye then explains that all these formulations mean 'I adjure you by an oath'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the formulation 'mashbi'a' actually means.

Rav Yehuda explains that each formulation refers to the corresponding Torah concept: 'mashbi'a' means 'by the oath stated in the Torah', 'metzaveh' means 'by the command stated in the Torah', and 'oser' means 'by the prohibition stated in the Torah'.
Abaye objects that Rabbi Chiyya's baraita includes the term 'koveil' (I bind you), which is not a Torah term, so Rav Yehuda's explanation cannot account for it.
Abaye resolves the objection by explaining that all formulations, including 'koveil', mean 'I adjure you by an oath'.

items.text: Gemara: Distinction between divine names and epithets
items.text_en: Gemara: Distinction between divine names and epithets
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'Channun ve-Rachum' is a divine name, citing a baraita that lists names that may not be erased: 'El', 'Elohim', 'Shaddai', 'Tzeva'ot', etc., but 'Channun ve-Rachum', 'Erech Apayim', and 'Rav Chesed' are epithets that may be erased. Abaye resolves that the Mishnah means 'by the One who is Channun' (merciful), not the name itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'Channun ve-Rachum' is considered a divine name, based on the Mishnah's inclusion of it among names that obligate one who swears by them.

The Gemara cites a baraita that lists names which may not be erased, including 'El', 'Elohim', 'Shaddai', 'Tzeva'ot', etc., and explicitly states that 'Channun ve-Rachum', 'Erech Apayim', and 'Rav Chesed' are epithets that may be erased, contradicting the Mishnah's implication.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah means 'by the One who is Channun' (merciful), referring to God's attribute, not the name itself.

items.text: Gemara's question about 'in heaven and on earth'
items.text_en: Gemara's question about 'in heaven and on earth'
