items.desc_en: Rava challenges the earlier interpretation that 'merciful' refers to God's attribute, arguing that 'in heaven and on earth' could similarly be interpreted as 'He whose are heaven and earth'. The Gemara distinguishes: since there is no other entity called 'merciful', it must refer to God; but since heaven and earth exist, the phrase refers to the physical objects.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that the phrase 'merciful' in the oath refers to God's attribute.
Rava objects that if 'merciful' is interpreted as God's attribute, then 'in heaven and on earth' could similarly be interpreted as 'He whose are heaven and earth'.
The Gemara resolves that since no other entity is called 'merciful', it must refer to God, but since heaven and earth exist, the phrase refers to the physical objects.

items.text: Baraita on partial divine names
items.text_en: Baraita on partial divine names
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that letters from the Tetragrammaton (אל from אלהים, יה from יהוה) are not erasable, but letters from other divine names (שד from שדי, אד from אדני, צב from צבאות) are erasable. Rabbi Yosei disagrees regarding 'צבאות', but Shmuel rules the halakha is not like Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that partial divine names from the Tetragrammaton (אל from אלהים, יה from יהוה) are not erasable, while letters from other divine names (שד from שדי, אד from אדני, צב from צבאות) are erasable.

Rabbi Yosei argues that the entire word 'צבאות' is erasable, because it is a name for Israel, not a divine name, citing the verse 'וְהוֹצֵאתִי אֶת צִבְאֹתַי' (and I will bring out my hosts, the children of Israel).
Shmuel rules that the halakha (binding law) does not follow Rabbi Yosei's opinion.

items.text: Baraita on prefixes and suffixes attached to God's name
items.text_en: Baraita on prefixes and suffixes attached to God's name
items.desc_en: A baraita rules that letters attached to God's name, whether before (e.g., ל of ליהוה) or after (e.g., נו of אלהינו), are erasable. Aḥerim argue that suffixes are not erasable because the name has already sanctified them. Rav Huna rules the halakha follows Aḥerim.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that any letter ancillary to God's name, whether a prefix or suffix, may be erased, and lists examples of prefixes that are erasable.
The baraita continues by listing examples of suffixes that are erasable, such as נו of אלהינו and הם of אלהיהם.
Aḥerim argue that suffixes are not erasable because the name of God has already sanctified them.
Rav Huna rules that the halakha follows Aḥerim, meaning suffixes are not erasable.
A mnemonic is provided listing the topics that follow: Abraham, Lot, Naboth, Gibeah of Benjamin, Solomon, and Daniel.

items.text: Names of Abraham in the Torah
items.text_en: Names of Abraham in the Torah
items.desc_en: All occurrences of 'Adonai' in the story of Abraham are sacred except one (Genesis 18:3). Ḥanina ben Aḥi Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya in the name of Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i argue that even that one is sacred. The Gemara connects this to Rav Yehuda's statement about hospitality being greater than receiving the Divine Presence.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states the general rule: all names of God in the Torah regarding Abraham are sacred, except for one instance in Genesis 18:3 which is non-sacred.

sub.text: Ḥanina ben Aḥi Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya in the name of Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i
sub.text_en: Ḥanina ben Aḥi Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya in the name of Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i
sub.desc_en: Ḥanina ben Aḥi Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, citing Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i, argue that even that one instance is sacred.
The Gemara asks in accordance with whose opinion Rav Yehuda's statement (that hospitality is greater than receiving the Divine Presence) aligns, and answers: in accordance with that pair of tanna'im.

items.text: Names of Lot
items.text_en: Names of Lot
items.desc_en: All occurrences of 'Adonai' in the story of Lot are profane except one (Genesis 19:18), which refers to God who has power over life and death.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states the general rule that all occurrences of 'Adonai' in the Lot narrative are profane, except one.
The Tanna Kamma cites Genesis 19:18 as the exception, where 'Adonai' refers to God who has power over life and death.

items.text: Names of Nabot and Mikhah
items.text_en: Names of Nabot and Mikhah
items.desc_en: All divine names in the story of Nabot are sacred; those in Mikhah are profane. Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes: in Mikhah, 'אל' is profane, 'יה' is sacred, except for one instance where 'אל' is sacred (Judges 18:31).

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states the general rule: all divine names in the story of Nabot are sacred, while those in Mikhah are profane.
Rabbi Eliezer agrees about Nabot but introduces a distinction for Mikhah: some names there are profane and some sacred.
Rabbi Eliezer specifies that the name 'אל' (El) is profane, while 'יה' (Yah) is sacred.
Rabbi Eliezer notes one exception where 'אל' (El) is sacred, citing the verse from Judges 18:31.

items.text: Names in the story of Gibeath Binyamin
items.text_en: Names in the story of Gibeath Binyamin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer says all divine names in the story of the concubine in Gibeath Binyamin are profane; Rabbi Yehoshua says they are sacred. Rabbi Eliezer argues that God would not promise and then fail to fulfill. Rabbi Yehoshua responds that God fulfilled His promise, but the people did not test whether they would win or lose; only at the end, when they tested, did God agree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says all divine names in the Gibeath Binyamin story are profane; Rabbi Yehoshua says they are sacred.
Rabbi Eliezer objects: Would God promise and then not fulfill?
Rabbi Yehoshua responds: God fulfilled His promise; the people failed to test whether they would win or lose, and only when they finally tested did God agree, as the verse shows.

items.text: Names of Solomon in Song of Songs
items.text_en: Names of Solomon in Song of Songs
items.desc_en: All occurrences of 'Solomon' in Song of Songs are sacred, referring to God, except for 'my vineyard, which is mine, is before me; the thousand shekels are for you, Solomon' (Song 8:12). Some say even that is profane, and also 'Behold his bed, which is Solomon's' (Song 3:7). The Gemara reconciles Shmuel's statement about a kingdom that kills one-sixth of the world not being punished, which uses the verse, with the opinions of the first tanna and the 'some say'.

sub.desc_en: The first tanna (תנא קמא) states that all occurrences of 'Solomon' in Song of Songs are sacred (קודש), referring to God, except for Song 8:12, where 'Solomon' is profane (referring to the human king) and 'the two hundred to those who guard its fruit' refers to the rabbis.
The 'some say' (יש אומרים) opinion adds that even Song 8:12 is profane, and also Song 3:7 ('Behold his bed, which is Solomon's') is profane.

The Gemara questions Shmuel's statement that a kingdom that kills one-sixth of the world is not punished, citing Song 8:12, and asks whether Shmuel aligns with the first tanna or the 'some say' opinion.
The Gemara resolves that the 'some say' opinion actually holds that Song 8:12 is sacred and only Song 3:7 is profane, and Shmuel's statement aligns with that 'some say' opinion.

items.text: Names of kings in Daniel
items.text_en: Names of kings in Daniel
items.desc_en: All occurrences of 'king' in Daniel are profane except one (Daniel 2:37). Some say even that one is sacred, because Daniel would not curse Israel by calling Nebuchadnezzar 'king of kings'. The first tanna holds that there are enemies of Israel but not enemies of Gentiles.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma rules that all occurrences of 'king' in Daniel are profane except one (Daniel 2:37), which is sacred.
Some say that even that one is sacred, citing the verse 'Mari helma lesana'akh ufishrei le'ara'akh' (Daniel 4:16).
The Gemara asks: To whom is Daniel speaking in that verse?
The Gemara objects: If Daniel is speaking to Nebuchadnezzar, his 'enemies' would be Israel — would Daniel curse Israel?
The Gemara resolves that the Tanna Kamma holds there are enemies of Israel but not enemies of Gentiles, so Daniel's phrase is not a curse.

items.text: Liability for curses using euphemisms
items.text_en: Liability for curses using euphemisms
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one is liable for cursing God using any euphemism. A contradiction is raised from a verse that seems to require the Tetragrammaton. Abaye resolves: one view (Rabbi Ḥanina bar Idi) requires the Tetragrammaton via a gezerah shavah; the other (the Rabbis) derives that 'alah' means oath from a verse, without requiring the Tetragrammaton. The Gemara clarifies that the Rabbis learn 'alah' as oath from the sotah passage.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one is liable for cursing God using any euphemism.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a verse that seems to require the Tetragrammaton for an oath, implying that only the ineffable name, not euphemisms, is valid.

Abaye resolves the contradiction by attributing the requirement for the Tetragrammaton to Rabbi Ḥanina bar Idi, who derives it via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), while the Rabbis hold that euphemisms suffice.
The Gemara questions the Rabbis' position: if they accept the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), they should require the Tetragrammaton; if not, how do they know that 'אלה' (alah) means an oath?
The Gemara answers that the Rabbis derive that 'אלה' (alah) means oath from a baraita that cites the sotah passage.
The Gemara objects that the verse says 'שבועת האלה' (oath of cursing), not just 'אלה' (alah), and clarifies that the baraita means 'אלה' (alah) is always used in the context of an oath.

items.text: Derivation that an imprecation without an oath is like an imprecation with an oath
items.text_en: Derivation that an imprecation without an oath is like an imprecation with an oath
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that an imprecation (alah) without an oath is like an imprecation with an oath, and an oath without an imprecation is like an oath with an imprecation? It answers with a verse: 'And she heard the voice of an imprecation' – she heard an imprecation, and she heard a voice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive that an imprecation (אלה) without an oath is like an imprecation with an oath, and an oath without an imprecation is like an oath with an imprecation.
The Gemara answers with a verse: 'And she heard the voice of an imprecation' – she heard an imprecation, and she heard a voice, equating the two.

items.text: Rabbi Abbahu's proof that 'alah' is a shevuah
items.text_en: Rabbi Abbahu's proof that 'alah' is a shevuah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abbahu proves that 'alah' is a shevuah from a verse about King Zedekiah, where the term 'alah' is used and then the text says he was made to swear by God.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu proves that 'alah' means an oath by citing verses where the same person is brought into an alah and then described as having been sworn.

items.text: The multiple meanings of 'arur'
items.text_en: The multiple meanings of 'arur'
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught that 'arur' (cursed) includes niddui (excommunication), kelalah (curse), and shevuah (oath). The Gemara provides scriptural proofs for each meaning, and then addresses a potential objection that Joshua and Saul might have done two things (swearing and cursing) separately. It concludes that since the verse does not say 'and cursed', it is clear that the curse itself is the oath.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that the word 'אָרוּר' (cursed) encompasses three meanings: excommunication (נִידּוּי), a curse (קְלָלָה), and an oath (שְׁבוּעָה).
The Gemara proves that 'אָרוּר' includes excommunication by citing the verse about Meroz and Ulla's statement that Barak excommunicated Meroz with four hundred shofar blasts.
The Gemara proves that 'אָרוּר' includes a curse by citing the verse from the blessings and curses at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.
The Gemara proves that 'אָרוּר' includes an oath by citing Joshua's oath, and then raises an objection that Joshua might have done two separate acts: swearing and cursing.
The Gemara offers a better proof from Saul's oath, but again raises the objection that Saul might have done two separate acts.
The Gemara resolves the objection by noting that the verse does not say 'וְאָרוּר' (and cursed), proving that the curse itself is the oath, not a separate act.

items.text: The multiple meanings of 'amen'
items.text_en: The multiple meanings of 'amen'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina teaches that 'amen' includes shevuah (oath), kabbalat devarim (acceptance of matters), and ha'amanat devarim (affirmation of matters). Each is proven from a verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina opens by stating that 'amen' encompasses three meanings: shevuah (oath), kabbalat devarim (acceptance of matters), and ha'amanat devarim (affirmation of matters).
The gemara cites a verse from the sotah (suspected adulteress) ritual to prove that 'amen' includes a shevuah (oath).
The gemara cites a verse from the blessings and curses at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal to prove that 'amen' includes kabbalat devarim (acceptance of matters).
The gemara cites a verse from Jeremiah to prove that 'amen' includes ha'amanat devarim (affirmation of matters).

items.text: The words 'lo' and 'hen' as oaths
items.text_en: The words 'lo' and 'hen' as oaths
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that 'lo' (no) and 'hen' (yes) can constitute oaths. The Gemara proves that 'lo' is an oath from the verse about the flood, and then argues that 'hen' is also an oath by logical inference. Rava adds that this applies only when one says 'lo lo' twice or 'hen hen' twice, as seen in the verses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that the words 'lo' (no) and 'hen' (yes) can constitute oaths.
The Gemara proves that 'lo' is an oath by citing the verse 'וְלֹא יִהְיֶה עוֹד הַמַּיִם לְמַבּוּל' (and there will no longer be a flood) which is linked to God's oath.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that 'hen' (yes) is an oath?
The Gemara answers by logical inference: since 'lo' is an oath, 'hen' is also an oath.
Rava adds that this applies only when one says 'lo lo' twice or 'hen hen' twice, as seen in the verses.

items.text: Liability for cursing with euphemisms: dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.text_en: Liability for cursing with euphemisms: dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who curses using any of these formulations is liable according to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages exempt. The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir derives from the verse that one is liable even for cursing with euphemisms (kinnuyim), while the Sages say that for the unique name the punishment is death, but for euphemisms it is only a prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who curses using any of these formulations is liable according to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages exempt.

A baraita explains that Rabbi Meir derives liability for cursing with euphemisms (kinnuyim) from the verse, while the Sages say that for the unique name the punishment is death, but for euphemisms it is only a prohibition.

items.text: The identity of the Sages and the source for cursing oneself and another
items.text_en: The identity of the Sages and the source for cursing oneself and another
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Sages as Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei, who holds that one who curses his father or mother is only liable if he curses them with the unique name. Rabbi Yannai says that everyone agrees that one who curses himself or another is liable, with proofs from verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who are the anonymous Sages in the Mishnah who disagree with Rabbi Meir regarding cursing one's parents.
The Gemara identifies the Sages as Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei, who holds that one who curses his father or mother is only liable if he curses them with the unique name of God.
Rabbi Yannai states that everyone agrees that one who curses himself or another is liable.

The Gemara provides scriptural proofs: for cursing oneself, the verse 'הִשָּׁמֶר לְךָ' (watch yourself) is interpreted as a negative commandment by Rabbi Avin in the name of Rabbi Ila; for cursing another, the verse 'לֹא תְקַלֵּל חֵרֵשׁ' (do not curse the deaf) is cited.

items.text: Euphemisms for curses and the principle of 'from a negative you hear a positive'
items.text_en: Euphemisms for curses and the principle of 'from a negative you hear a positive'
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses euphemisms like 'may God strike you' and the practice of using euphemisms (kinnuyim) in court. It then addresses a contradiction regarding Rabbi Meir's position on the principle of 'from a negative you hear a positive' (mikhlal lav atah shomea hen), resolving that Rabbi Meir rejects this principle in monetary matters but accepts it in prohibitions. However, a difficulty is raised from the Sotah case, where the principle is rejected even in a prohibition, as indicated by the word 'hinnaki'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines the euphemism 'יַכְּךָ ה׳ אֱלֹהִים' (may the Lord your God strike you) as the curse written in the Torah.

sub.text: Story: Rav Kahana before Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Story: Rav Kahana before Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana sits before Rav Yehuda and states the baraita; Rav Yehuda instructs him to use a euphemism (כַּנֵּה).

sub.text: Story: Another rabbi before Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Story: Another rabbi before Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Another rabbi sits before Rav Kahana and recites a verse of curse; Rav Kahana also instructs him to use a euphemism.
The Gemara asks why two stories are needed.
The Gemara explains that the second story teaches that euphemisms apply even to biblical verses, not just to mishnaic texts.
The baraita states that for euphemisms like 'אַל יַכְּךָ' (may He not strike you) and 'יְבָרֶכְךָ' (may He bless you), Rabbi Meir holds one liable, while the Sages exempt.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Meir does not accept the principle of 'from a negative you hear a positive' (מִכְּלָל לָאו אַתָּה שׁוֹמֵעַ הֵן), yet here he seems to apply it.
The Gemara suggests reversing the positions: Rabbi Meir exempts and the Sages hold liable.
Rav Yosef notes that when Rabbi Yitzchak came, he taught the baraita as originally stated, confirming that the original version is precise.
The Gemara raises a difficulty: the contradiction remains unresolved.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Meir rejects the principle in monetary matters but accepts it in prohibitions.
The Gemara objects that the case of the Sotah (suspected adulteress) is a prohibition, yet there the principle is rejected.

Rabbi Tanchum bar Chachinai cites that the verse writes 'הִנָּקִי' (you shall be cleansed), implying that without this word, the principle of 'from a negative you hear a positive' would not be applied even in a prohibition.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous sugya on Sotah and Rabbi Meir's view
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous sugya on Sotah and Rabbi Meir's view
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges the earlier attempt to reverse Rabbi Meir's positions, arguing that Rabbi Meir does apply the principle of 'is it not enough' to prohibitions as well, citing the case of those who drink wine and let their hair grow (during mourning). The Gemara resolves by saying that Rabbi Meir lacks the principle only in monetary matters, but has it in prohibitions; the case of Sotah is different because it involves both a prohibition and a monetary element.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes reversing Rabbi Meir's positions, claiming he lacks the principle of 'is it not enough' even in prohibitions.
Ravina objects, arguing that Rabbi Meir does apply the principle to prohibitions, citing the case of those who drink wine and let their hair grow during mourning.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Meir lacks the principle only in monetary matters but has it in prohibitions, and the case of Sotah is different because it involves both a prohibition and a monetary element.

items.text: Closing formula of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Closing formula of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The standard closing phrase 'Hadran alach Shevu'at HaEidut' marks the end of the chapter on the oath of testimony.

sub.desc_en: The standard closing phrase 'Hadran alach Shevu'at HaEidut' marks the end of the chapter on the oath of testimony.

items.text: Mishnah: Shevu'at HaPikadon
items.text_en: Mishnah: Shevu'at HaPikadon
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins by stating that the oath of deposit applies to all people, in or out of court, but liability for a false oath from others' testimony only applies if the denial was in court (Rabbi Meir). The Sages disagree. It then details the liability for intentional and unintentional oaths, the procedure of the oath, cases of multiple claims, and a general rule: one is liable only if they would pay on their own admission.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the oath of deposit applies to all people regardless of gender, proximity, or fitness.
Rabbi Meir rules that liability for a false oath from others' testimony requires denial in court, but from one's own mouth it applies anywhere.
The Sages disagree with Rabbi Meir and hold that one is liable for a false oath whether the denial is from his own mouth or from others' testimony.

The Mishnah states that one is liable for intentional false oaths and for unintentional oaths combined with intentional denial of the deposit, but not for purely unintentional oaths, and the penalty is a guilt offering worth two silver shekels.

sub.text: Mishnah's example of the oath procedure
sub.text_en: Mishnah's example of the oath procedure
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah illustrates the oath procedure: the claimant demands the deposit, the defendant denies it under oath, or the claimant administers an oath and the defendant says 'amen', making him liable.
The Mishnah rules that if one is administered five oaths and denies each, he is liable for each one; Rabbi Shimon explains the reason is that he could have retracted and admitted.

The Mishnah discusses a case of five claimants: a general denial yields one liability, but specifying each claimant yields liability for each; Rabbi Eliezer requires saying 'shevuah' at the end, and Rabbi Shimon requires saying 'shevuah' to each individually.

sub.text: Mishnah's case of multiple types of claims
sub.text_en: Mishnah's case of multiple types of claims
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one claims multiple types (deposit, bailment, theft, lost item), a general denial yields one liability, but specifying each type yields liability for each.

sub.text: Mishnah's case of multiple types of grain
sub.text_en: Mishnah's case of multiple types of grain
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one claims multiple types of grain, a general denial yields one liability, but specifying each type yields liability for each; Rabbi Meir adds that even saying 'wheat, barley, and spelt' in the singular form makes one liable for each.

sub.text: Mishnah's case of seduction and rape
sub.text_en: Mishnah's case of seduction and rape
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a claim of seduction or rape: the defendant is liable if he denies under oath; Rabbi Shimon exempts him because he does not pay a fine on his own admission, but the Sages respond that he pays for shame and degradation on his own admission.
The Mishnah rules that if one denies stealing an ox, he is liable; but if he admits to stealing but denies slaughtering or selling, he is exempt from the oath.

sub.text: Mishnah's case of goring ox and slave
sub.text_en: Mishnah's case of goring ox and slave
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one denies that his ox killed another's ox, he is liable; but if he denies that his ox killed another's slave, he is exempt.

sub.text: Mishnah's case of injury and slave's injury
sub.text_en: Mishnah's case of injury and slave's injury
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one denies causing injury to a free person, he is liable; but if a slave claims his master knocked out his tooth or blinded his eye, the master is exempt from the oath.
The Mishnah concludes with a general rule: one who would pay on his own admission is liable for the oath, and one who would not pay on his own admission is exempt.

items.text: Gemara: Opening anecdote about the rabbis who taught Shevuot in the house of Rabbah
items.text_en: Gemara: Opening anecdote about the rabbis who taught Shevuot in the house of Rabbah
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a narrative: Rav Acha bar Huna, Rav Shmuel bar Rabbah bar bar Chanah, and Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Yehudah were teaching the laws of oaths in the house of Rabbah. Rav Kahana encountered them and began to speak.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a narrative: Rav Acha bar Huna, Rav Shmuel bar Rabbah bar bar Chanah, and Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Yehudah were teaching the laws of oaths in the house of Rabbah, and Rav Kahana encountered them and began to speak.

items.text: Gemara's question on intentional false oath with warning
items.text_en: Gemara's question on intentional false oath with warning
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if one intentionally violates the oath of deposit and was forewarned, does he bring a guilt-offering (since this is a novel case where an intentional sin requires a sacrifice) or is he flogged instead, or perhaps both?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one intentionally violates the oath of deposit with forewarning, what is the law — does he bring a guilt-offering, receive lashes, or both?

items.text: First answer from a baraita: lashes, not sacrifice
items.text_en: First answer from a baraita: lashes, not sacrifice
items.desc_en: The students answer from a baraita that states the stringency of the oath of deposit is that one is liable to lashes for its intentional violation and a guilt-offering for its unintentional violation. This implies that with warning, one receives lashes and not a sacrifice. The Gemara explains the stringency: a person prefers to bring a sacrifice rather than be flogged.

sub.desc_en: The students answer from a baraita that the oath of deposit is stringent because one is liable to lashes for its intentional violation and a guilt-offering for its unintentional violation, implying that with warning one receives lashes and not a sacrifice.
The Gemara explains the stringency: a person prefers to bring a sacrifice rather than be flogged.

items.text: Rava bar Itai's objection: the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Rava bar Itai's objection: the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rava bar Itai objects that the baraita's ruling that intentional violation is not atoned for by a sacrifice follows Rabbi Shimon, but according to the Rabbis, one would still bring a sacrifice even if warned.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Itai objects that the baraita's ruling that intentional violation is not atoned for by a sacrifice follows Rabbi Shimon, but according to the Rabbis, one would still bring a sacrifice even if warned.

items.text: Rav Kahana's alternative version of the baraita
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's alternative version of the baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana presents a different version of the baraita: both intentional and unintentional violations require a guilt-offering of silver shekels. The stringency is that elsewhere a sin-offering is a lamb, but here it is a guilt-offering of silver shekels. The Gemara questions whether this can be used to infer the case of warning, and answers that it might refer to a case without warning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana presents an alternative version of the baraita: both intentional and unintentional violations require a guilt-offering of silver shekels.
The Gemara asks what the stringency is in this version, and Rav Kahana answers that elsewhere a sin-offering is a lamb (בת דנקא), but here it is a guilt-offering of silver shekels.
The Gemara questions whether this version can be used to infer the case of warning, and answers that it might refer to a case without warning.

items.text: Second attempt: a baraita on liability for intentional violation
items.text_en: Second attempt: a baraita on liability for intentional violation
items.desc_en: Another baraita states that one is not liable for unintentional violation, but for intentional violation one brings a guilt-offering. The Gemara asks if this implies warning, and answers that it too refers to a case without warning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a second version of a baraita that states one is not liable for unintentional violation but brings a guilt-offering for intentional violation.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita implies that the person was warned (התראה) before the act.
The Gemara answers that this baraita also refers to a case without warning (ללא התראה).

items.text: Third attempt: comparison with a nazirite
items.text_en: Third attempt: comparison with a nazirite
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita comparing a nazirite who became impure (who is flogged) to the oath of deposit, suggesting that the oath of deposit does not involve lashes but does involve a sacrifice. The Gemara reinterprets 'does not receive lashes' to mean 'is not exempted by lashes', and explains that the nazirite's sacrifice is to permit his naziriteship in purity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita comparing a nazirite who became impure (who is flogged) to the oath of deposit, suggesting that the oath of deposit does not involve lashes but does involve a sacrifice.
The Gemara reinterprets 'does not receive lashes' to mean 'is not exempted by lashes', and explains that the nazirite's sacrifice is to permit his naziriteship in purity.

items.text: Rabbah's inference: one who denies a loan without witnesses is exempt
items.text_en: Rabbah's inference: one who denies a loan without witnesses is exempt
items.desc_en: The Rabbis present a case before Rabbah, who infers that if there is no warning but there are witnesses, one would be liable. He then states that mere denial of words (without monetary loss) is exempt, indicating that one who denies a loan with witnesses is exempt from the oath of deposit.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis present a case before Rabbah, asking whether one who denies a loan with witnesses is liable.
Rabbah infers that mere denial of words (without monetary loss) is exempt, indicating that one who denies a loan with witnesses is exempt from the oath of deposit.

items.text: Rav Chanina's support and Rabbah's rejection
items.text_en: Rav Chanina's support and Rabbah's rejection
items.desc_en: Rav Chanina brings a baraita that seems to support Rabbah: the verse 'and he denied it' excludes one who admits to one of the brothers or partners, and 'swears falsely' excludes a borrower with a document or witnesses. Rabbah rejects this support, explaining that the baraita refers to one who says 'I borrowed but not with witnesses' or 'I borrowed but not with a document'. The Gemara analyzes the baraita to show that both the first and second clauses deal with mere denial of words.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanina cites a baraita that seems to support Rabbah's position, interpreting the verse 'וְכִחֵשׁ בָּהּ' (and he denied it) to exclude one who admits to a brother or partner, and 'וְנִשְׁבַּע עַל שָׁקֶר' (and swears falsely) to exclude a borrower with a document or witnesses.

Rabbah rejects the support, explaining that the baraita refers to a case where the borrower says 'I borrowed but not with witnesses' or 'I borrowed but not with a document' — a mere denial of words, not a denial of the debt itself.

The Gemara analyzes the baraita, demonstrating that both the first clause (about admitting to one brother) and the second clause (about borrowing with witnesses or a document) involve mere denial of words (כְּפִירַת דְּבָרִים), not denial of the actual debt.

items.text: Final attempts: baraitot on intentional violation and two sets of witnesses
items.text_en: Final attempts: baraitot on intentional violation and two sets of witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings two more baraitot: one about intentional violation (interpreted as intentional false testimony, not the oath itself) and another about two sets of witnesses where both are liable because testimony can be upheld by both. The Gemara questions why the first set is liable if the second set's testimony is still valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about intentional violation of the oath of deposit, and the Gemara initially interprets it as referring to intentional false testimony, but then rejects this interpretation, clarifying it refers to intentional violation of the oath itself.

The Gemara brings a baraita about two sets of witnesses where both are liable because testimony can be upheld by both, and questions why the first set is liable if the second set's testimony is still valid.

items.text: Ravina's resolution of the contradiction about the second witness
items.text_en: Ravina's resolution of the contradiction about the second witness
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that the case involves a second witness who was near death at the time of the first denial, and his wives were dying. The Gemara suggests that since most dying people die, one might think the second witness is considered dead, but the mishnah teaches that currently they are alive and not dead.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the second witness is standing alive, so how can the mishnah treat him as dead?

Ravina resolves that the second witness was near death at the time of the first denial, and his wives were dying; the mishnah teaches that despite the majority of dying people dying, currently they are alive.

items.text: Support from the Mishnah of the bailee who confessed
items.text_en: Support from the Mishnah of the bailee who confessed
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a mishnah about a bailee who claimed theft, swore, and then confessed. If he confessed before witnesses came, he pays principal, fifth, and guilt-offering; if after witnesses, he pays double payment and guilt-offering. The Gemara notes that this too is like Ravina's explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a bailee who falsely claimed theft, swore, and then confessed; the baraita distinguishes between confession before or after witnesses came, implying liability for a guilt-offering even when witnesses exist.
The Gemara resolves the baraita by applying Ravina's earlier explanation: the witnesses were related through moribund wives and thus unfit at the time of the oath.

items.text: Ravina's challenge from the oath of deposit
items.text_en: Ravina's challenge from the oath of deposit
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rava from a baraita that says the oath of deposit is more severe because one is liable for lashes for its intentional violation and a guilt-offering for its unintentional violation. The Gemara infers that lashes imply witnesses, yet the baraita says a guilt-offering is brought. Rav Mordechai deflects by citing Rav Kahana's version that both intentional and unintentional require a guilt-offering.

sub.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rava by citing a baraita that the oath of deposit is more severe, implying lashes (witnesses) yet a guilt-offering is brought.
Rav Mordechai deflects the challenge by citing Rav Kahana's version that both intentional and unintentional require a guilt-offering, removing the implication of witnesses.

items.text: Conclusive refutation of Rava
items.text_en: Conclusive refutation of Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a definitive refutation from a baraita comparing a nazirite and the oath of deposit. It shows that even when there are witnesses, one does not receive lashes for the oath of deposit but does bring a sacrifice, thus refuting Rava's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita comparing a nazirite and the oath of deposit, questioning whether the oath of deposit should be exempt from lashes.
The Gemara clarifies that the baraita assumes there are witnesses, and concludes that one does not receive lashes but does bring a sacrifice for the oath of deposit.
The Gemara declares this a conclusive refutation of Rava's position.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction between witnesses and documents
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction between witnesses and documents
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who denies a monetary claim with witnesses is liable to bring a sacrifice, but if the claim is based on a document, he is exempt. Rav Pappa explains the reason: witnesses might come, but a document is placed away. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua objects that a document might also be lost, and instead explains that the reason is because a document is a lien on land, and one does not bring a sacrifice for denial of a lien on land.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who denies a monetary claim supported by witnesses is liable to bring a sacrifice, but if the claim is based on a document, he is exempt.
Rav Pappa explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: witnesses might come to testify, but a document is placed away and thus not subject to denial.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua objects that a document might also be lost, undermining Rav Pappa's explanation.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua provides an alternative explanation: a document represents a lien on land, and one does not bring a sacrifice for denial of a lien on land.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar on oaths about land
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar on oaths about land
items.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar regarding one who administers an oath to witnesses about land. One says liable, the other exempt. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan holds exempt, based on his earlier ruling and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar regarding one who administers an oath to witnesses about land: one holds liable, the other exempt.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan holds exempt, based on his earlier ruling and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's explanation.

items.text: Connection to the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages
items.text_en: Connection to the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Abahu whether the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar corresponds to the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding a robber of a field. The Gemara explains the exegetical methods of Rabbi Eliezer (ribbui u'mi'ut) and the Sages (klal u'frat) and how they apply to the verses about oaths. Rabbi Abahu rejects the connection, arguing that even Rabbi Eliezer would exempt in the case of land because the verse says 'from all' and not 'all'.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Abahu
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Abahu
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Abahu whether the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar corresponds to the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding a robber of a field.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the dispute's basis
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the dispute's basis
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer uses the exegetical method of ריבויי ומיעוטי (amplifications and restrictions) while the Sages use כלל ופרט (general and specific), and details how each method applies to the verses about oaths.
The Gemara proposes that the one who obligates follows Rabbi Eliezer and the one who exempts follows the Sages.
Rabbi Abahu rejects the connection, arguing that even Rabbi Eliezer would exempt in the case of land because the verse says 'from all' and not 'all'.

items.text: Support from the Mishnah for exemption of slaves
items.text_en: Support from the Mishnah for exemption of slaves
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava cites the mishnah that lists 'you stole my ox' but not 'you stole my slave', implying that slaves are exempt because they are compared to land. Rav Pappi in the name of Rava adds that the general rule in the mishnah ('this is the rule') comes to include the case of 'you stole my slave'.

sub.text: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava cites the mishnah's listing of 'you stole my ox' but not 'you stole my slave' as evidence that slaves are exempt from the oath of deposit because they are compared to land.

sub.text: Rav Pappi in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Pappi in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappi in the name of Rava adds that the mishnah's general rule 'this is the rule' comes to include the case of 'you stole my slave', implying that the mishnah itself supports the exemption of slaves.

items.text: Transition from previous daf
items.text_en: Transition from previous daf
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that there is nothing to learn from the previous source, and introduces the Mishnah about the oath of deposit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that there is nothing to learn from the previous source, and transitions to the Mishnah about the oath of deposit.

items.text: Mishnah and Baraita on the oath of deposit
items.text_en: Mishnah and Baraita on the oath of deposit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the oath of deposit, and the Baraita records the dispute between Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Shimon regarding whether one is liable for each claim individually or only once.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of the oath of deposit and the Baraita records the general rule and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda.
The Baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir says one is liable only once for a general claim, but for each specific item; Rabbi Yehuda says one is liable for each 'not to you' statement.
Rabbi Eliezer states that if one says 'not to you, not to you, not to you, oath' he is liable for each one.
Rabbi Shimon holds that one is liable only if he says 'oath' for each and every one.

items.text: Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan's interpretations
items.text_en: Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan's interpretations
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that Rabbi Meir's general statement is Rabbi Yehuda's specific statement and vice versa. Rabbi Yochanan argues that all agree that 'and not to you' is specific, and they only dispute about 'not to you'.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that Rabbi Meir's general statement is Rabbi Yehuda's specific statement and vice versa.
Rabbi Yochanan argues that all agree that 'and not to you' is specific, and they only dispute about 'not to you'.

items.text: Analysis of the dispute between Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Analysis of the dispute between Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Shmuel deduces from the Baraita that Rabbi Yehuda considers 'and not to you' as specific, implying Rabbi Meir considers it general. Rabbi Yochanan argues both are specific to Rabbi Meir, and they dispute only about 'not to you'. The Gemara then supports Rabbi Yochanan's deduction from the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: On what basis do Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan dispute?
The Gemara explains that Shmuel deduces from the Baraita that Rabbi Yehuda considers 'וְלֹא לָךְ' (and not to you) specific, implying Rabbi Meir considers it general.
Rabbi Yochanan argues that both 'וְלֹא לָךְ' and 'לֹא לָךְ' are specific to Rabbi Meir, and they dispute only about 'לֹא לָךְ'; the Gemara then objects that Shmuel would not concede so much.
The Gemara supports Rabbi Yochanan's deduction from the Mishnah: since Rabbi Meir uses 'שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁאֵין לָכֶם בְּיָדִי' as a general statement, it implies that 'וְלֹא לָךְ' is specific.
Shmuel resolves that anyone who says 'וְלֹא לָךְ' is considered as saying 'שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁאֵין לָכֶם בְּיָדִי', equating the two formulations.

items.text: Challenges and resolutions regarding the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Challenges and resolutions regarding the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's wording, suggesting it should be read differently, and resolves that the Tanna is Rabbi, who holds that even 'like an olive, like an olive' is specific. It then discusses Rabbi Meir's statement about wheat and barley.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's wording, suggesting it should read 'לֹא לָךְ' (not yours) rather than 'לֹא לָךְ וְלֹא לָךְ וְלֹא לָךְ' (not yours, not yours, not yours).
The Gemara brings a supporting baraita where the Mishnah's list of claims should be read without the conjunctive 'ו' (and).
The Gemara brings another supporting baraita where the list of grains should be read without the conjunctive 'ו' (and).
The Gemara objects that the Tanna cannot be consistently mistaken, and resolves that the Tanna is Rabbi, who holds that even 'כְּזַיִת, כְּזַיִת' (like an olive, like an olive) is specific.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Meir's statement that even 'חִטָּה וּשְׂעוֹרָה וְכוּסֶּמֶת' (wheat, barley, and spelt) requires liability for each, and suggests the text should read without 'ו' (and).

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika resolves that 'אֲפִילּוּ' (even) means even a single wheat is included in the general category of wheat, and similarly for barley and spelt.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and dispute about combining claims
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and dispute about combining claims
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a perutah from each claim combines. Rav Acha and Ravina dispute whether one is liable for the details or also for the general categories. The Gemara cites a Baraita of Rabbi Chiya to support one view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's case of multiple claims and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that a perutah from each claim combines.
Rav Acha and Ravina dispute whether one is liable only for the details or also for the general categories.
The Gemara cites a Baraita of Rabbi Chiya listing fifteen sin-offerings, supporting the view that only details are counted.
The Gemara objects that another version of Rabbi Chiya's Baraita lists twenty sin-offerings, and resolves that the latter counts general categories as well.

items.text: Rava's inquiry to Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry to Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman about a case with five claimants and a single oath, questioning whether one is liable for each claimant or just one.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman: If five claimants say 'Give us the pikadon, tesumet yad, gazel, and aveidah that we have in your hand', and the defendant swears to one of them, what is the law? Is he liable for one?

items.text: Conclusion of the previous sugya: Is partial admission liable?
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous sugya: Is partial admission liable?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one who admits to part of a claim is liable for an oath, and brings a baraita of Rabbi Chiya to resolve the issue, concluding that partial admission is indeed considered a specific admission.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one who admits to part of a claim is liable for an oath on each individual item.
The Gemara brings a baraita of Rabbi Chiya about twenty sin-offerings to resolve the question, concluding that partial admission is considered a specific admission.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's rationale and Rava's analogy
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's rationale and Rava's analogy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning that the claimant is pursuing a penalty. Rava offers a mashal of wheat and barley to illustrate exemption, but Abaye objects and refines the analogy to show liability when the defendant denies the entire claim.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Shimon's rationale is that the claimant is pursuing a penalty (קנס), not compensation.
Rava offers a mashal (parable) of wheat and barley to illustrate that partial denial of a non-uniform claim leads to exemption, because the oath was truthful regarding the denied item.

Abaye objects that Rava's analogy is flawed: in the case at hand, the defendant denies the entire claim, so the correct analogy is one who swears 'I have nothing of yours' and is found to have some items, which renders him liable.

items.text: Ravin's version and the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages
items.text_en: Ravin's version and the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages
items.desc_en: Ravin reports Rabbi Yochanan's statement that according to Rabbi Shimon the claimant pursues a penalty, while according to the Sages he also pursues compensation for shame and degradation. Rav Papa explains the underlying disagreement about what a person would not abandon in their claim.

sub.desc_en: Ravin reports Rabbi Yochanan's statement that according to Rabbi Shimon the claimant pursues a penalty (קנס), while according to the Sages he also pursues compensation for shame and degradation (בושת ופגם).
The Gemara asks what is the underlying dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages.

Rav Papa explains that Rabbi Shimon holds a person does not abandon a fixed sum (מידי דקיץ) to claim a non-fixed sum, while the Sages hold a person does not abandon a claim that would exempt him if admitted, and claims something that would exempt him if admitted.

items.text: Mishnah: Shevuot HaDayanim
items.text_en: Mishnah: Shevuot HaDayanim
items.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the laws of the court oath, specifying the minimum claim (two silver coins) and admission (one perutah), and that the admission must be of the same type as the claim. It provides various examples of claims and admissions, including cases of partial admission, different types of property, and the rule that one does not swear on behalf of a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the laws of the court oath (שבועת הדיינים), stating the minimum claim is two silver coins and the admission must be worth at least one perutah.
The Mishnah adds the rule that if the admission is not of the same type as the claim, the defendant is exempt from the oath.

The Mishnah gives an example: if the claim is two silver coins and the admission is one perutah, the defendant is exempt; but if the claim is two silver coins and a perutah and the admission is one perutah, he is liable.
The Mishnah gives another example: if the claim is a maneh and the defendant denies everything, he is exempt; but if he admits to fifty dinars, he is liable.
The Mishnah states that if the claim is for a maneh belonging to the claimant's father, and the defendant admits to fifty dinars, he is exempt because he is like one returning a lost object.
The Mishnah rules that if the defendant initially admits to the debt but later claims he paid, he is exempt; but if he denies the debt entirely, he is liable.
The Mishnah rules that if the claimant stipulated payment in front of witnesses, and the defendant later claims he paid, he is liable because he needed to pay in front of witnesses.

The Mishnah rules that if the claim is for a litra of gold and the admission is for a litra of silver, the defendant is exempt; but if the claim is for a dinar of gold and the admission is for a dinar of silver and other coins, he is liable because all are one type of currency.

The Mishnah rules that if the claim is for a kor of grain and the admission is for a letekh of legumes, the defendant is exempt; but if the claim is for a kor of produce and the admission is for a letekh of legumes, he is liable because legumes are included in produce.
The Mishnah presents a dispute: if the claim is for wheat and the admission is for barley, the Sages exempt the defendant, but Rabban Gamliel holds him liable.

The Mishnah presents a dispute: if the claim is for jugs of oil and the admission is for jugs (without oil), Admon says he must swear because the admission is partially of the same type, the Sages say it is not, and Rabban Gamliel agrees with Admon.

The Mishnah rules that if the claim includes movable property (כלים) and land (קרקעות), and the defendant admits to one and denies the other, he is exempt; but if he admits to part of the movable property, he is liable, because movable property obligates an oath on land as well.

The Mishnah concludes that one does not administer an oath for a claim by a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor, nor does one swear on behalf of a minor; but one does swear to a minor and to the Temple treasury (הקדש).

items.text: Gemara: How is the oath administered?
items.text_en: Gemara: How is the oath administered?
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the formula for administering the oath, citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav that it is done with the oath mentioned in the Torah. Ravina questions whether this follows Rabbi Chanina bar Idi's view requiring the unique name, but Rav Ashi explains that even the Sages agree, and the practical difference is the requirement to hold a sacred object. The Gemara then rules in accordance with Rava's view that the judge who swears by 'the Lord God of Heaven' is considered mistaken and must return, but not with Rav Papa's view regarding phylacteries.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: How do we administer the oath to the defendant?

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers: We administer the oath with the oath mentioned in the Torah, as it is written: 'And I will make you swear by the Lord God of Heaven.'
Ravina asks Rav Ashi: Does this follow Rabbi Chanina bar Idi, who requires the unique name of God?
Rav Ashi answers: Even if you say it follows the Sages, who allow a substitute name, the practical difference is that one must hold a sacred object.
Rava rules that a judge who swears by 'the Lord God of Heaven' is considered mistaken in a Mishnah matter and must return.
Rav Papa rules that a judge who swears by phylacteries is considered mistaken in a Mishnah matter and must return.
The Gemara rules in accordance with Rava, because he did not hold a sacred object, and not in accordance with Rav Papa, because he did hold a sacred object.

items.text: Additional halakhot of the oath: standing, Torah scroll, and language
items.text_en: Additional halakhot of the oath: standing, Torah scroll, and language
items.desc_en: The Gemara records that the oath is administered standing, but a Torah scholar may sit; it is done with a Torah scroll, but a scholar may initially use phylacteries. A baraita teaches that the court oath is said in the language of the swearer, and the court informs him of the severity of the oath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the oath is administered standing, but a Torah scholar may sit; it is done with a Torah scroll, but a scholar may initially use phylacteries.
A baraita teaches that the court oath is said in the language of the swearer.
The court informs the swearer of the severity of the oath.

items.text: The unique severity of a false oath
items.text_en: The unique severity of a false oath
items.desc_en: The Gemara enumerates four ways in which a false oath is more severe than other transgressions: the world trembled at Sinai when 'Do not take God's name in vain' was given; for other sins forgiveness is implied, but here it says 'He will not clear'; punishment extends to the sinner's family and to the entire world; and punishment is immediate, not deferred for merit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the entire world trembled at Sinai when the prohibition against taking God's name in vain was given.
The Gemara contrasts other sins, where forgiveness is implied, with a false oath, where the verse says 'He will not clear'.
The Gemara states that for other sins punishment is only on the sinner, but for a false oath it extends to his family, citing the verse 'Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin'.
The Gemara states that for other sins punishment is only on the sinner, but for a false oath it extends to the entire world, citing the verse 'Swearing and lying'.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the punishment only comes when the entire world sins, but then rejects this by citing verses that show the land mourns because of the oath.
The Gemara states that for other sins punishment is deferred for merit, but for a false oath it is immediate, citing the verse 'I will bring it forth... and it shall consume his house'.

The Gemara explains the verse: 'I will bring it forth' means immediately; the thief of people's trust and the false swearer are both punished; and a false oath destroys even things that fire and water cannot destroy.

items.text: The procedure for administering the oath and the precedent of Moses
items.text_en: The procedure for administering the oath and the precedent of Moses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure: if the defendant says 'I will not swear,' he is immediately dismissed; if he says 'I will swear,' the bystanders say 'Depart from the tents of these wicked men.' The court then warns him that the oath is administered not according to his intent but according to the intent of God and the court, as Moses did when he adjured Israel, including future generations and future commandments like the reading of the Megillah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the court's procedure: if the defendant refuses to swear he is dismissed immediately; if he agrees, bystanders warn him to depart from the tents of the wicked, and the court informs him that the oath is administered according to God's intent and the court's intent, not his own.

The Mishnah cites the precedent of Moses, who adjured Israel not according to their intent but according to God's intent and his own, as derived from the verse 'וְלֹא אִתְּכֶם לְבַדְּכֶם' (not with you alone).
The Mishnah derives from the verse that the oath included not only those standing at Sinai but also future generations and converts.
The Mishnah further derives that future commandments, such as the reading of the Megillah, are included in the oath, based on the verse 'קִיְּמוּ וְקִבְּלוּ' (they fulfilled and accepted).

items.text: The meaning of 'even it is said in its language'
items.text_en: The meaning of 'even it is said in its language'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'even it is said in its language.' It explains that this refers to the list of things that may be said in any language, including the oath of testimony and the oath of deposit, and the Mishnah adds that the court-administered oath (שבועת הדיינין) is also said in its language.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'even it is said in its language'.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah refers to the list of things said in any language, and adds that the court-administered oath (שבועת הדיינין) is also said in its language.

items.text: Why the world trembled at the prohibition of false oaths
items.text_en: Why the world trembled at the prohibition of false oaths
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the world trembled specifically at the prohibition of false oaths. It considers and rejects the reasons that it was given at Sinai (since all Ten Commandments were given there) and that it is more severe (since the Mishnah lists it among the lighter transgressions). It concludes that the reason is that for other sins it says 'He will forgive,' but for this it says 'He will not clear.' The Gemara then addresses a contradiction: elsewhere it says 'He will by no means clear,' and resolves it with Rabbi Elazar's teaching that He clears those who repent but does not clear those who do not repent.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the court tells the defendant to know that the entire world trembled when God said at Sinai 'You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.'
The Gemara asks why specifically this prohibition caused the world to tremble, and rejects the possibility that it was because it was given at Sinai, since all Ten Commandments were given there.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the prohibition is more severe, citing the Mishnah that lists 'You shall not take' among the lighter transgressions, not the severe ones.
The Gemara concludes that the reason is that for other sins it says 'He will forgive,' but for this one it says 'He will not clear.'
The Gemara objects that other sins also have the phrase 'He will by no means clear,' citing the verse 'וְנַקֵּה לֹא יְנַקֶּה' (and forgiving, He will by no means clear).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction with Rabbi Elazar's teaching that the verse means He clears those who repent but does not clear those who do not repent.

items.text: Punishment extending to the family
items.text_en: Punishment extending to the family
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether punishment extends to the family for other sins, citing a verse that God sets His face against a man and his family. It brings Rabbi Shimon's explanation that the family is punished because they cover for the sinner. It then distinguishes between that case (where the family is punished in a different judgment) and the case of a false oath (where the sinner himself is punished), citing Rabbi's teaching that only the sinner is cut off, not the entire family.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether punishment extends to the family for other sins, citing the claim that for a false oath punishment extends to the family, and asking if that is not the case for all sins.
The Gemara cites a verse and Rabbi Shimon's explanation that the family is punished because they cover for the sinner.

The Gemara distinguishes between that case (where the family is punished in a different judgment) and the case of a false oath (where the sinner himself is punished), citing Rabbi's teaching that only the sinner is cut off, not the entire family.

items.text: Punishment extending to the entire world and the principle of collective responsibility
items.text_en: Punishment extending to the entire world and the principle of collective responsibility
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues with the claim that for a false oath punishment extends to the entire world, citing verses about the land mourning. It rejects the possibility that this only happens if everyone swears falsely, citing a verse that the land mourns because of the oath. It then questions whether for other sins punishment does not extend to the entire world, citing the principle that all Israel are sureties for one another, as per the verse 'they shall stumble each over his brother.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that for a false oath punishment extends to the entire world, citing the verse 'אָלֹה וְכַחֵשׁ' and the land mourning.
The Gemara questions whether the punishment only applies if everyone swears falsely, but rejects this based on the verse 'מִפְּנֵי אָלָה אָבְלָה הָאָרֶץ'.

The Gemara questions whether for other sins punishment does not extend to the entire world, citing the principle that all Israel are sureties for one another from the verse 'וְכָשְׁלוּ אִישׁ בְּאָחִיו'.

items.text: Distinction between the swearer and the wicked of his family
items.text_en: Distinction between the swearer and the wicked of his family
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the difference between the wicked of his family and other wicked people, and between the righteous of his family and other righteous people, in the context of the oath. It then applies these distinctions to the case of the oath itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the wicked of his family are those who could have protested but did not.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the wicked of his family and other wicked people, and between the righteous of his family and other righteous people.

The Gemara answers that regarding other sins, the swearer is judged by his own standard, the wicked of his family by a strict standard, other wicked people by a lenient standard, and the righteous are exempt.
The Gemara applies the distinction to the oath itself: the swearer and his family's wicked are judged by his own standard, other wicked by a strict standard, and the righteous by a lenient standard.

items.text: Why the one who administers the oath is also liable
items.text_en: Why the one who administers the oath is also liable
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the one who administers the oath is considered wicked, and answers with a teaching of Rabbi Shimon ben Tarfon that the oath applies to both parties.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the one who administers the oath is also called wicked, since only the one taking the oath is under an איסור (prohibition).
The Gemara answers by citing Rabbi Shimon ben Tarfon's teaching that the oath applies to both parties, based on the verse 'שבועת ה' תהיה בין שניהם' (the oath of the Lord shall be between them both).

items.text: The warning to the swearer and the reason for it
items.text_en: The warning to the swearer and the reason for it
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when they administer the oath, they tell the swearer that it is not according to his own mind, and this is due to the reed of Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, describing that when they administer the oath, they tell the swearer it is not according to his own mind.
The Gemara asks why it is necessary to tell the swearer this warning.
The Gemara answers that it is due to the reed of Rava (a known principle about the severity of false oaths).

items.text: The dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the minimum claim
items.text_en: The dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the minimum claim
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the claim must be two silver [ma'ah]. Rav says this refers to the denial of the claim, while Shmuel says it refers to the claim itself, and even if he denied only a perutah and admitted only a perutah, he is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the claim must be two silver [ma'ah].
Rav says the two silver refers to the denial of the claim.
Shmuel says the two silver refers to the claim itself, and even if he denied only a perutah and admitted only a perutah, he is liable.

items.text: Rava's analysis: Mishnah supports Rav, verses support Shmuel
items.text_en: Rava's analysis: Mishnah supports Rav, verses support Shmuel
items.desc_en: Rava states that the Mishnah supports Rav because it mentions the claim of two silver and the admission of a perutah but not the denial of a perutah, while the verses support Shmuel because they derive from 'kesef' and 'keilim' that the claim must be of significant value.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that the Mishnah supports Rav because it lists the claim of two silver and the admission of a perutah but omits the denial of a perutah.
Rava then argues that the verses support Shmuel, deriving from 'kesef' and 'keilim' that the claim must be of significant value, and the Torah says 'כי הוא זה' (for it is this).

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's interpretations of the verses
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's interpretations of the verses
items.desc_en: Rav uses the verse for admission in part of the claim, while Shmuel uses both 'hu' and 'zeh' to teach that if he denied in part and admitted in part, he is liable. Rav uses both for admission in part and admission from the same type of claim.

sub.desc_en: Rav explains that the verse 'כי הוא זה' is needed to teach the law of admission in part of the claim (הודאה במקצת הטענה).
Shmuel argues that the two words 'הוא' and 'זה' teach that if one denied part and admitted part, he is liable.

items.text: Rav's alternative derivation and Shmuel's response
items.text_en: Rav's alternative derivation and Shmuel's response
items.desc_en: Rav argues that 'kesef' comes for denial, otherwise it would be superfluous. Shmuel counters that without 'kesef', one might think that only the number of items matters, not their value.

sub.desc_en: Rav argues that the word 'כֶּסֶף' (silver) in the verse comes primarily for the requirement of denial (כְּפִירָה), because if it were only for the claim, it would be superfluous, so it is applied to the denial.
Shmuel counters that without 'כֶּסֶף' (silver), one might think that only the number of items matters, not their value, so the word teaches that a valuable item is required.

items.text: Challenge to Shmuel from the Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to Shmuel from the Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel from a Mishnah where a claim of two silver and an admission of a perutah results in exemption, implying the claim is lacking. Shmuel explains the Mishnah as 'davka' (exact). The Gemara then challenges Rav from another case, and Rav distinguishes the case of a litra of gold.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel from a Mishnah where a claim of two silver and an admission of a perutah results in exemption, implying the claim is lacking.
Shmuel explains that the Mishnah is 'דווקא' (exact), meaning the claim and admission do not match at all.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah is exact, the second case where the claim includes a perutah should also be exempt, but it is liable.
Rav Nachman cites Shmuel's principle that if one claims wheat and barley and admits to one, he is liable, resolving the objection.

sub.text: Gemara's supporting evidence from the Mishnah's end
sub.text_en: Gemara's supporting evidence from the Mishnah's end
sub.desc_en: The Gemara adduces support from the Mishnah's end case of a litra of gold vs. silver, which is exempt only if the Mishnah is exact.
The Gemara concludes that since the end case is exact, the beginning case is also exact, supporting Shmuel.
The Gemara asks whether this constitutes a refutation of Rav's position.
Rav distinguishes the case of a litra of gold as exceptional, maintaining that the rest of the Mishnah is 'שווה' (equal).

items.text: Gemara's challenge from the Mishnah's seifa
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge from the Mishnah's seifa
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's position (that the claimant must specify the exact coin) by citing the seifa of the Mishnah, where a claim of 'a gold dinar' and a partial admission of 'a silver dinar, a trisit, a pundyon, and a perutah' is deemed liable. If Rav is correct, why is the defendant liable?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's position by citing the Mishnah's seifa, where a claim of 'a gold dinar' and a partial admission of smaller coins is liable, asking: if Rav requires exact specification, why is the defendant liable?

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's resolution in support of Shmuel
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's resolution in support of Shmuel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that the case involves a claim of a 'dinar of coins' (a generic coin), not a specific gold dinar, and the Mishnah teaches that a perutah is included in the category of coinage. This supports Shmuel's view that equivalent value suffices.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar answers that the case involves a claim of 'a dinar of coins' (generic), and the Mishnah teaches that a perutah is included in the category of coinage, as indicated by the phrase 'all are one type of coin'.

items.text: Rav's alternative reading of the seifa
items.text_en: Rav's alternative reading of the seifa
items.desc_en: Rav reads the seifa as saying 'all are of the same legal category of coinage' (דין מטבע), not 'type' (מין), thus allowing liability even under his view that the claim must be precise, because all coins are legally equivalent for shevuah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav reads the Mishnah's phrase as 'all are subject to the law of one coin' (i.e., they are all coins, but not necessarily the same type).

items.text: Gemara's inference about Rabbi Elazar's consistency
items.text_en: Gemara's inference about Rabbi Elazar's consistency
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Elazar, who resolves the seifa like Shmuel, also holds Shmuel's view in the reisha. It answers that the seifa is indeed precise (supporting Shmuel), but the reisha remains ambiguous between Rav and Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: since Rabbi Elazar resolves the seifa (later clause) in accordance with Shmuel, does he also hold like Shmuel regarding the reisha (first clause)?

The gemara answers: no — the seifa is precise (דווקא) because it explicitly says 'all are the same type of coinage', but the reisha remains ambiguous and could be interpreted according to either Rav or Shmuel.

items.text: Proof from a baraita with 'gold gold dinar'
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita with 'gold gold dinar'
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if one claims 'a gold gold dinar' and the other admits to a silver dinar, he is liable, implying that a simple 'gold dinar' claim is about equivalent value. Rav Ashi explains that saying 'gold dinar' is like saying 'gold gold dinar' (emphasizing the gold).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where claiming 'a gold gold dinar' and the defendant admitting to a silver dinar makes him liable, implying that a simple 'gold dinar' claim is about equivalent value.
Rav Ashi explains that saying 'gold dinar' is equivalent to saying 'gold gold dinar', so the baraita does not prove the general rule.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Chiyya supporting Rav
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Chiyya supporting Rav
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya teaches a baraita: if one claims a sela and the other admits to a sela missing two silver coins, he is liable; if missing a ma'ah, he is exempt. This supports Rav's position that the admission must match the specific coin claimed.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Chiya supporting Rav
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Chiya supporting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya taught a baraita supporting Rav: if one claims 'a sela' and the defendant admits to a sela missing two silver coins, he is liable; if missing a ma'ah, he is exempt, showing that exact specification matters.

items.text: Shmuel's distinction between borrower and witness
items.text_en: Shmuel's distinction between borrower and witness
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak quotes Shmuel: the rule of partial admission applies only to a borrower's admission, but if a single witness testifies, even a perutah claim obligates shevuah, as derived from the verse 'for every iniquity and sin' – a witness does not stand for punishment but stands for shevuah.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites Shmuel: the rule that one must claim at least a perutah applies only to a case of lender's claim and borrower's admission, but if there is a single witness, even a claim of a perutah obligates an oath.

The gemara explains the reason: the verse 'a single witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity or any sin' implies that for monetary matters a single witness does obligate an oath, and a baraita confirms that wherever two witnesses would obligate payment, one witness obligates an oath.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on mixed claims and Rabbi Yochanan's approval
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on mixed claims and Rabbi Yochanan's approval
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Shmuel: if one claims wheat and barley and the other admits to one of them, he is liable. Rabbi Yitzchak says 'yishar' and reports that Rabbi Yochanan agrees, implying Resh Lakish disagrees, though there is a dispute about whether Resh Lakish was silent or drinking.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports Shmuel's ruling that if one claims wheat and barley and the other admits to one of them, he is liable.
Rabbi Yitzchak says 'yishar' (may you be strong) and reports that Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Shmuel's ruling.
The gemara asks whether Resh Lakish disagrees with Shmuel's ruling, since Rabbi Yochanan's explicit approval implies a dispute.
The gemara resolves the question with two versions: either Resh Lakish was delayed and silent, or he was drinking and silent, so his silence does not indicate disagreement.

items.text: Attempted proof from a Mishnah and its rejection
items.text_en: Attempted proof from a Mishnah and its rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove Shmuel's ruling from a Mishnah where claiming wheat and admitting barley is exempt, implying that claiming wheat and barley and admitting one is liable. It is rejected: even in that case it is exempt, and the Mishnah only teaches about Rabban Gamliel's stringency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove Shmuel's ruling from a Mishnah: if one claims wheat and the defendant admits to barley, he is exempt, implying that if one claims wheat and barley and admits to one, he is liable.
The Gemara rejects the proof: even in the case of claiming wheat and barley and admitting to one, the defendant is exempt; the Mishnah only teaches about Rabban Gamliel's stringency.

items.text: Baraita on claims of movables and land
items.text_en: Baraita on claims of movables and land
items.desc_en: A baraita states: if one claims vessels and land, and admits to vessels but denies land, or admits to land but denies vessels, he is exempt from shevuah. This further illustrates the rules of partial admission.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita: if one claimed vessels and land and admitted to one and denied the other, he is exempt, which may challenge Shmuel's position.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Partial admission of land vs. movables
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Partial admission of land vs. movables
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one admits to part of a claim involving land, he is exempt from an oath, but if he admits to part of a claim involving movables, he is liable. This sets up the basic distinction between land (which is not subject to an oath) and movables.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: partial admission of land exempts from an oath, but partial admission of movables obligates one.

items.text: Gemara's inference and resolution: The case of two types of movables
items.text_en: Gemara's inference and resolution: The case of two types of movables
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if the claim involved two types of movables (e.g., vessels and vessels), the defendant would be liable, since land is not subject to an oath. It then rejects this inference, explaining that the Mishnah's real point is to teach that partial admission to movables makes one liable even for the land (through the principle of זוקין). The Gemara notes that this principle is already known from another source, but the Mishnah mentions it incidentally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if the claim involved two types of movables (vessels and vessels), the defendant would be liable, since land is not subject to an oath.

The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that even with two types of movables the defendant is exempt, and the Mishnah's real point is to teach that partial admission to movables makes one liable even for the land.
The Gemara objects that the principle of זוקין (linking movables to land for the oath) is already known from a baraita.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah mentions this principle only incidentally (אגב גררא), not as its primary teaching.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's opinion: Wheat and barley claim
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's opinion: Wheat and barley claim
