items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that if one claimed wheat and barley and the defendant admitted to one of them, he is exempt. This contradicts another statement attributed to Rabbi Yochanan. The Gemara resolves that these are different Amoraic interpretations of Rabbi Yochanan's view.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that if one claimed wheat and barley and the defendant admitted to one, he is exempt.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yitzchak reported Rabbi Yochanan's approval of a contradictory ruling, implying Rabbi Yochanan held the defendant is liable.
The Gemara resolves that the two statements are different Amoraic interpretations of Rabbi Yochanan's view, not direct contradictions.

items.text: Challenge from a Baraita: Wheat and barley vs. wheat admitted as barley
items.text_en: Challenge from a Baraita: Wheat and barley vs. wheat admitted as barley
items.desc_en: A Baraita states that if one claimed wheat and the defendant admitted to barley, he is exempt (except Rabban Gamliel who obligates). The Gemara infers that if the claim was wheat and barley and he admitted to one, he would be liable. The Gemara rejects this, explaining that the Baraita's formulation is only to highlight Rabban Gamliel's stringent view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges with a Baraita: if one claimed wheat and the defendant admitted to barley, he is exempt (except Rabban Gamliel who obligates); the Gemara infers that if the claim was wheat and barley and he admitted to one, he would be liable.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the Baraita's formulation is only to highlight Rabban Gamliel's stringent view, but the underlying law is that even in the mixed claim one is exempt.

items.text: Second challenge from a Mishnah: Vessels and land again
items.text_en: Second challenge from a Mishnah: Vessels and land again
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another Mishnah that explicitly states the same law as the opening Mishnah, and again infers that vessels and vessels would be liable. The Gemara gives the same answer: the Mishnah's point is to teach that partial admission to vessels obligates an oath even for the land, and this is incidental.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah that states partial admission to vessels obligates an oath, and infers that if the claim were vessels and vessels, the defendant would be liable.
The Gemara answers that even vessels and vessels would be exempt, and the Mishnah's point is to teach that partial admission to vessels obligates an oath even for the land, which is incidental.

items.text: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's objection: Ox and sheep claim
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's objection: Ox and sheep claim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects to Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba with a Baraita: if one claimed an ox and a sheep and admitted to one, he is liable. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba deflects by saying the Baraita follows Rabban Gamliel, but then corrects himself, stating it follows Admon, and that this was a well-established tradition from Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects to Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba by citing a Baraita: if one claimed an ox and a sheep and admitted to one, he is liable.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's initial deflection
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's initial deflection
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba deflects by saying the Baraita follows Rabban Gamliel, but Rabbi Abba bar Memel immediately objects that even the first clause would then be liable.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba corrects himself, stating the Baraita follows Admon, and that this was a well-established tradition from Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: Rav Anan in the name of Shmuel: Intent and needles
items.text_en: Rav Anan in the name of Shmuel: Intent and needles
items.desc_en: Rav Anan reports two statements from Shmuel: (1) If one claimed wheat and the defendant preemptively admitted to barley, if he did so cunningly (מערים) he is liable, but if unintentionally (מתכוין) he is exempt. (2) If one claimed two needles and the defendant admitted to one, he is liable, which explains why vessels (even small ones) are subject to the oath.

sub.desc_en: Rav Anan reports Shmuel's first statement: if one claimed wheat and the defendant preemptively admitted to barley, if done cunningly (מערים) he is liable, but if unintentionally (מתכוין) he is exempt.
Rav Anan reports Shmuel's second statement: if one claimed two needles and the defendant admitted to one, he is liable, which explains why vessels (even small ones) are subject to the oath.

items.text: Rav Papa: Vessels and a perutah
items.text_en: Rav Papa: Vessels and a perutah
items.desc_en: Rav Papa rules: If one claimed vessels and a perutah (small coin) and admitted to the vessels but denied the perutah, he is exempt; if he admitted to the perutah and denied the vessels, he is liable. The Gemara explains that this ruling combines two views: one like Rav (that the denial must be of at least two silver coins) and one like Shmuel (that admitting to one of two types obligates).

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa rules that if one claimed vessels and a perutah (small coin) and admitted to the vessels but denied the perutah, he is exempt; if he admitted to the perutah and denied the vessels, he is liable.
The Gemara explains that Rav Papa's ruling combines two views: one like Rav (that the denial must be of at least two silver coins) and one like Shmuel (that admitting to one of two types obligates).

items.text: Rav Nachman: The case of total denial and the oath of hesset
items.text_en: Rav Nachman: The case of total denial and the oath of hesset
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one claims 'I have a maneh in your hand' and the defendant says 'I have nothing of yours', he is exempt. Rav Nachman adds that we administer an oath of hesset (a rabbinic oath) because it is assumed that a person does not sue unless he has a claim. The Gemara objects that the defendant may be evading payment, and the oath is to deter evasion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one claims 'I have a maneh in your hand' and the defendant says 'I have nothing of yours', he is exempt from a biblical oath.
Rav Nachman adds that we administer an oath of היסת (a rabbinic oath) to the defendant.
The Gemara asks the reason for Rav Nachman's ruling, explaining the presumption that a person does not sue unless he has a valid claim.
The Gemara objects with a counter-presumption: a person does not have the audacity to deny a debt in front of his creditor.
The Gemara resolves that the defendant is merely evading payment, thinking 'until I have money and I will pay him', so the oath is administered to deter evasion.

items.text: Rav Idi bar Avin: The difference between loan and deposit
items.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin: The difference between loan and deposit
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin reports in the name of Rav Chisda that one who denies a loan is still fit to testify, but one who denies a deposit is disqualified. This supports the idea that denial of a loan may be due to evasion, while denial of a deposit is considered outright theft.

sub.text: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin reports in the name of Rav Chisda that one who denies a loan is still fit to testify, but one who denies a deposit is disqualified, supporting the idea that denial of a loan may be due to evasion while denial of a deposit is considered outright theft.

items.text: Rav Nachman on the case of 'I gave it to you'
items.text_en: Rav Nachman on the case of 'I gave it to you'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues: If the defendant initially admitted ('yes') and later said 'I gave it to you', he is exempt. Rav Nachman again imposes an oath of hesset. The Gemara notes that one who teaches this ruling for the first case (total denial) certainly applies it to the second case (claim of payment).

sub.desc_en: Rav Chaviva teaches the Mishnah's second case: the defendant initially admits and later claims payment, and is exempt.
Rav Nachman imposes an oath of היסת (hesset) on the defendant in this case as well.
The Gemara notes that one who teaches Rav Nachman's ruling for the first case (total denial) certainly applies it to the second case (claim of payment).

items.text: Clarification of the dispute's scope
items.text_en: Clarification of the dispute's scope
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute between the two versions of the Mishnah (whether the oath applies to the beginning or the end of the Mishnah) is limited to cases where there is a monetary loss involved, but not where there is no monetary loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute between the two Mishnah versions by limiting the oath's application to cases involving monetary loss.

items.text: Difference between biblical and rabbinic oaths: reversing the oath
items.text_en: Difference between biblical and rabbinic oaths: reversing the oath
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between a biblical oath and a rabbinic oath. One difference is that a biblical oath cannot be reversed (imposed on the other party), while a rabbinic oath can be reversed. Mar bar Rav Ashi holds that even a biblical oath can be reversed, so another difference is needed: for a biblical oath, the court seizes the defendant's property, but for a rabbinic oath, it does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between a biblical oath (שבועה דאורייתא) and a rabbinic oath (שבועה דרבנן).
The Gemara answers that one difference is reversing the oath (מיפך שבועה): for a biblical oath, the court does not reverse the oath onto the other party, but for a rabbinic oath, it does.
Mar bar Rav Ashi holds that even a biblical oath can be reversed, so the Gemara asks what difference remains.
The Gemara resolves that another difference is seizing property (מיחת לנכסיה): for a biblical oath, the court seizes the defendant's property, but for a rabbinic oath, it does not.

items.text: Rabbi Yose's view and further differences
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose's view and further differences
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers Rabbi Yose's opinion that even for a rabbinic oath, the court seizes property, citing a Mishnah about finding lost items. Rav Chisda explains that Rabbi Yose's 'complete robbery' is rabbinic. The Gemara then asks what difference remains between biblical and rabbinic oaths, and answers: if the opposing party is suspected of perjury, for a biblical oath we reverse the oath onto him, but for a rabbinic oath we do not make a rabbinic enactment on top of another enactment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Yose, who says that even for a rabbinic oath we seize property, what difference remains between biblical and rabbinic oaths?

The Gemara cites a Mishnah about finding lost items of a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor, where Rabbi Yose says it is 'complete robbery' (גזל גמור), and Rav Chisda explains that this robbery is only rabbinic, and the practical difference is that the court can seize property.

The Gemara answers: the difference is that if the opposing party is suspected of perjury, for a biblical oath we reverse the oath onto him, but for a rabbinic oath we do not make a rabbinic enactment on top of another enactment.

items.text: What to do when property cannot be seized
items.text_en: What to do when property cannot be seized
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is done to a defendant who refuses to take a rabbinic oath, according to the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Yose and do not seize property. Ravina suggests that if we seize his cloak, we have already taken his property. Rav Ashi answers that we excommunicate him until the time for flogging arrives, then we flog him and release him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is done to a defendant who refuses to take a rabbinic oath, according to the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Yose and do not seize property.
Ravina suggests that if we seize his cloak, we have already taken his property, so the proposed solution is ineffective.
Rav Ashi answers that we excommunicate him until the time for flogging arrives, then we flog him and release him.

items.text: Case of a creditor with a promissory note and the debtor claims payment
items.text_en: Case of a creditor with a promissory note and the debtor claims payment
items.desc_en: Rav Papa states that if a creditor produces a promissory note and the debtor claims it was paid, we tell the debtor to pay. If the debtor demands an oath from the creditor, we tell the creditor to swear. Rav Acha bar Rava asks how this differs from the case of one who impairs his note (admitting partial payment). Rav Ashi explains that in the latter case, we claim on his behalf even if he does not, but here we only tell the debtor to pay, and if he demands an oath, we tell the creditor to swear. However, if the creditor is a Torah scholar, we do not make him swear.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa rules that when a creditor produces a promissory note and the debtor claims it was paid, we tell the debtor to pay, and if the debtor demands an oath, we tell the creditor to swear.
Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi how this case differs from the case of one who impairs his promissory note (admitting partial payment).

Rav Ashi distinguishes: in the case of impairing the note, we claim on the debtor's behalf even if he does not; here we only tell the debtor to pay, and if he demands an oath we tell the creditor to swear, but if the creditor is a Torah scholar we do not make him swear.

items.text: Exception for a Torah scholar: no involvement in his case
items.text_en: Exception for a Torah scholar: no involvement in his case
items.desc_en: Rav Yemar questions Rav Ashi's ruling that a Torah scholar does not swear, arguing that a Torah scholar would not send someone's cloak (i.e., would not be suspected of lying). Rather, we do not get involved in his case at all (we do not adjudicate it).

sub.text: Rav Yemar's objection to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Yemar's objection to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Yemar objects to Rav Ashi's ruling that a Torah scholar does not swear, arguing that a Torah scholar would not send someone's cloak (i.e., would not be suspected of lying), so we should not adjudicate his case at all.

items.text: Dispute about repaying a loan made in front of witnesses
items.text_en: Dispute about repaying a loan made in front of witnesses
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav Asi: one who lends to another in front of witnesses must repay in front of witnesses. Shmuel disagrees, saying the debtor can claim he repaid in front of witnesses who went overseas. The Gemara challenges this from the Mishnah: if the creditor claims 'I have a maneh in your hand' and the debtor admits, then later says 'I gave it to you,' he is exempt. Since the creditor claimed in front of witnesses, it is like lending in front of witnesses, yet the Mishnah says he is exempt (contradicting Rav Asi).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Asi states that one who lends to another in front of witnesses must repay in front of witnesses.
Shmuel objects that the debtor can claim he repaid in front of witnesses who have since gone overseas, so repayment in front of witnesses is not always required.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah where the creditor claims in front of witnesses, yet the debtor is exempt if he claims repayment, contradicting Rav Asi's rule.

items.text: Rav Asi's response to the refutation
items.text_en: Rav Asi's response to the refutation
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially raises a refutation against Rav Asi's position. Rav Asi defends himself by distinguishing his earlier statement, which applied only when the loan was originally given with witnesses and the borrower did not trust himself, whereas here the borrower explicitly trusted himself by agreeing to repay with witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a refutation (תיוּבְתָּא) against Rav Asi's position.

Rav Asi defends himself by distinguishing his earlier statement, which applied only when the loan was originally given with witnesses and the borrower did not trust himself, whereas here the borrower explicitly trusted himself by agreeing to repay with witnesses.

items.text: Rav Yosef's version of Rav Asi's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's version of Rav Asi's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef transmits Rav Asi's ruling in a different formulation: one who lends with witnesses does not need to repay with witnesses, but if the lender stipulated repayment only with witnesses, then repayment must be with witnesses. Shmuel adds that the borrower can claim he repaid in front of witnesses who have since gone overseas.

sub.desc_en: The stam introduces Rav Yosef's alternative version of Rav Asi's ruling.
Rav Asi rules that a lender who lent with witnesses does not need repayment with witnesses, unless the lender stipulated repayment only with witnesses.
Shmuel adds that the borrower can claim he repaid in front of witnesses who have since gone overseas.

items.text: Refutation of Shmuel and resolution via Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Refutation of Shmuel and resolution via Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that contradicts Shmuel's position, where the borrower is liable because he must repay with witnesses. Shmuel deflects this by claiming it is a Tannaitic dispute, citing a beraita where Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira allows the borrower to claim repayment in front of witnesses who have gone overseas, while the first Tanna requires either payment or proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where a borrower who claims repayment is liable because he must pay in front of witnesses, refuting Shmuel's position.

Shmuel deflects the refutation by claiming it is a Tannaitic dispute, citing a beraita where Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira allows the borrower to claim repayment in front of witnesses who have gone overseas, while the first Tanna requires either payment or proof.

items.text: Rav Acha's challenge to the beraita's interpretation
items.text_en: Rav Acha's challenge to the beraita's interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Acha questions the assumption that the beraita refers to the time of the loan; it might refer to the time of the claim, where the lender says 'Did I not lend you with witnesses? You should have repaid me with witnesses!' But at the time of the loan, all agree the borrower is liable.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha challenges the assumption that the beraita refers to the time of the loan, suggesting it might refer to the time of the claim, where the lender says 'Did I not lend you with witnesses? You should have repaid me with witnesses!' — but at the time of the loan, all agree the borrower is liable.

items.text: Conflicting halakhic rulings from Rava's students
items.text_en: Conflicting halakhic rulings from Rava's students
items.desc_en: Rav Pappi and Rav Pappa each report a different halakha in Rava's name: one requires repayment with witnesses for a loan given with witnesses, the other requires it only if stipulated. The latter also allows the borrower to claim repayment in front of witnesses who have gone overseas. A mnemonic lists the key terms.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappi reports in Rava's name that one who lent with witnesses must repay with witnesses.

Rav Pappa reports a conflicting ruling in Rava's name: repayment with witnesses is not required unless stipulated, and the borrower is believed if he claims he repaid before witnesses who went overseas.
A mnemonic lists key terms from the two conflicting reports: Reuven and Shimon, who taught halakha, borrowed and repaid, Ploni and Ploni, witnesses on both sides, trustworthiness like two.

items.text: Case of repayment in front of unspecified witnesses
items.text_en: Case of repayment in front of unspecified witnesses
items.desc_en: A borrower was told to repay in front of Reuven and Shimon but repaid in front of two other people. Abaye says he fulfilled the condition since he repaid in front of two witnesses, but Rava argues the lender specified Reuven and Shimon to avoid being pushed off.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a borrower was told to repay in front of Reuven and Shimon, but he repaid in front of two other people.
Abaye rules that the borrower fulfilled the condition because he repaid in front of two witnesses, as specified.
Rava objects that the lender specified Reuven and Shimon specifically to prevent the borrower from pushing him off, so the condition was not fulfilled.

items.text: Case of repayment to a Torah scholar and the ruling of Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Case of repayment to a Torah scholar and the ruling of Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: A borrower was told to repay in front of two Torah scholars but repaid privately; the coins were then lost. The lender admitted receiving them as a deposit until he could fulfill the condition. Rav Nachman ruled that since the lender admitted receiving the money, it is a valid repayment, and if he wants to fulfill the condition, he must bring the witnesses himself, as Rav Nachman and Rav Sheishet are qualified.

sub.desc_en: A borrower was told to repay in front of two Torah scholars, but repaid privately, and the coins were subsequently lost.
The lender admitted receiving the money as a deposit until the condition could be fulfilled.

Rav Nachman ruled that since the lender admitted receiving the money, it is a valid repayment, and if he wants to fulfill the condition, he must bring the witnesses himself, as Rav Nachman and Rav Sheishet are qualified.

items.text: Case of denial of the loan and contradictory witnesses
items.text_en: Case of denial of the loan and contradictory witnesses
items.desc_en: A borrower denied ever receiving a loan, but witnesses testified that he both borrowed and repaid. Abaye is uncertain how to rule, but Rava says that one who says 'I never borrowed' is like one who says 'I never repaid,' and is liable.

sub.desc_en: A borrower denies ever receiving a loan, but witnesses testify that he both borrowed and repaid, prompting Abaye's uncertainty.
Abaye questions how to rule when the same witnesses contradict each other about the loan and repayment.
Rava rules that one who denies borrowing is treated as one who denies repaying, making him liable.

items.text: Case of denial of repayment with witnesses who deny the event
items.text_en: Case of denial of repayment with witnesses who deny the event
items.desc_en: A borrower claimed he repaid in front of Ploni and Almoni, but those witnesses denied it. Rav Sheishet thought the borrower is established as a denier, but Rava said a person does not remember things that are not incumbent upon him.

sub.desc_en: A borrower claimed he repaid in front of Ploni and Almoni, but those witnesses denied it.
Rav Sheishet thought the borrower is established as a denier (כַּפְרָן) because his claim of repayment was contradicted by witnesses.
Rava rejected Rav Sheishet's reasoning, arguing that a person does not remember things that are not incumbent upon him, so the borrower is not necessarily a denier.

items.text: Case of partial repayment claim
items.text_en: Case of partial repayment claim
items.desc_en: A lender demanded six hundred zuz, and the borrower claimed he had repaid one hundred kav (a measure). The text is cut off, but the case involves a dispute over partial repayment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case where a lender demands six hundred zuz and the borrower claims he repaid one hundred kav (a measure).

items.text: Rava's principle of 'established as a denier'
items.text_en: Rava's principle of 'established as a denier'
items.desc_en: Rava states that if witnesses testify that the debtor admitted to the debt, he is established as a denier. Rami bar Chama objects, saying people don't remember what isn't on their mind, but Rava responds that the amount of the doorpost is remembered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where witnesses testify that the debtor admitted to a debt, establishing him as a denier.
Rami bar Chama objects that people do not remember details that are not on their mind.
Rava responds that the amount of the doorpost is remembered by people.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Pappa on a promissory note
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Pappa on a promissory note
items.desc_en: A debtor claims he repaid, but the creditor says the note is for other loans. Rav Nachman says the note is invalidated; Rav Pappa disagrees. The Gemara distinguishes this from a case where the debtor claimed the creditor took a bribe, which Rav Pappa agreed invalidates the note.

sub.desc_en: A debtor claims he repaid, but the creditor says the note is for other loans.
Rav Nachman rules that the promissory note is invalidated.
Rav Pappa disagrees and rules that the note is not invalidated.
The Gemara asks why Rav Pappa distinguishes this case from a similar case where he agreed the note is invalidated.
The Gemara explains that in the other case the creditor admitted taking a bribe, which invalidates the note, but here the creditor merely says the note is for other loans.

items.text: Final ruling on the promissory note dispute
items.text_en: Final ruling on the promissory note dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Pappei and Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi debate the ruling, and the halakha is that the note is invalidated. The Gemara adds that this applies only if he paid in front of witnesses and didn't mention the note.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the final ruling is on the dispute regarding the promissory note.
Rav Pappei rules that the promissory note is not invalidated.

sub.text: Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi's position
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi's position
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi rules that the promissory note is invalidated.
The Gemara concludes that the halakha follows Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi: the note is invalidated.

items.text: Distinction between payment with and without witnesses
items.text_en: Distinction between payment with and without witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the ruling applies only when he paid in front of witnesses and didn't mention the note. If he paid privately, he can claim it was for other loans, citing the case of Avimi bar Rabbi Avahu.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the previous ruling applies only when the debtor paid in front of witnesses without mentioning the promissory note.
The Gemara distinguishes that if the debtor paid privately, he can claim the payment was for other debts, citing the precedent of Avimi bar Rabbi Avahu.

items.text: Case of 'you are believed whenever you say I didn't pay'
items.text_en: Case of 'you are believed whenever you say I didn't pay'
items.desc_en: A debtor said to his creditor, 'You are believed whenever you say I didn't pay.' He then paid in front of witnesses. Abaye and Rava say he is believed, but Rav Pappa objects that he believed him more than himself, not more than witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a debtor told his creditor 'you are believed whenever you say I didn't pay,' and then paid in front of witnesses.
Abaye and Rava rule that the debtor is believed (he is exempt) because he had already empowered the creditor to claim non-payment.
Rav Pappa objects: although the debtor believed the creditor more than himself, he did not believe him more than witnesses, so the witnesses' testimony should override the creditor's claim.

items.text: Case of 'you are believed like two witnesses'
items.text_en: Case of 'you are believed like two witnesses'
items.desc_en: A debtor said 'you are believed like two witnesses' and paid in front of three. Rav Pappa says he believed him like two, not three. Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua objects that for testimony, many are like two and two like many.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a debtor said 'you are believed like two witnesses' and later paid in front of three witnesses.
Rav Pappa rules that the debtor believed him like two witnesses, not like three, so the payment before three does not disprove the claim.
Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua objects that for testimony, many witnesses are like two and two are like many, so the debtor's belief in two should extend to three.

items.text: Alternative version of the 'like two witnesses' case
items.text_en: Alternative version of the 'like two witnesses' case
items.desc_en: An alternative version presents the same case. Rav Pappa rules he believed him like two, not three. Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua objects that two are like a hundred and a hundred like two, and if he said 'like three' and paid before four, since it descends to opinions, it descends.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version presents the same case: one who said 'I trust you like two witnesses' and later paid before three; Rav Pappa rules he trusted him like two, not three.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua objects that two are like a hundred and a hundred like two, and if he said 'like three' and paid before four, since it descends to opinions, it descends.

items.text: Oaths on claims of a deaf-mute, insane person, or minor
items.text_en: Oaths on claims of a deaf-mute, insane person, or minor
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one does not swear on the claim of a deaf-mute, insane person, or minor, nor does one administer an oath to a minor. The Gemara explains the scriptural basis and discusses a case where one swears on the claim of a minor regarding his father's debt, citing Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one does not swear on the claim of a deaf-mute, insane person, or minor, nor does one administer an oath to a minor.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural basis of the Mishnah's rule.
The Gemara cites the verse 'כי יתן איש אל רעהו' (When a man gives to his fellow) to show that a minor's deposit is legally void.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah itself later says one does swear for a minor and for consecrated property, contradicting the opening rule.
Rav resolves the contradiction by explaining that the later clause refers to a case where the claimant comes on behalf of his father, and it follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

A baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rules that one sometimes swears on his own claim, giving the example of a son claiming his father's debt, while the Sages exempt him as one who returns a lost object.
The Gemara questions how Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov can require an oath when the principle of 'one who returns a lost object is exempt' should apply.
Rav answers that the case involves a minor who made the claim, so the exemption of returning a lost object does not apply.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly says one does not swear on the claim of a minor, contradicting Rav's explanation.
The Gemara answers that the claimant is actually an adult, but he is called a 'minor' relative to his father's affairs.
The Gemara objects that if the claimant is an adult, the baraita's phrase 'his own claim' is inaccurate, since it is actually the claim of others (the father).
The Gemara resolves that the baraita means the claim is of others (the father), but the admission is of himself (the son admits he owes the father).

items.text: Rabbah's rationale for the partial admission oath
items.text_en: Rabbah's rationale for the partial admission oath
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Rabbis is based on Rabbah's principle: a person is not brazen enough to deny a debt entirely in the creditor's presence, but may delay payment by admitting part. The Torah imposes an oath to force full admission.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah's cases are not all classified as a claim of others and an admission of oneself.
The Gemara explains that the dispute is based on Rabbah's principle: a person is not brazen enough to deny entirely in the creditor's presence, so the Torah imposes an oath to force full admission.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that one is not brazen even before the creditor's son, so the partial admission is not a 'returner of a lost object'. The Rabbis hold that one is brazen before the son, so the admission shows honesty and exempts from oath.

sub.text: Stam (anonymous statement of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position)
sub.text_en: Stam (anonymous statement of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that a person is not brazen (מעיז) even before the creditor's son, so the partial admission does not qualify as returning a lost object (משיב אבידה).

sub.text: Stam (anonymous statement of the Rabbis' position)
sub.text_en: Stam (anonymous statement of the Rabbis' position)
sub.desc_en: The Rabbis hold that one is brazen before the son but not before the creditor himself, so the admission before the son demonstrates honesty and exempts from the oath as a returning of a lost object.

items.text: Rejection of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position
items.text_en: Rejection of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah can be aligned with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, since the first clause rules 'exempt' because the defendant is a 'returner of a lost object'. The answer distinguishes: there the claimant did not say 'I am certain', here he does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah can be aligned with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, citing the first clause that rules 'exempt' because the defendant is a 'returner of a lost object'.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's case is different: there the claimant did not say 'I am certain', but here he does.

items.text: Shmuel's teaching on collecting from orphans and hekdesh
items.text_en: Shmuel's teaching on collecting from orphans and hekdesh
items.desc_en: Shmuel teaches that 'to a minor' means collecting from the minor's property, and 'to hekdesh' means collecting from hekdesh property. The Gemara questions redundancy with existing Mishnayot and explains that Shmuel's teaching is necessary to counter a possible assumption that one does not act deceitfully with hekdesh.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel teaches that the Mishnah's phrase 'to a minor' means collecting from the minor's property, and 'to hekdesh' means collecting from hekdesh property.
The Gemara questions why Shmuel's teaching is needed, since a Mishnah already states that one collects from orphans only with an oath.
The Gemara answers that Shmuel's teaching conveys the ruling of Abaye Keshisha, that 'orphans' includes both adults and minors, and applies both to the oath and to collecting inferior land.
The Gemara questions why Shmuel's teaching about hekdesh is needed, since a Mishnah already requires an oath for collecting from encumbered property, and hekdesh is analogous.

The Gemara answers that Shmuel's teaching is necessary to counter a possible assumption that one does not act deceitfully (עושה קנוניא) with hekdesh, so Shmuel teaches that even for hekdesh an oath is required.

items.text: Distinction between a dying man and a healthy person regarding hekdesh
items.text_en: Distinction between a dying man and a healthy person regarding hekdesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Huna that a dying man who dedicates all his property and claims a debt is believed because one does not act deceitfully with hekdesh. The Gemara distinguishes: that applies to a dying man who has nothing to gain, but for a healthy person we are concerned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Huna's ruling that a dying man who dedicates all his property and claims a debt is believed because one does not act deceitfully with hekdesh.
The Gemara distinguishes: Rav Huna's leniency applies only to a dying man who has nothing to gain, but for a healthy person we are concerned about deceit.

items.text: Mishnah: Items not subject to oaths
items.text_en: Mishnah: Items not subject to oaths
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that are not subject to oaths: slaves, documents, land, and consecrated property. It also states that there is no double payment or four/five payment for them, and a unpaid watchman does not swear, a paid watchman does not pay. Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Meir add qualifications.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing items not subject to oaths: slaves, documents, land, and consecrated property, and states that there is no double payment, four/five payment, and that an unpaid watchman does not swear and a paid watchman does not pay.
Rabbi Shimon adds a qualification: for consecrated property that one is responsible for, oaths are taken; for those not under responsibility, oaths are not taken.
Rabbi Meir states that there are items attached to land that are not treated as land, and the Sages disagree.
Rabbi Meir gives an example: if one says 'I gave you ten laden vines' and the other says 'only five', Rabbi Meir obligates an oath, but the Sages say anything attached to land is like land.

The Mishnah concludes that oaths are only taken on items measured, weighed, or counted, with examples: a full house or full bag where the other says 'I don't know' is exempt, but if one says 'up to the ledge' and the other 'up to the window', he is liable.

items.text: Derivation of exemption from double payment
items.text_en: Derivation of exemption from double payment
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the exemption from double payment via a brayta using a general-particular-general hermeneutic: the particular items are movable with intrinsic monetary value, excluding land, slaves (assimilated to land), documents (no intrinsic value), and hekdesh (excluded by 'his fellow').

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where is the exemption from double payment derived?

The baraita cites the verse 'על כל דבר פשע' (concerning any matter of trespass) and applies the כלל ופרט וכלל (general-particular-general) hermeneutic to derive that only movable property with intrinsic monetary value is included.
The Gemara concludes that land, slaves (assimilated to land), documents (no intrinsic value), and hekdesh (excluded by the word 'רֵעֵהוּ' — his fellow) are all exempt from double payment.

items.text: Derivation of exemption from four/five payment and unpaid watchman's oath
items.text_en: Derivation of exemption from four/five payment and unpaid watchman's oath
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the exemption from four/five payment is derived from the verse, and begins to derive the exemption for an unpaid watchman's oath from a brayta.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists exemption from four/five payment separately from double payment, and answers that the Torah only exempts from four/five payment, not from three/four.
The Gemara introduces a brayta to derive the exemption of an unpaid watchman from the oath.

items.text: Derivation of liability for movables
items.text_en: Derivation of liability for movables
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse "כי יתן איש אל רעהו" that a bailee is liable only for movable property with intrinsic value, excluding land, slaves, documents, and consecrated property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara applies the hermeneutic principle of כלל ופרט וכלל (general-particular-general) to the verse 'כי יתן איש אל רעהו' to derive that a bailee is liable only for movable property with intrinsic value.
The Gemara excludes land, slaves (assimilated to land), documents (movable but lacking intrinsic value), and consecrated property (based on the word 'רֵעֵהוּ' meaning a fellow person).

items.text: Paid bailee exempt from paying
items.text_en: Paid bailee exempt from paying
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the rule that a paid bailee does not pay, citing a similar derivation from the verse about a paid bailee.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the rule that a paid bailee does not pay, citing a similar derivation from the verse about a paid bailee.

items.text: Dispute about attached produce
items.text_en: Dispute about attached produce
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis disagree about whether attached produce is considered land; Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains they argue about grapes ready to be harvested.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir states that there are items that are like land but not land, introducing the dispute about attached produce.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Meir's position, asking why the dispute is about claims rather than about the status of attached produce itself.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains that the dispute concerns grapes ready to be harvested, with Rabbi Meir considering them as already detached and the Sages disagreeing.

items.text: Requirement for measurable claim
items.text_en: Requirement for measurable claim
items.desc_en: Abaye limits the mishnah's rule to a vague claim, but Rava argues that one is never liable unless the claim and admission are on a measurable item; a beraita supports Rava.

sub.desc_en: Abaye limits the mishnah's rule to a vague claim of 'a house,' but if one claims 'this house is full,' the claim is measurable and actionable.
Rava objects that if Abaye were correct, the mishnah should have distinguished between vague and specific claims within its own case, rather than only in the later clause.
Rava resolves that one is never liable for an oath unless both the claim and the admission are on a measurable, weighable, or countable item.

items.text: Beraita supporting Rava
items.text_en: Beraita supporting Rava
items.desc_en: A beraita illustrates that one is exempt when the claim and admission are on different types, but liable when they are on the same type with different measures.

sub.desc_en: The beraita presents cases where the claim and admission are on different types (e.g., 'large menorah' vs. 'small menorah'), ruling the defendant exempt.
The beraita presents cases where the claim and admission are on the same type with different measures (e.g., 'a kor' vs. 'a letekh'), ruling the defendant liable.
The beraita concludes with the general principle that liability requires the claim and admission to be on a matter of measure, weight, or count.

items.text: Analysis of the beraita's cases
items.text_en: Analysis of the beraita's cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the beraita's distinction between a large and small candelabrum versus a ten- and five-litrai candelabrum, and resolves it with explanations about a sectional candelabrum or one that can be reduced.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the beraita's phrase 'כללו של דבר' (the general principle) comes to include, suggesting it might include the case of 'בית זה מלא' (this house is full).

The Gemara objects that the distinction between a large and small candelabrum (patut) versus a ten- and five-litrai candelabrum (chayav) is inconsistent, since in both cases the claim and admission do not match.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak answers that the case involves a sectional candelabrum (מנורה של חוליות), where the defendant admits to owning part of it.
The Gemara objects that if the answer is about a sectional candelabrum, the beraita should also have taught a case of a sectional belt (אזור) that can be reduced, but it did not.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel resolves that the candelabrum is different because one can drag it and reduce it to five litrai, making the admission a partial admission of the same item.

items.text: Mishnah: Lender and pledge
items.text_en: Mishnah: Lender and pledge
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents cases where a lender and borrower dispute the value of a lost pledge, determining liability based on whether the admission is of a different type or a partial admission of the same type.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah presents the first case: a lender claims he lent a sela (סלע) on a pledge worth a shekel (שקל), and the borrower claims the pledge was worth a sela — the borrower is exempt from an oath.
The mishnah presents the second case: the lender claims a sela loan and a shekel value, the borrower admits to a sela loan but claims a three-dinar value — the borrower is liable to swear.

The mishnah presents the third and fourth cases: when the borrower claims a lower value and the lender claims a higher value, the borrower is exempt if the lender's claim equals the loan amount, but liable if the lender's claim exceeds the loan amount.
The mishnah concludes: the one who currently holds the pledge takes the oath, to prevent a scenario where the lender swears and the borrower then produces the pledge.

items.text: Identifying the clause of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Identifying the clause of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Shmuel's statement refers to the latter clause of the Mishnah, but objects that there the oath is with the lender. Shmuel, Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav, and Rabbi Yochanan all say it refers to the first clause.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which clause of the Mishnah Shmuel's statement refers to, and raises an objection that if it refers to the latter clause, the oath would be with the lender, contradicting Shmuel's ruling.

sub.text: Shmuel, Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav, and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Shmuel, Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav, and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Shmuel, Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav, and Rabbi Yochanan all state that Shmuel's statement refers to the first clause of the Mishnah.

items.text: Explaining the first clause
items.text_en: Explaining the first clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the first clause refers to the case where the borrower claims the collateral was worth less, and the oath is with the borrower, but the Sages transferred it to the lender.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the first clause refers to and explains that it is the sub-clause of the first clause, where the borrower claims the collateral was worth less, and the Sages transferred the oath from the borrower to the lender.

items.text: Rav Ashi's interpretation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah's ruling is based on the principle that each party swears: the bailee that the deposit is not in his possession, and the lender as to its value. The question is who swears first, and the answer is the bailee, lest he swear and then the lender produce the deposit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the Mishnah's ruling by stating that the bailee swears first to prevent the lender from producing the deposit after the bailee's oath.

items.text: Shmuel's and Rav Nachman's rulings on lost collateral
items.text_en: Shmuel's and Rav Nachman's rulings on lost collateral
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that if one lent a thousand zuz and took a single sickle-handle as collateral, and it is lost, the entire debt is lost. But if there were two handles, the loss of one does not cancel the whole debt. Rav Nachman disagrees, saying that even with two handles, each is worth half. The Nehardeans say that even with a handle and a cup, the loss of the cup cancels half, and the loss of the handle cancels the whole.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that if one lent a thousand zuz and took a single sickle-handle as collateral, its loss cancels the entire debt, but if there were two handles, the loss of one does not cancel the whole.

Rav Nachman disagrees, ruling that even with two handles, each is worth half, so the loss of one cancels half the debt and the loss of the other cancels the rest, but a handle and a cup are not treated the same.
The Nehardeans rule that even with a handle and a cup, the loss of the cup cancels half the debt and the loss of the handle cancels the entire debt.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the Mishnah: the borrower claims the collateral was worth less, yet he is liable. The borrower could say 'you accepted it as collateral for the full amount.' The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah deals with a case where the lender specified the value, while Shmuel's case is where he did not specify.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the Mishnah: the borrower claims the collateral was worth less, yet he is liable; the borrower could say 'you accepted it as collateral for the full amount.'
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah deals with a case where the lender specified the value, while Shmuel's case is where he did not specify.

items.text: Support from a Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Support from a Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says the lender swears and collects his money if the collateral is lost; Rabbi Akiva says the lender loses his money. The Gemara then asks about the case of a loan with a document and a collateral, where all agree the money is lost. It then asks what the case is, and begins to analyze whether the collateral is worth the loan amount.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says the lender swears and collects his money if the collateral is lost; Rabbi Akiva says the lender loses his money.
The Gemara notes that in a case of a loan with a document and a collateral, all agree the money is lost.
The Gemara asks what the case is, and begins to analyze whether the collateral is worth the loan amount.

items.text: Gemara's question about Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning, suggesting that the dispute is about a pledge worth less than a perutah and whether Shmuel's principle applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning, suggesting that the dispute is about a pledge worth less than a perutah and whether Shmuel's principle applies.

items.text: Rejection of Shmuel's principle and introduction of Rabbi Yitzchak
items.text_en: Rejection of Shmuel's principle and introduction of Rabbi Yitzchak
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous suggestion, stating that all agree on Shmuel's principle when the pledge is not worth a perutah. Instead, the dispute is about a pledge worth a perutah, and it revolves around Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching that a creditor acquires the pledge, as derived from the verse 'and it shall be righteousness for you.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous suggestion, clarifying that all agree on Shmuel's principle when the pledge is not worth a perutah, and the dispute is about a pledge worth a perutah and revolves around Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching.
Rabbi Yitzchak cites the verse 'וּלְךָ תִּהְיֶה צְדָקָה' (and it shall be righteousness for you) to prove that a creditor acquires the pledge.

items.text: Challenge: Is Rabbi Yitzchak's view a Tannaic dispute?
items.text_en: Challenge: Is Rabbi Yitzchak's view a Tannaic dispute?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yitzchak's principle is actually a dispute among Tannaim, but then clarifies that Rabbi Yitzchak only spoke about a pledge taken not at the time of the loan, not one taken at the time of the loan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that a creditor acquires the pledge is actually a dispute among Tannaim.
The Gemara rejects the question with a rhetorical 'would you think so?'
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yitzchak only spoke about a pledge taken not at the time of the loan, not one taken at the time of the loan.

items.text: Refinement: Dispute about a pledge taken at the time of the loan and the laws of a finder
items.text_en: Refinement: Dispute about a pledge taken at the time of the loan and the laws of a finder
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that all agree on Rabbi Yitzchak's principle for a pledge not taken at the time of the loan. The actual dispute here concerns a pledge taken at the time of the loan, and it revolves around the laws of a finder as a bailee, citing the Amoraim Rabbah and Rav Yosef.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that all agree on Rabbi Yitzchak's principle for a pledge not taken at the time of the loan, and the actual dispute concerns a pledge taken at the time of the loan, revolving around the laws of a finder as a bailee.
The Gemara cites the dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef regarding the status of a finder as a bailee, with Rabbah holding he is like an unpaid bailee (שומר חנם).

items.text: Rav Yosef's position and the dispute about the lender's status
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's position and the dispute about the lender's status
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef holds that a lender with collateral is like a paid guardian. The Gemara considers whether this is a dispute between Tanna'im, but concludes that all agree on Rav Yosef's view regarding a finder of lost property; the dispute here is about whether the lender performs a mitzvah by taking collateral.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that a lender who holds collateral is classified as a שומר שכר (paid guardian).
The Gemara asks whether Rav Yosef's position is actually a dispute between Tanna'im (earlier sages).
The Gemara rejects the question, explaining that regarding a finder of lost property (שומר אבידה), everyone agrees with Rav Yosef.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute here is about whether the lender performs a מצוה (commandment) by taking collateral: one opinion (Mar) holds it is a מצוה, the other holds it is not.

items.text: Analysis of the Tannaic dispute about a loan on collateral and shemittah
items.text_en: Analysis of the Tannaic dispute about a loan on collateral and shemittah
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines a Tannaic dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi regarding whether a loan on collateral is subject to shemittah cancellation. It analyzes whether the dispute is about the value of the collateral or about Samuel's principle, and concludes that the first Tanna holds the collateral cancels the debt, while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds it does not, and the collateral is merely a reminder.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to examine a Tannaic dispute about a loan on collateral and shemittah, citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position that the debt is not cancelled.

The Gemara questions the meaning of the first Tanna's statement 'does not cancel' and challenges that if it means only up to the collateral's value, then Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would absurdly cancel even that, undermining the purpose of taking collateral.
The Gemara suggests that the first Tanna means the entire debt is not cancelled, and the dispute is about Samuel's principle that a loan on collateral is not subject to shemittah.

The Gemara rejects the alternative and concludes that the first Tanna holds the collateral cancels the debt up to its value, while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds even that is cancelled, and the collateral serves merely as a reminder (לזכרון דברים בעלמא).

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous chapter with the phrase 'Hadran alach Shevu'at HaDayyanim'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous chapter with the standard formula 'Hadran alach Shevu'at HaDayyanim' (we return to you, Oath of the Judges).

items.text: Mishnah: Those who swear and collect
items.text_en: Mishnah: Those who swear and collect
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those who swear and collect: the hired worker, the robbed, the injured, one whose opponent is suspect regarding oaths, and a storekeeper regarding his ledger. It details the cases of the hired worker, the robbed, and the injured, with Rabbi Yehuda requiring a partial admission.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing those who swear and collect: the hired worker, the robbed, the injured, one whose opponent is suspect regarding oaths, and a storekeeper regarding his ledger.

sub.text: Mishnah's detail on the hired worker
sub.text_en: Mishnah's detail on the hired worker
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah details the case of the hired worker: the worker swears and collects, with Rabbi Yehuda requiring a partial admission, illustrated by a dispute over fifty dinars with a gold dinar acknowledged.

The Mishnah details the case of the robbed: witnesses saw entry without permission, the claimant swears and collects, with Rabbi Yehuda requiring a partial admission, illustrated by a dispute over two vessels with one acknowledged.

The Mishnah details the case of the injured: witnesses saw entry healthy and exit injured, the claimant swears and collects, with Rabbi Yehuda requiring a partial admission, illustrated by a dispute over two injuries with one acknowledged.

sub.text: Mishnah's transition to the suspect case
sub.text_en: Mishnah's transition to the suspect case
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah transitions to the case of one whose opponent is suspect regarding oaths, asking how this applies.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Those who swear and collect
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Those who swear and collect
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where one swears and collects, including a worker, a victim of theft, and a creditor. It then discusses the case where one of the parties is suspected of swearing falsely, and the dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Meir regarding when both are suspected.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing types of oaths and then enumerates cases where the opposing party swears and collects, including a gambler, usurer, pigeon-flyer, and Sabbatical-year trader.

The Mishnah presents the dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Meir regarding when both parties are suspected of swearing falsely: Rabbi Yosei says the oath returns to its place, Rabbi Meir says they divide.

items.text: The case of the storekeeper and his ledger
items.text_en: The case of the storekeeper and his ledger
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a storekeeper who claims he paid workers, while the workers deny receiving payment. The storekeeper swears and collects, and the workers swear and collect. Ben Nannas objects, arguing this leads to a vain oath, and proposes that both take without an oath.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a storekeeper and his ledger, where the storekeeper claims he paid workers and they deny receiving payment, so both swear and collect.
Ben Nannas objects that this leads to a vain oath (שבועת שוא) and proposes that both take without an oath.

items.text: Disputes between a householder and a storekeeper or money changer
items.text_en: Disputes between a householder and a storekeeper or money changer
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details cases where a householder asks a storekeeper for produce or a money changer for coins, and disputes arise about payment. In each case, the one who denies receiving payment swears. Rabbi Yehuda offers a different ruling based on who holds the item.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a householder asks a storekeeper for produce for a dinar, and after receiving it, the storekeeper claims the dinar was not paid; the householder swears he paid it.
The Mishnah presents a second case where the storekeeper claims he already gave the produce; the storekeeper swears.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that the one holding the produce has the upper hand, and similarly for the money changer, he does not give small change until he receives the dinar.

items.text: Cases where a woman collects her ketubah with an oath
items.text_en: Cases where a woman collects her ketubah with an oath
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a woman collects her ketubah only with an oath, such as when she impairs her ketubah, when one witness testifies it is paid, or when collecting from encumbered property. It then discusses the oath of heirs and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing cases where a woman collects her ketubah only with an oath: when she impairs it, when one witness testifies it is paid, from encumbered property, from orphans' property, and when collecting not in the husband's presence.
The Mishnah adds that heirs also collect only with an oath, reciting a formula that they did not find the debt paid among their father's documents.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka rules that even a son born after the father's death may swear and collect.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that if witnesses testify that the father declared at his death that the debt is unpaid, the heir collects without an oath.

items.text: Those who swear without a claim and the rule of gilgul shevuah
items.text_en: Those who swear without a claim and the rule of gilgul shevuah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists partners, sharecroppers, guardians, and others who swear without a specific claim. It then states that after division, partners cannot impose an oath, but if a shevuah is triggered from another source, it can be expanded via gilgul. The shemittah year cancels the oath.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those who swear without a specific claim: partners, sharecroppers, guardians, a woman managing the household, and a household steward, and states that if the defendant says 'I want you to swear to me,' the plaintiff is obligated.

The Mishnah rules that after partners or sharecroppers divide the property, one cannot impose an oath, but if an oath is triggered from another source, it can be expanded via גילגול (rolling over), and the shemittah year cancels the oath.

items.text: Gemara: Why does a hired worker swear and collect?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why does a hired worker swear and collect?
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by establishing the general principle that those who swear in the Torah swear and do not pay. It then asks why the rabbis instituted that a hired worker swears and collects. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says they taught 'great halakhot' here, but the Gemara objects and Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel clarifies: they taught 'fixed enactments' – the rabbis uprooted the oath from the householder and placed it on the worker for the sake of the worker's livelihood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes the general principle that those who swear in the Torah swear and do not pay, citing the verse 'וְלָקַח בְּעָלָיו וְלֹא יְשַׁלֵּם' (the owner shall take and not pay) to show that the oath is given to the one who would otherwise pay.
The Gemara asks why the rabbis instituted that a hired worker swears and collects, deviating from the general principle.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers that they taught 'great halakhot' here, implying the rule is a fundamental law.
The Gemara objects that these are mere halakhot, not 'great' ones, questioning the characterization.
The Gemara corrects the statement to say 'great enactments' were taught here, not halakhot.
The Gemara objects that calling them 'great' implies there are 'small' enactments, which is problematic.

sub.text: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel resolves that they taught 'fixed enactments' – the rabbis uprooted the oath from the householder and placed it on the worker for the sake of the worker's livelihood, and the householder is content because it ensures workers will hire themselves to him.

items.text: Gemara: Further analysis of the enactment
items.text_en: Gemara: Further analysis of the enactment
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the reasoning, suggesting the worker would prefer the householder swear, but the Gemara responds that the householder is busy with his workers. It then asks why not give the worker without an oath, and answers that it is to appease the householder. Further questions about witnesses and immediate payment are answered with practical considerations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the worker would prefer the householder swear and be exempt, so the worker would be hired.
The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that the householder is forced to hire and is busy with his workers.
The Gemara asks why the householder should not simply pay the worker without an oath.
The Gemara answers that the oath is to appease the householder.
The Gemara asks why the householder does not pay with witnesses.
The Gemara answers that arranging witnesses is burdensome for the householder.
The Gemara asks why the householder does not pay the worker immediately at the outset.
The Gemara answers that both parties prefer credit (הקפה).

items.text: Gemara's objection: if so, even for cutting?
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: if so, even for cutting?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the worker's oath is based on the employer's forgetfulness, then even in a case of cutting (where the worker claims two cuts and the employer says one), the worker should swear and take. But the Mishnah says the burden of proof is on the claimant, implying the worker does not swear. The Gemara explains that cutting is certainly remembered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the worker's oath is based on the employer's forgetfulness, then even in a case of cutting (where the worker claims two cuts and the employer says one), the worker should swear and take, but the Mishnah says the burden of proof is on the claimant, implying the worker does not swear; the Gemara explains that cutting is certainly remembered.

items.text: Gemara's objection: if so, even after the time has passed?
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: if so, even after the time has passed?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the worker's oath is due to the employer's forgetfulness, then even after the time for payment has passed, the worker should swear and take. But a baraita says that after the time has passed, the worker does not swear and take. The Gemara answers that there is a presumption that the employer does not violate the prohibition of delaying wages, and when the time of obligation arrives, he reminds himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the worker's oath is due to the employer's forgetfulness, then even after the time for payment has passed, the worker should swear and take, but a baraita says that after the time has passed, the worker does not swear and take.
The Gemara answers that there is a presumption that the employer does not violate the prohibition of delaying wages, and when the time of obligation arrives, he reminds himself.

items.text: Gemara's question: does the worker violate 'bal tigzol'?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: does the worker violate 'bal tigzol'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the worker violates the prohibition of robbery by delaying his wages. It answers that regarding the employer, there are two presumptions: that the employer does not violate 'bal talin' and that the worker does not delay his wages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the worker violates the prohibition of robbery (בל תגזול) by delaying his wages.

The Gemara answers that regarding the employer, there are two presumptions: that the employer does not violate בל תלין (the prohibition of delaying wages) and that the worker does not delay his wages.

items.text: Rav Nachman citing Shmuel: distinction based on witnesses
items.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Shmuel: distinction based on witnesses
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman says in the name of Shmuel that the Mishnah's rule (that the worker swears and takes) applies only when he was hired with witnesses. But if hired without witnesses, since the employer could say 'I never hired you,' he can also say 'I hired you and paid you.' Rabbi Yitzchak praises this statement and says Rabbi Yochanan said the same.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states in Shmuel's name that the Mishnah's rule (worker swears and takes) applies only when hired with witnesses; without witnesses, the employer can deny hiring altogether and thus claim payment.
Rabbi Yitzchak praises Rav Nachman's statement and confirms that Rabbi Yochanan said the same ruling.

items.text: Gemara's note: does Resh Lakish disagree?
items.text_en: Gemara's note: does Resh Lakish disagree?
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that from Rabbi Yitzchak's praise, it implies that Resh Lakish disagreed. There are two versions: one says Resh Lakish was drinking and silent, another says he was delaying and silent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Resh Lakish's silence implies disagreement with Rabbi Yitzchak's praise of Rav Nachman's statement.
The Gemara offers two versions: one says Resh Lakish was drinking and silent, another says he was delaying and silent, explaining that his silence was not necessarily disagreement.

items.text: Rav Menashya bar Zevid citing Rav: same ruling
items.text_en: Rav Menashya bar Zevid citing Rav: same ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Zevid says in the name of Rav the same ruling as Shmuel: the Mishnah applies only when hired with witnesses; without witnesses, the employer can claim he never hired him.

sub.text: Rav Menashya bar Zevid citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Menashya bar Zevid citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Zevid reports in the name of Rav the same ruling as Shmuel: the Mishnah's oath applies only when the employer hired the worker with witnesses; without witnesses, the employer can claim he never hired him.

items.text: Rami bar Chama praises the statement; Rava challenges with bailees
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama praises the statement; Rava challenges with bailees
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama praises the statement, but Rava challenges: if so, how can we ever find a case where a bailee is liable for an oath? Since the bailee could say 'it never happened,' he could also say 'it was an accident.' The Gemara answers: when the deposit was made with witnesses, and when it was made with a document. It follows that both agree: one who deposits with witnesses does not need to return with witnesses; with a document, he needs to return with witnesses.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama praises the previous statement (of Rav Menashya bar Zevid/Rav) as excellent.

Rava challenges: if the principle applies, how can we ever find a case where a bailee is liable for an oath of bailment, since the bailee could always deny the deposit entirely and thus also claim an accident?
The Gemara answers: the case is where the deposit was made with witnesses, and then further refined: where it was made with a document.

The Gemara concludes that both Rami bar Chama and Rava agree: one who deposits with witnesses does not need to return with witnesses, but one who deposits with a document does need to return with witnesses.

items.text: Rami bar Chama praises Rav Sheshet; Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's statement
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama praises Rav Sheshet; Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's statement
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama applies the verse about David to Rav Sheshet, who found Rabba bar Shmuel and asked him to teach a Mishnah about a hired worker. Rabba bar Shmuel taught the Mishnah distinguishing between wage claim and cutting. The Gemara infers that the first clause is without witnesses. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak begins a statement.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama applies the verse about David to Rav Sheshet, praising his ability to retain teachings.
Rav Sheshet found Rabba bar Shmuel and asked him to teach a Mishnah about a hired worker; Rabba bar Shmuel taught the Mishnah distinguishing between a wage claim and a cutting claim.
The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's structure that the first clause (wage claim) applies without witnesses, while the second clause (cutting claim) requires evidence.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak begins a statement, which is cut off at the section boundary.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction in the Mishnah: it mentions 'evidence' for payment but not for the oath, implying that the oath is not considered a form of evidence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction in the Mishnah: it mentions 'evidence' for payment but not for the oath, implying the oath is not considered evidence.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on the craftsman's case
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on the craftsman's case
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba reports that the academy sent a question to Shmuel: if a craftsman says 'you cut two for me' and the homeowner says 'I only cut one', who takes the oath? Shmuel answers that the homeowner swears and the craftsman loses, because people certainly remember cutting.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba reports that the academy sent to Shmuel a case of a craftsman claiming two cuts and the homeowner claiming one, and Shmuel ruled that the homeowner swears and the craftsman loses, because people remember a cut.
Shmuel answers that the homeowner swears and the craftsman loses, because people certainly remember cutting.

items.text: Objection from Rabba bar Shmuel's baraita
items.text_en: Objection from Rabba bar Shmuel's baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabba bar Shmuel taught that in a case of cutting, the burden of proof is on the claimant, and if he doesn't bring proof, he loses. Why doesn't the homeowner swear and the craftsman lose? Rav Nachman explains that the baraita means either he brings proof and takes, or the homeowner swears and the craftsman loses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from a baraita of Rabbah bar Shmuel that in a case of a cut, the burden of proof is on the claimant, implying the homeowner does not swear.
Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita means either the craftsman brings evidence and takes payment, or the homeowner swears and the craftsman loses.

items.text: Challenge from the baraita about the cloak
items.text_en: Challenge from the baraita about the cloak
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: if a craftsman says 'you cut two' and the homeowner says 'only one', while the cloak is in the craftsman's hand, the homeowner must bring proof. If the craftsman returned it on time, he swears and takes; if time passed, the burden is on the claimant. The Gemara asks: why does the craftsman swear and take? Let the homeowner swear and the craftsman lose!

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a cloak given to a craftsman, which states that within the time limit the craftsman swears and takes payment, contradicting Shmuel's ruling.
The Gemara challenges: why does the craftsman swear and take when the cloak was returned on time? Let the homeowner swear and the craftsman lose!

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's answer: it is Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's answer: it is Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, who says that whenever the oath leans toward the homeowner, the hired worker swears and takes.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that whenever the oath leans toward the homeowner, the hired worker swears and takes payment.

items.text: Clarifying which Rabbi Yehuda: the one from the baraita
items.text_en: Clarifying which Rabbi Yehuda: the one from the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: which Rabbi Yehuda? If it is the one from the Mishnah, he is more stringent (requiring partial admission). Rather, it is Rabbi Yehuda from the baraita, which states that a hired worker swears and takes only within the time, and only when the claim is about a specific number of cuts, but if the homeowner denies hiring altogether or claims payment, the burden is on the claimant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Rabbi Yehuda is meant, and rejects the possibility that it is the Rabbi Yehuda of the Mishnah, who is more stringent (requiring partial admission).

The Gemara concludes that it is Rabbi Yehuda of the baraita, who rules that a hired worker swears and takes only within the time, and only when the claim is about a specific number of cuts, but if the homeowner denies hiring altogether or claims payment, the burden is on the claimant.

items.text: Rav Shisha's objection and the difficulty with Rabba bar Shmuel's baraita
items.text_en: Rav Shisha's objection and the difficulty with Rabba bar Shmuel's baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi objects: if the baraita about cutting follows Rabbi Yehuda, then where Rabbi Yehuda is stringent, the Rabbis are lenient, and where he is lenient, they are stringent. But then Rabba bar Shmuel's baraita (which says the burden is on the claimant) would fit neither Rabbi Yehuda nor the Rabbis.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi objects: if the baraita about cutting follows Rabbi Yehuda, then the Rabbis would be lenient where he is stringent and stringent where he is lenient, which is inconsistent.
The Gemara asks: if the baraita is attributed to the Rabbis, then Rabba bar Shmuel's baraita fits neither Rabbi Yehuda nor the Rabbis.

items.text: Rava's resolution: the dispute is about a takkanah for a Torah obligation
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: the dispute is about a takkanah for a Torah obligation
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the dispute is about a fundamental principle: Rabbi Yehuda holds that a takkanah was made for the hired worker in Torah law (the oath of the hired worker), but in rabbinic law (the case of cutting), since it is already a takkanah, we do not make a takkanah for a takkanah. The Rabbis hold that we do make a takkanah for the hired worker even in rabbinic law, and cutting is something people remember.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda holds that a rabbinic enactment was made for the worker in Torah law, but not for a rabbinic enactment on top of another enactment; the Rabbis hold that an enactment is made even for rabbinic matters, and a cut is remembered.
Rava explains that the Rabbis hold that we do make a takkanah for the hired worker even in rabbinic law, and cutting is something people remember.

items.text: Discussion of the Mishnah's case of the robbed person
items.text_en: Discussion of the Mishnah's case of the robbed person
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's case of a robbed person: witnesses saw him enter his house to take a pledge. The Gemara questions whether he actually took it, citing Rav Nachman's principle that a person may threaten but not act. It then explains that the Mishnah refers to a case where he took items that can be hidden under his arms, as taught by Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Yehuda adds that they saw him hide items under his arms and leave.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case of a robbed person, asking whether the witnesses' testimony that he entered to take a pledge actually proves he took it.
The Gemara cites Rav Nachman's principle that a person may threaten (גוזם) but not act, suggesting the same could apply here.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah must mean he actually took the pledge, not just threatened.
The Gemara asks what specific items he took, since the witnesses must have seen something.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the case involves items that can be hidden under one's arms, so the witnesses could see the taking.
